questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presents with a cough lasting 15 days and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Histopathological examination of a lymph node biopsy reveals characteristic features suggestive of a particular condition. Based on the clinical presentation and biopsy findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of chronic cough and cervical lymphadenopathy (scrofula) in a pediatric patient is a classic presentation for Tuberculosis (TB). The biopsy image provided shows "caseating granulomas," which are diagnostic of TB. These consist of a central area of "caseous necrosis" (acellular, cheese-like material) surrounded by epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells with horseshoe-shaped nuclei, and a rim of lymphocytes. Sarcoidosis (Option C) also presents with granulomas, but they are characteristically "non-caseating" (no central necrosis). Leprosy (Option B) and Syphilis (Option D) present with different cutaneous and systemic findings and do not typically cause isolated cervical caseating lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis of TB is further confirmed by Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) staining or CBNAAT (GeneXpert) testing. Early identification is essential to begin the intensive six-month multi-drug anti-tubercular therapy (AKT) regimen and prevent local complications or miliary spread
questions.learning: The clinical combination of chronic cough and cervical lymphadenopathy (scrofula) in a pediatric patient is a classic presentation for Tuberculosis (TB).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Dehydration occurs in both adults and children, but children become dehydrated more easily than adults. How does the ratio of extracellular fluid (ECF) to intracellular fluid (ICF) in children differ from that in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ECF is higher than ICF

In infants and young children, the ECF is higher than ICF. This higher ECF-to-ICF ratio in children explains why they are more susceptible to dehydration.

At birth, ECF is approximately 1.5 times that of ICF. However, this changes rapidly to become almost equal to ICF by day 10 of life. ICF gradually increases in proportion to become twice as much as ECF by age 3 years, and this proportion (two-thirds of TBW is ICF and one-third of TBW is ECF) is maintained thereafter.

Higher ECF volume in children is physiologically necessary for rapid growth and development but makes them more vulnerable to fluid losses through fever, diarrhea, or vomiting. This distinctive fluid distribution gradually shifts toward adult proportions as the child grows, with ICF increasing and ECF decreasing relatively.

This is markedly different from adults where ICF predominates. In newborns, extracellular fluid makes up about 45% of body weight compared to about 15% in adults.

Other Options

Option A (ICF is higher than ECF) describes the adult fluid distribution, not children's.

Option B (Total body water is high) is true but doesn't address why children are more susceptible to dehydration.

Option D (ECF is equal to ICF) is incorrect as the ECF clearly predominates in children.
questions.learning: ECF is higher than ICF — In infants and young children, the ECF is higher than ICF. This higher ECF-to-ICF ratio in children explains why they are more susceptible to dehydration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is true about the Hayflick limit?
options: Human cells can divide a finite number of times only
Free radical oxidation level is unrestricted
RNA polymerase can function for. a finite number of times only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human cells can divide a finite number of times only

The Hayflick limit says that human cells can divide for a finite number of times.

The Hayflick limit is the number of divisions a cell population can go through in culture before division stops and enters a state known as senescence. With the exception of stem cells, all the other human cells have only a limited capacity for cell division. This biological clock is of great help in the study of the normal ageing process.

The number of cell divisions of the cultured cell is roughly related to:

• The age of the cell donors
• The longevity of the species

For example, fibroblasts from the human embryos, when sustained in tissue culture, divide about 50 times before they die. Those taken from person after birth divide only 20 to 30 times.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A professional boxer wants vision correction surgery. Which of the following is not recommended?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RK

RK (Radial Keratotomy) would not be recommended to this boxer who wants vision correction surgery.
Radial keratotomy (RK) involves making deep (90% of corneal thickness) radial incisions in the peripheral part of cornea leaving the central 4 mm optical zone. These incisions on healing flatten the central cornea reducing its refractive power. This procedure was done to correct low to moderate myopia (2 to 6 D). However, because of its disadvantages and advent of safe techniques (LASIK and PRK), RK is now obsolete.
Disadvantages of RK:
- Cornea is weakened, increasing chances of globe rupture following trauma (RK more than PRK). Hence this procedure should not be done for patients who are at high risk of blunt trauma, such as sports persons and military personnel.
- Irregular astigmatism from uneven healing.
- Glare at night.
Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) (Option C) is the most commonly done surgery for myopia. An excimer laser beam reshapes the cornea by ablating the superficial stroma to a predetermined extent after lifting a flap of the cornea with a sharp microkeratome. It is safer than RK.

Patient selection criteria:

- In individuals aged 21 years and above.
- In individuals who have a stable refractive error for at least 1 year.
- In individuals who have had unsatisfactory results with non-surgical treatment.
- In individuals in whom corneal-thinning disorders such as keratoconus have been ruled out.

Complications:

- Tear instability (dry eye)
- Wrinkling, distortion, or dislocation of the flap
- Subepithelial haze with resultant glare, especially at night.
- Persistent epithelial defects.
- Epithelial ingrowth under the flap.
- Diffuse lamellar keratitis
- Corneal ectasia
- Keratoconus

Other options :

Option B : PRK (Photorefractive keratectomy) corrects myopia by using an excimer laser to photoablate a central optical zone of anterior corneal stroma. This causes flattening of the central cornea. Like RK, the PRK also gives very good correction for up to -6 D of myopia but is safer.

Option D : SMILE (Small incision lenticule extraction) is a technique in which a lenticule of corneal stroma is extracted using a femtosecond laser. This can correct myopia, with and without astigmatism up to 10 D.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Can you identify the active toxic compound found in the poisonous plant shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image shows Atropa belladonna (Deadly Nightshade), identifiable by its characteristic shiny black berries, bell-shaped purple flowers, and broad oval leaves. The active toxic compound found in this plant is 1-hyoscyamine (which racemizes to atropine upon extraction). Key Plant Identification Features visible in image : The plant shows classic Atropa belladonna features — glossy black round berries, drooping purple bell-shaped flowers, and broad green leaves growing alternately. All parts of the plant are toxic, especially the berries which are attractive to children. Mechanism of Toxicity : 1-Hyoscyamine is a tropane alkaloid that acts as a potent competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, producing classic anticholinergic toxidrome — dry mouth, mydriasis, flushing, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, and delirium ("mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, red as a beet"). Why other options are wrong: (A) Calotropis gigantea is incorrect because Calotropis contains calotropin and calactin (cardenolide glycosides). It appears as a shrub with thick fleshy leaves and purple crown-shaped flowers — entirely different morphology. (B) Digitalin is incorrect because digitalin is the toxic compound found in Digitalis purpurea (Foxglove), which has tall spikes of tubular pink/purple flowers — completely different appearance from the plant shown. (C) Ricin is incorrect because ricin is the toxic compound found in Ricinus communis (Castor bean plant), which has distinctive star-shaped leaves and spiny seed pods — morphologically very different from Atropa belladonna
questions.learning: The image shows Atropa belladonna (Deadly Nightshade), identifiable by its characteristic shiny black berries, bell-shaped purple flowers, and broad oval leaves.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the mode of insertion of this contraceptive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hysteroscopic

The image shows an Essure coil which is inserted hysteroscopically to occlude both the fallopian tubes.

Essure(not yet licensed in India):

* It is a spring-like device introduced using a hysteroscope inserted through the vagina into the uterus and then into each fallopian tube.

* In 3 months' time, scar tissue grows into the device and plugs the fallopian tube; hence, sperms cannot pass through to fertilize an egg.

* Made of nickel and titanium alloy and is considered irreversible.

* Contraindicated in patients who are uncertain about ending fertility, can have only one insert placed (including contralateral proximal tubal occlusion or suspected unicornuate uterus), an abnormal uterine cavity that makes visualization of the tubal ostia impossible, and/or abnormal tubal anatomy or previous tubal ligation (including failed ligation), pregnant or suspect pregnancy, delivered or terminated a pregnancy less than 6 weeks, an active upper or lower genital tract infection, unexplained vaginal bleeding, a gynecological malignancy, known allergy to contrast media.

* Side effects-cramping, nausea/vomiting, back pain, abdominal pain, and dyspareunia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The graph below shows oxygen dissociation curves. What does the curve marked as 'A' indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myoglobin

The curve 'A' shows a hyperbolic curve that is characteristic of oxygen dissociation in myoglobin.

Myoglobin is an iron-containing component of the skeletal muscle. Myoglobin can bind only to one oxygen molecule and hence lacks co-operative binding. It has a higher affinity to oxygen than hemoglobin and hence releases oxygen only at low PO2 values. This leads to a leftward shift in the myoglobin oxygen dissociation curve.

Myoglobin is present in large quantities in muscles that are commonly used for sustained contraction. During such contractions, muscle blood supply is decreased due to compression. Myoglobin facilitates oxygen supply in these conditions.

Other options:

Option B: Carbon monoxide (CO) reacts with hemoglobin to form carbon monoxyhemoglobin (carboxyhemoglobin or COHb). The affinity of hemoglobin for CO is 210 times its affinity for O2, and COHb liberates CO very slowly. An additional difficulty is that when COHb is present, the dissociation curve of the remaining HbO2 shifts to the left, decreasing the amount of O2 released.

Option C: Hemoglobin normally has ferrous ion. When it is oxidized to ferric iron, it is called methemoglobin. It causes dark-coloured blood.

Option D: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is structurally similar to hemoglobin A except for the gamma chains. It binds less avidly to 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate and hence has higher affinity for oxygen leading to left ward shift in the dissociation curve.
questions.learning: Myoglobin — The curve 'A' shows a hyperbolic curve that is characteristic of oxygen dissociation in myoglobin. Myoglobin is an iron-containing component of the skeletal muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with gait instability, particularly noticeable when standing on one leg. On examination, standing on the left leg causes the right side of the pelvis to drop. Paralysis of which muscle group is responsible for this finding?
options: Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
questions.explanation: The physical exam finding described is a positive Trendelenburg sign. In this case, the drooping of the right pelvis when standing on the left leg indicates that the hip abductors of the stance leg (left) are paralyzed or weak. These abductors are the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. Normally, these muscles contract on the weight-bearing side to prevent the pelvis from tilting toward the unsupported side. Paralysis of the right-sided muscles (Options A and C) would cause the left pelvis to sag. The gluteus maximus (Option B) is primarily an extensor of the hip rather than an abductor, and its weakness leads to a "lurching" gait but not pelvic sagging in the coronal plane. Instability while walking, or a "waddling gait," is common when these muscles are compromised. Therefore, the sag on the right side while weight-bearing on the left side definitively localizes the pathology to the left gluteus medius and minimus
questions.learning: The physical exam finding described is a positive Trendelenburg sign. In this case, the drooping of the right pelvis when standing on the left leg indicates that the hip abductors of the stance leg (left) are paralyzed or weak.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with type 2 diabetes experiences hypoglycemia and falls. Due to incoherent speech, a CT scan is performed, revealing a large subdural hematoma (SDH) >30 cc. What is the immediate next step in management?
options: Stabilize the patient and urgently seek a neurosurgical consultation
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a subdural hematoma (SDH) greater than 10 mm in thickness or with a volume greater than 30 cc is an indication for immediate surgical intervention, regardless of the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. In this case, the hematoma is "substantial" and likely causing significant mass effect and brain compression, which explains the incoherent speech. Performing a craniotomy for evacuation of the clot is the definitive and urgent next step. Administering Mannitol (Option A) is a temporary measure to lower intracranial pressure but does not address the cause. Administering Aspirin and Clopidogrel (Option B) would be disastrous, as antiplatelets would exacerbate the bleeding. While stabilizing the patient (Option D) is necessary, "seeking a neurosurgical consultation" should not delay the obvious need for surgery in a large hematoma. In acute SDH, the time from injury to surgery is the most important factor for survival and neurological outcome
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a subdural hematoma (SDH) greater than 10 mm in thickness or with a volume greater than 30 cc is an indication for immediate surgical intervention, regardless of the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Nadas criteria include all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Raised Troponin T level

• Nada's criteria are used for clinical diagnosis of congenital heart disease in children.
• They include features like congestive cardiac failure, diastolic murmur, and abnormal chest X-ray findings.
• They rely on clinical findings + basic investigations, not cardiac biomarkers.

Major Criteria

Presence of any one major criterion strongly suggests organic heart disease.

1. Diastolic murmur
2. Grade ≥ 3/6 systolic murmur
3. Cyanosis
4. Congestive heart failure

Minor Criteria

1. Abnormal ECG
2. Abnormal chest X-ray
3. Abnormal blood pressure (hypertension or significant discrepancy)
4. Systolic murmur of grade <3/6
5. Abnormal second heart sound (S2)
6. Abnormal precordial activity (thrill/heave)
7. Abnormal cardiac examination (e.g., clicks, gallops)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is deficient in breast milk?
questions.explanation: Human breast milk is a complete nutritional source for infants, but it is naturally deficient in Vitamin K (Option D). This deficiency, combined with the lack of intestinal flora in neonates to synthesize the vitamin, puts breastfed infants at high risk for Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB), also known as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. To prevent this, a prophylactic dose of Vitamin K is administered to all newborns at birth. Breast milk is generally rich in Vitamin A (Option A), Vitamin C (Option B), and Vitamin E (Option C), providing sufficient amounts for the infant's needs. Vitamin D is also relatively low in breast milk, but Vitamin K is the classic academic answer for a "major" deficiency that mandates immediate intervention at birth. Therefore, the low concentrations of Vitamin K are a critical clinical consideration in neonatal care

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is true about chromic catgut?
options: It is made from cat gut
It is made from rabbit gut
It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis
It is tanned with nickel salts to improve handling and to resist degradation in tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis

Chromic catgut is absorbed through macrophage phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within 90 days.

It is made from collagen derived from healthy sheep or cattle. It is then tanned with chromium salts to improve handling and resist degradation in tissue.

The tensile strength lasts for 21-28 days. It has a moderate tissue reaction as compared to plain catgut, which has a high tissue reactivity.

It is used to ligate superficial vessels, suture subcutaneous tissues, and is used for stomas and other tissues that heal rapidly. It is not used in tissues that heal slowly and require prolonged support.
questions.learning: It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis Chromic catgut is absorbed through macrophage phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within 90 days.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery is administered succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. Shortly after administration, he develops hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dantrolene sodium

• Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder triggered by succinylcholine and volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane). It is caused by a mutation in the RYR1 (ryanodine receptor), leading to uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, resulting in sustained muscle contraction and a hypermetabolic state.
• The drug of choice for treatment is intravenous dantrolene sodium, which inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Why not the other options?

• A. Neostigmine: Reverses non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers; ineffective in malignant hyperthermia.
• C. Atropine: Used for bradycardia or to reduce secretions; no role in MH.
• D. Midazolam: Provides sedation but does not treat the underlying pathophysiology.
questions.learning: Dantrolene sodium • Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder triggered by succinylcholine and volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image below shows a pressure sore. Which stage does this belong to ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 4

The given image shows a pressure sore with extensive tissue destruction, including damage to the muscle layer and thus it belongs to stage 4.

Pressure sores also referred known as bed sores, pressure ulcers and decubitus ulcers are ulcers that occur due to prolonged pressure on certain sites thereby leading to tissue necrosis. The commonest sites involved are ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral >medial), and occiput. Paraplegic patients, elderly patients, and severely ill patients are at a higher risk of developing pressure sores.

They are staged as:

• Stage 1 - Erythema with no blanching and no breach in the epidermis.
• Stage 2- Partial-thickness skin loss with epidermal and dermal involvement.
• Stage 3- Full-thickness skin loss with intact fascia but the involvement of the subcutaneous tissue.
• Stage 4- Full-thickness skin loss extending to the fascia with massive tissue destruction and involvement of muscle, bone, tendon, or joint.

Management is primarily proper skin care with pressure dispersion cushions, air-fluidized beds, and urinary or fecal diversion if required. Patients who are bed-bound should be turned once in 2 hours. Those in a wheelchair should lift themselves off the seat for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgery is the last resort and is done after a proper initial debridement and vacuum-assisted closure. Vacuum-assisted closure is a wound closure technique in which negative pressure is applied to the wound which leads to a decrease in edema. This hastens the debridement and formation of granulation tissue. Skin flaps with a muscle are also used for closure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents with colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura. Urinalysis reveals only red blood cells without other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura in a 35-year-old patient is highly characteristic of IgA vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura. This small-vessel vasculitis often presents with a tetrad of symptoms: palpable purpura (typically on lower extremities), arthralgia/arthritis, abdominal pain (often colicky), and renal involvement. The presence of red blood cells in the urinalysis indicates glomerulonephritis, a common complication of this condition. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option B) usually involves the respiratory tract and is associated with c-ANCA. Microscopic polyangiitis (Option C) also causes glomerulonephritis but lacks the characteristic palpable purpura and abdominal findings of IgA vasculitis. Behçet's disease (Option D) typically presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers and uveitis. Therefore, given the specific combination of systemic symptoms and the age of the patient, IgA vasculitis is the most likely diagnosis. The pathology involves the deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in vessel walls
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura in a 35-year-old patient is highly characteristic of IgA vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient with hypertension is prescribed Drug X, which has an oral bioavailability of 30%. Which of the following statements most appropriately explains the implication of this bioavailability for the patient’s prescription?
options: 70% of drug reach systemic circulation in unchanged form
70% of drug is potent in giving therapeutic effect
70% of the drug undergoes 1st pass metabolism in the liver
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of an administered dose of a drug that reaches the systemic circulation in its unchanged form. If a drug has a bioavailability of 30%, it means only 30% of the oral dose enters the bloodstream intact. The remaining 70% is lost during the process of absorption and, most significantly, during first-pass metabolism as it passes through the gut wall and the liver before reaching the heart. Therefore, statement D is the most appropriate physiological explanation. Statement A is the exact opposite of the definition. Statement B confuses bioavailability with chemical purity. Statement C is incorrect as potency refers to the amount of drug needed to produce a specific effect, not the percentage absorbed. Low bioavailability often requires clinicians to use significantly higher oral doses compared to intravenous doses to achieve the same therapeutic plasma concentration
questions.learning: Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of an administered dose of a drug that reaches the systemic circulation in its unchanged form. If a drug has a bioavailability of 30%, it means only 30% of the oral dose enters the bloodstream intact.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The SAFE strategy given by WHO forms the mainstay of the management of trachoma. What does the S in this acronym represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Surgery

The S in the acronym stands for surgery.

Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFEstrategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the TRIC (trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis) serovars A, B, Ba, C. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage. The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show:

* Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes)

* Corneal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

The cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. The patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. Conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include:

* Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles)

* Corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

The below image shows Herbert's pits.

There can be associated trichiasis ( when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion.

At present WHO grading with `FISTO’ is in use.

Pearl PF1843: WHO Programme to Control Trachoma: SAFE Strategy

* S—Surgery: Trichiasis and entropion correction surgery → 3° prevention.

* A—Antibiotics: Oral azithromycin, topical 1% tetracycline, topical 1% azithromycin → 2° prevention

* F—Facial hygiene → 1° prevention.

* E—Environmental cleanliness → primordial prevention

The strategy depends on the prevalence of trachoma follicle in children (aged 1–9 yrs)

* >10% → Mass antibiotic treatment at the community level and FE measures

* 5 to 10% → Targeted antibiotic treatment (affected families) and FE measures

* < 5% → FE measures
questions.learning: Surgery — The S in the acronym stands for surgery. Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFEstrategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Given the RNA sequence CAAGGU, what would be the corresponding template DNA strand?
questions.explanation: To determine the template DNA strand from a given RNA sequence, remember that RNA is synthesized complementary to the DNA template strand during transcription. Given RNA sequence: 5′–CAAGGU–3′ Base pairing rules: 1. C ↔ G 2. A ↔ T (in DNA) 3. G ↔ C 4. U ↔ A Now, find the complementary DNA template strand: RNA: C A A G G U DNA: G T T C C A So, the template DNA sequence is: 3′–GT TCCA–5′, which is written as GTTCCA However, if written in the 5′→3′ direction, it becomes: TGGAAC Why other options are wrong: (A) CAAGGT → Coding strand (similar to RNA, U→T) (B) GTTCCA → Correct sequence but in 3′→5′ direction (C) ACCTTG → Reverse complement, incorrect
questions.learning: To determine the template DNA strand from a given RNA sequence, remember that RNA is synthesized complementary to the DNA template strand during transcription.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct about hair cells?

1. There is 1 row of inner hair cells and 3 rows of outer hair cells
2. Inner hair cells are responsible for transmitting auditory impulses
3. Majority of the afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells.
4. Outer hair cells primarily initiate the electrical signals sent to the brain in response to sound vibrations.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. i, ii, iii

Statements i, ii, and iii are correct.

Statement i: There is 1 row of inner hair cells and 3 rows of outer hair cells is a correct statement.

Statement ii: Inner hair cells are responsible for transmitting auditory impulses is a correct statement. Inner hair cells are richly supplied by afferent cochlear fibres and are probably more important in the transmission of auditory impulses.

Statement iii: The majority of the afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells is a correct statement. Ninety-five percent of afferent fibres of spiral ganglion supply the inner hair cells while only five percent supply the outer hair cells. Efferent fibres to the hair cells come from the olivocochlear bundle.

Statement iv: Outer hair cells are important in the modulation of basilar membrane action is an incorrect statement. Outer hair cells mainly receive efferent innervation from the olivary complex and are concerned with modulating the function of inner hair cells.
questions.learning: i, ii, iii Statements i, ii, and iii are correct. Statement i: There is 1 row of inner hair cells and 3 rows of outer hair cells is a correct statement.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A female patient with a history of fall few months back presents with the deformity shown in the image. Probing into history reveals it was managed with traditional treatment. This deformity is likely to be due to ____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extra-articular fracture of wrist

The given image shows the dinner-fork deformity seen in Colle's fracture which is an extra-articular fracture of the wrist.

Colle's fracture is a fracture of corticocancellous junction of the distal end of the radius. The dinner fork deformity is the prominence on the back of the wrist and depression in the front. It is due to the dorsal angulation of the distal fracture fragment. It is treated by a Colles’ cast, which immobilizes the wrist in palmar flexion, pronation, and ulnar deviation.

Displacements that may be seen in Colles' fracture:

• Dorsal tilt
• Dorsal shift
• Lateral tilt (Radial tilt)
• Lateral shift (Radial shift)
• Supination
• Impaction of fragments

The given radiograph shows the dorsal tilt of the distal fragment leading to dinner fork deformity.
questions.learning: Extra-articular fracture of wrist — The given image shows the dinner-fork deformity seen in Colle's fracture which is an extra-articular fracture of the wrist.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An AIDS-positive patient came with a history of fever, vomiting, and meningismus. Which of the following tests help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen

Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis.

Latex agglutination tests are mainly used for the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms. In latex agglutination tests, an antigen-specific antibody (either polyclonal or monoclonal) is fixed to latex beads. When the clinical specimen from the patient is added to a suspension of the latex beads, the antibodies bind to the antigens on the microorganism forming a lattice structure, and agglutination of the beads occurs.

Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis in an immunocompromised HIV patient. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL.

It presents with subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs. The CSF profile shows elevations in WBC with lymphocyte predominance, elevated protein levels, and reduced to normal levels of glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated

Diagnosis is made by demonstration of yeast cells or cryptococcal antigen in CSF. India ink stain is used to demonstrate capsulated budding yeast cells in CSF as they have a distinctive appearance because their capsules exclude ink particles. But its very much subjective and hence is less preferred over other methods for rapid diagnosis. Rapid detection of cryptococcal antigen in CSF and blood can also be done. Colonies develop within a few days on most media at room temperature or 37°C.

Treatment

*  Induction – IV or Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with Amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative.

*  Maintenance -  Oral Fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART.

*  Primary Prophylaxis - Oral Fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.
questions.learning: Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis. Latex agglutination tests are mainly used for the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A male patient presented with complaints of imbalance, numbness of the foot, and muscle weakness. On history taking, he revealed that he has been taking multivitamin tablets more than the prescribed dose for 1 year. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the associated symptoms seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B6 toxicity

The above clinical vignette points towards the diagnosis of vitamin B6 toxicity due to excess intake of vitamin B6 supplements.

The active form of vitamin B6/pyridoxine is pyridoxal phosphate(PLP). PLP acts as a coenzyme for many reactions such as transaminations, decarboxylations, metabolism of sulfur-containing amino acids, heme synthesis, niacin synthesis, and glycogenolysis.

Excessive intake of food-based sources of pyridoxine doesn’t cause toxicity, the only source of pyridoxine toxicity is from the intake of supratherapeutic dosing of supplements, more than 100-200mg/day or iatrogenic. Pyridoxine toxicity manifests as neurological symptoms, including numbness, tingling sensations, muscle weakness, and difficulty in ambulation in severe cases.

Drugs that decrease pyridoxine levels include isoniazid, cycloserine, oral contraceptives, and alcohol. Deficiency manifestations of vitamin B6 include convulsions, peripheral neuritis, pellagra due to decreased niacin synthesis, and hypochromic microcytic anaemia due to inhibition of heme synthesis. Vitamin B6 levels can be measured by erythrocyte transaminase assay.

Other options:

Option A: Intake of vitamin D of more than 10,000 units per day can cause toxicity and it manifests as weakness, polyuria, intense thirst, difficulty in speaking, hypertension, weight loss, and metastatic calcification(calcinosis).

Option C: Clinical features of Vitamin C toxicity:

* Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea

* Increased prevalence of kidney stones (oxalate)

* Iron overload (in patients on supplemental iron)

* Hemolysis (G6PD deficiency)

Option D: Acute vitamin A toxicity manifests with headaches, vision changes, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, myalgias and arthralgias. Weight loss can be observed with chronic intoxication.
questions.learning: Vitamin B6 toxicity — The above clinical vignette points towards the diagnosis of vitamin B6 toxicity due to excess intake of vitamin B6 supplements. The active form of vitamin B6/pyridoxine is pyridoxal phosphate(PLP).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are not included in the School Health Programme under Ayushman Bharat?
options: Monthly IFA tablets for all children
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monthly IFA tablets for all children

Weekly Iron Folic Acid Supplementation is included in School Heath Programme not monthly IFA tablets for all children.

The Weekly Iron Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) program is a school health program that provides iron and folic acid (IFA) tablets which aims to reduce the prevalence of anemia in school going children.

The school health programs are managed by the primary health center (PHC).

The School Health Committee (1961) in India recommended that the school health services should be a part of the general health services administered through PHCs. Formation of school health committees at the village, block, district, state, and national levels was recommended. The National School Health Council was created as an advisory and coordinating body.

PHCs provide the following school health services:

• Screening and general assessments for

1. Anemia/nutritional status
2. Visual acuity and hearing problems
3. Dental check-up
4. Physical disabilities
5. Learning disorders and behavior problems

• Basic medicines for common ailments
• Immunization
• Micronutrient management (vitamin A, iron, and folic acid)
• Deworming
• Mid-day meal
• Provison of sanitary napkins

Note: National Programme for Mid-Day Meal in Schools has recently been renamed Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN).
questions.learning: Monthly IFA tablets for all children Weekly Iron Folic Acid Supplementation is included in School Heath Programme not monthly IFA tablets for all children.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the best method to preserve a blood-stained handkerchief recovered from a crime scene?
options: Dry over spirit lamp and preserve it
Stained area folded and preserved in plastic bag
Rinse with water to prevent contamination
Stained area folded and preserved in paper bag
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stained area folded and preserved in paper bag

The stained handkerchief should be folded and preserved in a paper bag.

Preservation of Blood stains:

* The stained item should be allowed to air dry at room temperature without applying additional heat, as heat can degrade the stain.

* Failure to dry stained clothing may result in putrefaction, making it challenging or impossible to determine whether the blood is of human or animal origin. It's advisable to label the stained object with initials and the date. If labelling is not feasible, attaching a tag or similar identifier is necessary.

* Avoid using air-tight containers to prevent trapped moisture, which can promote bacterial growth and damage the stains. Each garment should be individually wrapped to prevent contact with other clothing, ensuring that no two stains touch each other.

* Placing a clean sheet of paper between each stain is recommended.

* All types of stains should be sent to the State Forensic Science Laboratory for examination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents with high-grade fever and a purpuric rash. Cerebrospinal fluid examination shows gram-negative diplococci. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic triad of high-grade fever, purpuric rash (petechiae/ecchymoses), and signs of meningitis. The definitive diagnostic clue is the CSF finding of gram-negative diplococci. This is the pathognomonic microscopic appearance of Neisseria meningitidis (the meningococcus). Pseudomonas (Option B) and E. coli (Option D) are Gram-negative rods (bacilli). Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) is a major cause of meningitis but would appear as Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. The purpuric rash is highly characteristic of meningococcemia, resulting from vascular damage and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Neisseria meningitidis is a leading cause of bacterial meningitis in young adults and can cause rapid clinical deterioration. Immediate treatment with intravenous Ceftriaxone and respiratory isolation are required. Given the Gram-stain morphology and the characteristic rash, Neisseria meningitidis is the only possible causative agent
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic triad of high-grade fever, purpuric rash (petechiae/ecchymoses), and signs of meningitis. The definitive diagnostic clue is the CSF finding of gram-negative diplococci.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent bleeding for the past 1 year. Transnasal endoscopic results are shown below. A contrast-enhanced CT revealed a mass extending from the posterior choana to the nasopharynx. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The above clinical scenario with recurrent spontaneous bleeding with unilateral nasal obstruction and contrast-enhanced CT showing a growth protruding into the nasopharynx, along with the transnasal endoscopic image, is suggestive of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor. It is predominantly seen in adolescent males and is thought to be testosterone-dependent. It arises from the posterior part of the nasal cavity near the sphenopalatine foramen.

The clinical features include epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction, and denasal speech. Other symptoms include conductive hearing loss, broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis leading to frog-face deformity, cheek swelling, and involvement of II, III, IV, and VI cranial nerves.

Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is the investigation of choice that reveals anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (Antral sign/Holman Miller sign), which is pathognomonic of angiofibroma as shown below.

Carotid angiography shows the extent of the tumor with its vascularity. The feeding vessels mostly come from the external carotid artery. In large tumors with intracranial extension, vessels come from the internal carotid system also.

Biopsy of the mass is avoided due to the risk of bleeding.

Surgical approach is the treatment of choice. Embolization of the vessels can be done prior to surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding during the surgery.

Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy can also be considered.

Other options:

Option B: Antrochoanal polyp (Killian's polyp) arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum. They are usually unilateral and are seen in children and young adults. They present with unilateral nasal obstruction with minimal to no bleeding. X-rays of the paranasal sinuses show opacity of the maxillary sinus.

Option C: Rhinoscleroma is caused by a gram-negative coccobacillus Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It causes this progressive granulomatous infection starting in the nose and extending into the upper respiratory tract. It presents initially with foul-smelling nasal discharge, and then with granulomatous nodules in the nose giving it a woody feeling. The last stage is the cicatricial stage, with stenosis of nares, and adhesions in the nose.

Option D: Concha bullosa is pneumatization of the middle turbinate that leads to an enlarged middle turbinate, which is ballooned out.

The CT image shown below depicts concha bullosa

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following blood groups can be given to a patient having Bombay blood group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oh

Among the given options, Oh (Bombay) blood group blood can be transfused to Bombay blood group patients.

The H antigen is present in all four blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). A rare blood group where there is an absence of the H antigen is known as the Bombay blood group. The absence of this H antigen results in the absence of A and B antigens. Their plasma contains anti-A, anti-B, and strong anti-H antibodies. Therefore, they do not react with anti-A, anti-B, and anti-AB antiserums, and get recognized as O blood group on cell typing.

However, the O blood group has an H antigen. Thus if a patient with the Bombay blood group is transfused with the O blood group blood, the anti-H antibodies in the Bombay blood group patient react with the H antigen present in the O blood group. This can lead to fatal transfusion reactions. Therefore, patients with the Bombay blood group require the same blood group during transfusion.

Other less common systems of blood grouping include MNSs, Lutheran, Kell, and Kidd systems of blood grouping.

ABO blood typing is performed by mixing the individual's red blood cells with antisera that contains the various agglutinins on a slide and observing for the presence of clumping or agglutination.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lady presented with a pelvic mass which was hyperintense on T1-weighted image, hyperintense on T1-fat saturated image, and hypointense on T2-weighted image with T2 shading. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrioma

Endometriomas (chocolate cysts) show T1 hyperintensity due to blood, remain bright on fat-sat, and T2 shading from repeated hemorrhage. Teratomas contain fat, carcinoma/dysgerminoma lack these features.

Key Radiological Signs

1. T1 Hyperintensity

• Due to blood products (methemoglobin)

2. No Fat Suppression

• Remains bright on T1 fat-sat → confirms blood, not fat

3. T2 Shading Sign

• Progressive loss of signal on T2
• Due to chronic repeated hemorrhage

| Feature | Endometrioma | Teratoma | Ovarian Carcinoma | Dysgerminoma

| ------- | ------------ | -------- | ----------------- | ------------

| T1 | Hyperintense | Hyperintense | Variable | Iso/hypo

| Fat suppression | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | No | No

| T2 | Shading (hypo) | Variable | Heterogeneous | Solid

| Nature | Blood cyst | Fat tumor | Malignant | Solid tumor

| Key sign | T2 shading ⭐ | Fat suppression | Solid nodules | Lobulated mass
questions.learning: Endometrioma Endometriomas (chocolate cysts) show T1 hyperintensity due to blood, remain bright on fat-sat, and T2 shading from repeated hemorrhage. Teratomas contain fat, carcinoma/dysgerminoma lack these features.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a hard, irregular left- sided scrotal mass that does not reduce in size when lying down or on manipulation, lacks a cough impulse, and is associated with para- aortic lymph node enlargement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of a hard, irregular, and non-reducible scrotal mass (no cough impulse) in the presence of para-aortic lymphadenopathy are pathognomonic for a testicular malignancy . The lymphatic drainage of the testes follows their embryological path of descent from the high posterior abdominal wall; therefore, testicular cancer typically bypasses the inguinal nodes and spreads first to the para-aortic nodes at the level of the renal vessels (L1-L2). Hydrocele (Option A) presents as a soft, cystic, transilluminant swelling. Inguinal hernias (Option B and C) would typically have a positive cough impulse and reduce when lying down. Because the mass is solid, non-reducible, and has a specific pattern of deep abdominal lymphatic spread, a metastasizing testicular tumor is the definitive diagnosis. Further evaluation requires serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) and a radical orchidectomy for tissue diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical findings of a hard, irregular, and non-reducible scrotal mass (no cough impulse) in the presence of para-aortic lymphadenopathy are pathognomonic for a testicular malignancy .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a fracture visible on X-ray. In this type of fracture, which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a spiral fracture of the humerus midshaft. This fracture type is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve because the nerve courses directly against the bone within the spiral (radial) groove. Trauma at this specific location frequently causes radial nerve palsy, which manifests clinically as "wrist drop"—the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. The median nerve (Option A) is situated medially and is rarely affected by midshaft humeral injuries. The ulnar nerve (Option C) runs near the medial epicondyle and is more commonly injured in distal fractures. The axillary nerve (Option D) is located near the surgical neck of the humerus and is typically injured in proximal fractures or shoulder dislocations. Given the close anatomical proximity of the radial nerve to the humeral shaft, it is the most likely structure to be damaged
questions.learning: The X-ray displays a spiral fracture of the humerus midshaft. This fracture type is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve because the nerve courses directly against the bone within the spiral (radial) groove.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presents to the ER with a history of RTA. On examination, GCS is 15/15, heart rate = 110/min, BP = 90/60 mmHg, and there is elevated JVP. The right chest is hyperresonant on percussion with decreased breath sounds. The left chest appears normal. But the patient is dyspneic and ecchymosis is noted over the chest wall. The abdomen was soft. The probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tension pneumothorax

The given clinical scenario of trauma with decreased breath sounds and a hyper-resonant note on percussion indicates pneumothorax. The presence of tachycardia, hypotension and elevated JVP is suggestive of tension pneumothorax.

Tension pneumothorax develops when there is a parietal or visceral pleural tear. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e. air enters the pleural space from the lung or chest wall during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration, leading to the collapse of the affected lung.

It is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea, acute dyspnea, sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness), neck vein distention, tracheal deviation away from the side of injury, decreased chest movements on the affected side, hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side and absent or decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed awaiting radiological confirmation.

Management includes:

• Immediate management: Needle decompression or needle thoracostomy with a wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line. In the pediatric age group, the needle thoracostomy location is at the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.
• Definitive management: Tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th intercostal space in the triangle of safety.

The triangle of safety is bounded anteriorly by the lateral border of the pectoralis major, posteriorly by latissmus dorsi and inferiorly by a horizontal line at the level of the nipple.

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing to the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Other options:

Options A:  Pericardial tamponade can mimic tension pneumothorax, but the absence of a tympanic note on percussion rules out its possibility. A patient with pericardial tamponade can present with hypotension, raised JVP, and muffled heart sounds (Beck’s triad), with normal breath sounds and no tracheal shift.

Option C: Dullness in percussion at the base of the left inferior angle of scapula in conjunction with tubular breath sounds (Ewart’s sign), chest pain that improves while sitting upright and worsens when lying down and pulsus paradoxus are indicative of pericardial effusion. Pericardial effusion develops into tamponade when the effusion leads to increased pressure, impairing ventricular filling and reducing cardiac output.

Option D: Massive hemothorax is the accumulation of >1500 ml of blood or one-third or more of the patient’s blood volume in the chest cavity. The patient will have collapsed neck veins, decreased breath sounds and a dull note on percussion.
questions.learning: Tension pneumothorax — The given clinical scenario of trauma with decreased breath sounds and a hyper-resonant note on percussion indicates pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which pair of neurotransmitters is associated with depression?
questions.explanation: The "monoamine hypothesis" of depression proposes that the condition results from a deficiency of certain neurotransmitters in the brain. The two most critical neurotransmitters involved are Serotonin and Norepinephrine (Option B). Serotonin (5-HT) regulates mood, sleep, and appetite, while norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is involved in energy, focus, and the stress response. Most modern antidepressants work by increasing the synaptic levels of these two chemicals . For example, SSRIs target serotonin, while SNRIs target both. While dopamine (Option C) also plays a role in the brain's reward system and its lack can contribute to anhedonia (loss of pleasure), the most standard pairing taught in medical and psychiatric texts regarding the core pathophysiology of depression is serotonin and norepinephrine. GABA (Option A and D) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter and is more closely associated with anxiety disorders. Therefore, the "monoamine" pair is the correct answer
questions.learning: The "monoamine hypothesis" of depression proposes that the condition results from a deficiency of certain neurotransmitters in the brain. The two most critical neurotransmitters involved are Serotonin and Norepinephrine (Option B).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive mother with a viral load of 1200 copies/mL delivers a newborn baby. What is the most appropriate antiretroviral prophylaxis for the newborn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nevirapine + Zidovudine for 12 weeks

In infants born to HIV-positive mothers, the choice and duration of antiretroviral prophylaxis depend on the risk of transmission, primarily determined by maternal viral load.

• High-risk exposure (maternal viral load >1000 copies/mL or unknown) requires combination prophylaxis
• Recommended regimen: dual therapy with Nevirapine + Zidovudine for extended duration (e.g., 12 weeks)
• Low-risk exposure (viral load <1000 copies/mL, good ART adherence) may receive single-drug prophylaxis

Clinical importance:

• Early initiation (within hours of birth) significantly reduces vertical transmission
• Adherence to prophylaxis and follow-up testing is essential

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved as a secondary messenger in the mechanism of gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cAMP

cAMP is the secondary messenger involved in the mechanism of gastric acid secretion.

cGMP is not involved in gastric acid secretion. Ach acts on the synapses, and CCK-B receptors interact with gastrin to contribute to gastric acid secretion. They also act via secondary messengers such as IP3 and increased intracellular Ca2+.

Pearl PF0546: Stimuli for gastric secretion

Stimuli

Mechanism

Applied aspects

Vagal stimulation

Direct pathway

Vagus nerve innervates parietal cells and stimulates H+ secretion directly.

The neurotransmitter at these synapses is Ach, the receptor on the parietal cells is muscarinic (M3)

The second messengers for CCK are IP3 and increased intracellular [Ca2+].

Atropine, a cholinergic muscarinic antagonist, inhibits H+ secretion by blocking the direct pathway, which uses ACh as a neurotransmitter. However, it does not block H+ secretion completely because it does not inhibit the indirect pathway, which uses GRP as a neurotransmitter

Indirect pathway

Vagus nerve innervates G cells and stimulates gastrin secretion, which then stimulates H+ secretion.

The neurotransmitter at these synapses is GRP (not ACh).

Vagotomy eliminates both direct and indirect pathways.

Gastrin

Released in response to eating a meal (small peptides, distension of the stomach, vagal stimulation).

Stimulates H+ secretion by interacting with the cholecystokinin B (CCKB) receptor on the parietal cells.

The second messenger for gastrin on the parietal cell is IP3/Ca2+.

Histamine

Released from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa and diffuses to the nearby parietal cells.

Stimulates H+ secretion by activating H2 receptors on the parietal cell membrane.

The H2 receptor is coupled to adenylyl cyclase via a Gs protein.

The second messenger for histamine is cAMP.

H2 receptor–blocking drugs, such as cimetidine, inhibit H+ secretion by blocking the stimulatory effect of histamine.
questions.learning: cAMP cAMP is the secondary messenger involved in the mechanism of gastric acid secretion. cGMP is not involved in gastric acid secretion. Ach acts on the synapses, and CCK-B receptors interact with gastrin to contribute to gastric acid secretion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Para-sagittal section of the abdomen is given below. What is the superior border of the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Caudate lobe of liver

The structure marked in the given image is epiploic foramen. The superior border of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe of the liver.

Epiploic foramen is a vertical slit of about 3 cm behind the free right border of the lesser omentum. It connects the lesser sac to the greater sac. The pearl summarizes the various relations of the foramen.

The image attached shows the various peritoneal reflections.

Clinical note: Pringle maneuver (as shown below) is a technique where the free margin of the lesser omentum is compressed to obtain rapid control of the hepatic artery and portal vein in liver trauma and surgery.
questions.learning: Caudate lobe of liver — The structure marked in the given image is epiploic foramen. The superior border of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe of the liver.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the deformity displayed in the image.
questions.explanation: The image illustrates a "Boutonniere deformity," a classic hand finding often seen in rheumatoid arthritis or following trauma to the finger. It is characterized by persistent "flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint" and "hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint." This occurs due to a rupture or weakening of the central slip of the extensor tendon, allowing the lateral bands to slide volarly and act as flexors of the PIP joint. Swan neck deformity (Option A) is the opposite: hyperextension of the PIP and flexion of the DIP. Z-line deformity (Option C) specifically refers to a thumb deformity in RA involving CMC subluxation and MCP hyperextension. Trigger finger (Option D) involves a "locking" of the finger in flexion due to a tendon nodule. Treatment for Boutonniere deformity involves PIP joint splinting in extension to allow the central slip to heal, or surgical repair in chronic, fixed cases

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) due to contraceptive failure can be done up to:
questions.explanation: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act (India), termination of pregnancy due to failure of contraception is permitted up to 20 weeks of gestation. This applies to both married and unmarried women as per recent amendments. Between 20–24 weeks, MTP is allowed only under specific conditions (such as rape survivors, minors, or other special categories) and requires approval by two registered medical practitioners. Contraceptive failure alone is not sufficient for termination beyond 20 weeks. Why other options are incorrect: (B) 24 weeks: Allowed only for special categories, not routine contraceptive failure (C) 32 weeks: Not permitted under MTP Act (D) 12 weeks: Earlier limit for single doctor opinion, but not the maximum limit Therefore, for contraceptive failure, the legal limit is 20 weeks
questions.learning: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act (India), termination of pregnancy due to failure of contraception is permitted up to 20 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with diabetes presents with severe ear pain and persistent ear discharge that does not improve with antibiotics. Otoscopic examination shows granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, along with facial nerve palsy. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Malignant otitis externa (MOE), also known as necrotizing otitis externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal and skull base. It typically occurs in elderly diabetic patients or immunocompromised individuals. The causative organism is almost always Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Key clinical features—intense ear pain out of proportion to clinical signs, persistent foul-smelling otorrhea, and the presence of granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction—are classic. Facial nerve paralysis indicates that the infection has spread to the skull base, causing osteomyelitis. Option A (Otomycosis) involves fungal growth and itching rather than deep pain. Option B (Serous otitis media) presents with hearing loss and fluid behind the drum, not external canal findings. Option D is an allergic/inflammatory condition with itching and redness. MOE requires urgent intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics and meticulous diabetic control to prevent further cranial nerve involvement or intracranial complications
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa (MOE), also known as necrotizing otitis externa, is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal and skull base.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which chemical form is nitrogenous waste predominantly excreted from the human body?
questions.explanation: Humans are "ureotelic" organisms, meaning that the primary vehicle for the excretion of nitrogenous waste from protein metabolism is urea. Urea is synthesized in the liver through the urea cycle (ornithine cycle), which converts highly toxic ammonia into the less toxic, water-soluble urea. This urea is then transported through the blood to the kidneys, where it is eliminated in the urine. Nitric oxide (Option B) is a signaling molecule. Ammonia (Option C) is a toxic metabolic intermediate that is only eliminated in large quantities by aquatic animals (ammonotelic). Glutamine (Option D) acts as a safe carrier of ammonia in the blood but is not the final excretory product. The measurement of Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) is a standard clinical indicator of renal and hepatic function. Therefore, urea is the final, non-toxic form in which nitrogen is safely concentrated and eliminated from the human body

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-year-old unusually tall child with disproportionately long limbs presents with diminished vision. Ophthalmic examination reveals bilateral lens subluxation. Which underlying defect is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fibrillin 1

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 (Fibrillin-1) gene on chromosome 15. It classically presents with tall stature, disproportionately long limbs (arachnodactyly), ectopia lentis (lens subluxation), and cardiovascular abnormalities.

Key differentiating features:

• Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation):

• Tall, thin habitus with long limbs
• Lens subluxation upward and outward (superotemporal)
• Aortic root dilatation → aortic aneurysm/dissection
• Mitral valve prolapse

• Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (PLOD1/COL5A2 mutations):

• Hyperextensible skin
• Joint hypermobility
• Tissue fragility

• Homocystinuria:

• Marfanoid habitus with downward and inward lens subluxation
• Intellectual disability
• Thromboembolic events

questions.text: Type of voice associated with the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image shows a lateral skull X-ray with narrowing/obstruction in the nasopharyngeal airway, most consistent with conditions like adenoid hypertrophy. This leads to blockage of nasal airflow, which directly affects speech resonance. In such cases, the voice becomes hyponasal (denasal), a condition known as rhinolalia clausa. Here, nasal sounds like “m” and “n” are reduced or altered, and the patient’s speech appears muffled or congested, similar to speaking with a blocked nose. Key Concept: 1. Rhinolalia clausa → nasal obstruction → decreased nasal resonance 2. Rhinolalia aperta → palatal defect → increased nasal resonance Why other options are incorrect: (B) Rhinolalia aperta : Seen in cleft palate → excessive nasal sound (opposite condition) (C) Hot potato voice : Due to peritonsillar abscess; muffled but not nasal (D) Hypernasality : Feature of rhinolalia aperta, not clausa

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with Cryptococcal meningitis. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: The standard induction therapy for Cryptococcal meningitis is the combination of Flucytosine and Liposomal Amphotericin B (L.Amp) for 2 weeks. This combination is superior in rapidly clearing the fungal load from the CSF. Flucytosine (Option A) or L.Amp (Option C) alone are less effective and associated with higher mortality. Fluconazole (Option B) is used for the subsequent maintenance phase (typically 8–10 weeks) after the initial induction is complete, but it is not the first-line induction treatment. Cryptococcal meningitis is a major opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients and is diagnosed by CSF India ink staining or antigen tests. Managing increased intracranial pressure via frequent lumbar punctures is also a critical adjunctive management step alongside this combination antifungal regimen

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following cataract surgery prefers suturing with nylon 10-0?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extracapsular cataract extraction

Suturing with nylon 10-0 is preferred in extracapsular cataract extraction.

In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydro dissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.

The newer techniques of cataract surgery like phacoemulsification, MICS and FLACS doesn't require a suturing either because they use self sealing incisions or doesn't require a long incision.,

Pearl PF1395: Different extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) techniques

Conventional ECCE

* Incision: 10 to 2 o'clock

* Anterior capsulotomy

* Can opener’s technique

* Envelope technique

* Continuous circular capsulorrhexis

Manual SICS

* Incision: 4-6 mm

* A self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision is made.

Phacoemulsification

* Incision:1.5–2.4 mm

* Phacoprobe and foldable IOL is used

* Sutureless surgery is possible with self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel or clear corneal incision.
questions.learning: Extracapsular cataract extraction Suturing with nylon 10-0 is preferred in extracapsular cataract extraction. In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the type of cataract seen following a blunt trauma?
questions.explanation: A Rosette-shaped cataract is the classic finding associated with blunt (concussive) trauma to the eye. The mechanical shock causes fluid to infiltrate the lens fibers, typically following the lines of the lens sutures, which creates a characteristic flower-like or star-shaped opacity. Christmas tree cataract (Option B) is a polychromatic opacity seen in myotonic dystrophy. Snowflake cataract (Option C) is the hallmark of uncontrolled, acute juvenile diabetes mellitus. Sunflower cataract (Option D) is caused by copper deposition (chalcosis) and is classically seen in Wilson's disease. While traumatic cataracts can also appear as a "Vossius ring" (pigment deposit on the lens), the rosette pattern is the most frequently tested morphological description for trauma. Surgery is required if the opacity significantly impairs the patient's vision or if there is associated lens instability

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young female presented with the following findings on the face. Which among the following will not be useful for its treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical fluocinolone

The age of the patient and the presence of papules and pustules with an erythematous base on the face are suggestive of acne. All the above agents are useful in the treatment of acne except topical fluocinolone (topical steroid). Corticosteroids may provoke an acneform reaction irrespective of their route of administration.

Acne is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit. It is commonly seen in teenagers. It can vary from very mild comedonal acne to severe aggressive pustular acne. These eventually may lead to scarring due to sinus formation.

Acne results from the combination of:

• Increased sebaceous gland activity under the influence of androgens - oily skin
• Abnormal follicular differentiation with increased keratinization- hypercornification of the duct due to increased IL-1
• Microbial hypercolonization of the follicular canal leading to its inflammation.

Management-

• Mild comedonal acne is treated with a topical retinoid. Mild papular and pustular acne is treated with topical retinoid and topical antibiotics.
• Moderate papular/pustular acne and moderate nodular acne are treated with oral antibiotic + topical retinoid with or without benzoyl peroxide.
• Severe nodular and conglobate acne are treated with oral isotretinoin.

Tazarotene is a third‐generation retinoid, which is available for the treatment of acne.
