questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Following exposure to a blast, a patient presents with lung injury and tympanic membrane rupture. Which level of blast wave effect is responsible for these injuries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary

The primary level of blast wave effect is responsible for these injuries.

A blast causes the most damage at an interface between tissues in contact with the atmosphere, which is why the lung usually suffers the most severe damage. Lungs are considered to be severely damaged organs in the air due to variations in density between the alveolar walls and the contained air.

Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT.

Blast injuries are classified as:

* Primary injuries – effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. External injuries are absent and are characterised by internal injuries. The middle ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this.

* Secondary injuries – injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries.

* Tertiary injuries – caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects.

* Quaternary injuries – all other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. e.g., flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc.

The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes and lungs.

Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion. Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries, as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure. The liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury.

Pearl PF2146: Types of Blast Injuries

Blast injury type

Mechanism of injury

Health impact

Primary

Rapid crushing over pressure

Tympanic membrane (most common), Lung (2nd most common), eyes, GIT

Secondary

Flying debris

MARSHAL’s triad (triad of abrasions, contuisions, lacerations)

Tertiary

Blast wind

Victim is thrown in air and strikes other objects leading to fracture and blunt trauma

Quaternary

Any complicating factor not in the other three categories

Burns, histotoxic anoxia, and crush injuries

* The specific pulmonary injury of air blast is known as blast lung.

* When the explosion is in the water the pressure changes are called underwater blast. Intestinal damage is very common in underwater blast injuries.

* Solid blast refers to the wave of energy that spreads through the rigid structure when an explosive is detonated near it and people in contact with its structure can be injured.

* Caecum is most sensitive to intestinal blast injury.
questions.learning: Primary — The primary level of blast wave effect is responsible for these injuries. A blast causes the most damage at an interface between tissues in contact with the atmosphere, which is why the lung usually suffers the most severe damage.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A type 1 diabetic mother is on magnesium sulfate infusion post-cesarean section for preeclampsia. She develops delirium and is drowsy. She has a respiratory rate of 10/min, random blood glucose level of 240 mg/dL, oliguria, and bilaterally absent knee reflex. What is the cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Magnesium sulfate toxicity

The given clinical scenario and examination finding of bilaterally absent knee reflex following magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) administration for preeclampsia suggest the cause of her condition to be magnesium sulfate toxicity.

MgSO4 is used as an anticonvulsant in the management of eclampsia and as prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia. It can also be used as a tocolytic to stop preterm labor. The therapeutic level of magnesium in eclampsia is 4–7 mEq/L.

Patients must be monitored for magnesium toxicity:

• Loss of deep tendon reflexes
• Decreased respiratory rate <12/min
• Urine output <30 mL/h
• Chest pain and heart block
• Visual changes, flushing, muscle paralysis, and drowsiness

Measurement of serum magnesium levels is indicated to monitor magnesium toxicity if serum creatinine >1.0 mg/dL.

Management of magnesium toxicity is as follows:

• Stop magnesium therapy
• Estimation of serum magnesium and creatinine levels
• Intravenous injection of calcium gluconate 10 mL (10% solution)

The two commonly used MgSO4 regimens are described below:

Regimen

Loading Dose

Maintenance Dose

Intramuscular (Pritchard)

4 g (20% solution) IV over 3–5 minutes, followed by 10 g (50%) deep IM (5 g in each buttock)

5 g (50%) IM 4 hourly in the alternate buttock

Intravenous (Zuspan or Sibai)

4 g IV slow over 15–20 minute

1–2 g/h IV infusion

Repeated/maintenance dose IM injections of magnesium sulfate are continued only under the following conditions:

• The patellar reflex is present
• Respiration is not depressed
• Urine output >30 mL/h

Other options:

Option B: Pregnant women with diabetic ketoacidosis present with hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) and their blood glucose level is around 380 mg/dL.

Option C: Eclampsia patients present with generalized tonic-clonic convulsions.

Option D: Diabetes insipidus patients present with polyuria and polydipsia.
questions.learning: Magnesium sulfate toxicity — The given clinical scenario and examination finding of bilaterally absent knee reflex following magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) administration for preeclampsia suggest the cause of her condition to be magnesium sulfate toxicity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows granulomatous necrotizing inflammation. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Metastatic calcification with normal serum calcium level
Dystrophic calcification with normal serum calcium level
Metastatic calcification with increased serum calcium level
Dystrophic calcification with increased serum calcium level
questions.explanation: The biopsy findings of granulomatous necrotizing inflammation (classic for tuberculosis) indicate tissue damage and cell death. In such areas of necrosis, calcium salts often deposit; this is called dystrophic calcification. A hallmark of dystrophic calcification is that it occurs in damaged or dead tissues even when serum calcium levels are normal. In contrast, metastatic calcification (Options A and C) refers to calcium deposition in normal tissues due to high serum calcium levels (hypercalcemia) from conditions like hyperparathyroidism or bone malignancy. Dystrophic calcification with increased calcium (Option D) is incorrect because the process itself is independent of serum calcium levels. Grossly, dystrophic calcification appears as gritty, white, sand-like deposits. Microscopically, it appears as basophilic (blue/purple) amorphous clumps. In the case of old tubercular lymph nodes or lung lesions, these calcifications are often visible on X-rays as bright radio-opaque spots, serving as permanent markers of past infection and tissue injury
questions.learning: The biopsy findings of granulomatous necrotizing inflammation (classic for tuberculosis) indicate tissue damage and cell death. In such areas of necrosis, calcium salts often deposit; this is called dystrophic calcification.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which parameter is the best guide to monitor the adequacy of fluid resuscitation in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urine output

Urine output is the best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor for adequacy of fluid resuscitation.

Adequate end-organ perfusion is best indicated by urine output of  >0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h. However, it does not give a minute-to-minute value.

The level of consciousness is an important marker for cerebral perfusion.

The only clinical indicators of perfusion of the gastrointestinal tract and muscular beds are measures of lactic acidosis (lactate and base deficit) and mixed venous oxygen saturation.

Other options:

Option A: Central venous pressure (CVP) is the mean pressure in the superior vena cava, used for estimation of preload and right atrial pressure. Normal CVP ranges from 2 to 7 mm Hg (3 to 9 cm H2O). A sick or injured patient with a CVP <3 mm Hg is presumed to be volume depleted and may be given fluids with relative safety. However, CVP is unreliable in assessing volume status or left ventricular function with respect to resusitation.

Options C and D: Blood pressure and oxygen saturation do not reflect body fluid levels.
questions.learning: Urine output Urine output is the best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor for adequacy of fluid resuscitation. Adequate end-organ perfusion is best indicated by urine output of >0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following is not done during the primary survey in trauma management?

1. NCCT brain
2. Endotracheal intubation
3. Intercostal drainage
4. Chest X Ray
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 only

NCCT brain is not done during the primary survey in trauma management. (Option C)

Endotracheal intubation is part of airway management in the primary survey. Intercostal drainage for hemothorax or pneumothorax and chest X-ray especially AP view is part of breathing component assessment of the primary survey in trauma management.

NCCT brain is a part of the secondary survey of trauma management and is performed after initial resuscitation and stabilisation. A CT scan of the head is performed within 1 hour if the GCS is <14 at the initial assessment. Other indications include a tense fontanelle, suspicion of an open/ depressed or base of skull fracture, abnormal pupillary response, abnormal posturing, and a focal neurological defect. A head CT scan should also be performed if there are three or more vomiting episodes, a witnessed loss of consciousness or amnesia for >5 minutes.
questions.learning: 1 only NCCT brain is not done during the primary survey in trauma management. (Option C) Endotracheal intubation is part of airway management in the primary survey.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the primary referral centers in India's healthcare system?
options: Primary health centres and district hospitals
Community health centres and medical colleges
Sub-district hospitals and community health centres
questions.explanation: India’s healthcare system is organized into a three-tier structure: primary, secondary, and tertiary care. Primary referral centres refer to facilities where patients are first referred from lower-level institutions (like sub-centres or primary health centres) for more specialized care. Community Health Centres (CHCs) function as the first referral units (FRUs) in rural areas. They provide specialist services such as medicine, surgery, pediatrics, and obstetrics. When cases require even more advanced care, patients are referred further to tertiary care centres, such as medical colleges, which are equipped with highly specialized services, advanced diagnostics, and teaching facilities. Other options are incorrect: (A) Primary health centres and district hospitals PHCs are first-contact facilities, not referral centres (B) Medical colleges and district hospitals district hospitals are referral centres, but PHCs are missing (D) Sub-district hospitals and CHCs these are secondary-level facilities but do not represent the full referral hierarchy

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A teenager is brought to the OPD with history of amenorrhea. On examination, she is short statured, has a webbed neck, low hairline at the back of the neck. Further examination revealed widely spaced nipples. Karyotyping in this patient would reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 45 X0

This patient most likely has turner's syndrome, with 45 XO.

Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality with partial or complete monosomy of the X chromosome (45+XO). In Turner's syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis causes primary ovarian failure that is hypogonadism. The clinical picture of amenorrhea, short stature, webbed neck, low hairline at the back of the neck, widely spaced nipples, and lack of secondary sexual characteristics is seen in Turner's syndrome.

Important features associated with Turner's syndrome: (mnemonic: See A Baby CLOWN Here)

* Short stature, Short fourth metacarpal, Sensorineural hearing loss, Shield chest

* Amenorrhea (primary), infertility

* Barr body absent

* Cardiac defects, Cubitus valgus, Congenital lymphedema

* L: Learning disabilities

* Ovaries underdeveloped (streak ovaries), Gonadoblastoma (increased risk if Y chromosome material is present)

* Webbed neck

* Nipples widely spaced

* Horseshoe kidneys

The image below shows webbed neck.

Option D - 47 XXY: Klinefelter's syndrome occurs in males with a 47 XXY karyotype and is associated with testicular dysfunction and male infertility.
questions.learning: 45 X0 This patient most likely has turner's syndrome, with 45 XO. Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality with partial or complete monosomy of the X chromosome (45+XO).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the Tillaux sign?
options: Mass is felt in the periumbilical region
Mass is mobile perpendicular to mesentery attachment line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mass is mobile perpendicular to mesentery attachment line

Tillaux's sign is said to be positive if the mass/swelling is mobile perpendicular to the mesentery attachment line. Tillaux’s sign is seen in a mesenteric cyst.

Mesenteric cysts occur either in the small intestine (60%) or the colon (40%) and can be classified as the following:

• Chylolymphatic (most common type)
• Enterogenous
• Urogenital remnant
• Dermoid
• Other causes: traumatic hematoma and cyst formation, tuberculous cold abscess of mesentery and hydatid cyst of the mesentery

They most commonly occur in adults with a mean age of 45 years. It is more common in females than males (2:1). The most common presentation is a painless abdominal swelling near the umbilicus, which is smooth and not moving with respiration with Tillaux's triad:

• Soft, smooth swelling in the umbilical region
• Freely mobile in a direction perpendicular to the mesentery (Tillaux's sign)
• Zone of resonance around the cyst

Other presentations include recurrent attacks of abdominal pain due to temporary impaction of a food bolus in a segment of the bowel narrowed by the cyst and vomiting.

Complications of mesenteric cyst include torsion, rupture, infection and hemorrhage into the cyst.

Ultrasonography and CT are used to demonstrate mesenteric cysts.

Treatment:

• Chlyolymphatic cyst is managed by enucleation.
• Enterogenous cyst is managed by removal of the cyst with resection of the adjacent bowel as it arises as a diverticulum or duplication from the adjacent bowel.

In cases where complete excision is not possible due to the close proximity to vital structures, partial excision or marsupialization should be performed.
questions.learning: Mass is mobile perpendicular to mesentery attachment line Tillaux's sign is said to be positive if the mass/swelling is mobile perpendicular to the mesentery attachment line.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat initiative, mild to moderate anemia in pregnant women < 34 weeks of gestation is treated using:
options: 3 iron and folic acid (IFA) tablets, taken OD
IV iron sucrose for non-compliance with oral tablets
2 iron and folic acid tablets OD + IV iron sucrose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IV iron sucrose for non-compliance with oral tablets

According to the Anemia Mukt Bharat initiative, pregnant women with mild and moderate anemia is treated with

• Two iron and folic acid tablets (60 mg elemental iron and 500 mcg folic acid) daily, orally given by the health provider during the ANC contact
• Parenteral iron (IV iron sucrose or ferric carboxy maltose [FCM]) may be considered as the first line of management in pregnant women who are detected to be anemic late in pregnancy or in whom compliance is likely to be low (high chance of loss to follow-up)

Anemia Mukt Bharat 2018 scheme:

This is an initiative that aims to strengthen the existing mechanisms and foster newer strategies for tackling anemia. It focuses on six target beneficiary groups, through six interventions and six institutional mechanisms to achieve their target by 2022.

Interventions:

• Prophylactic iron and folic acid supplementation.
• Deworming.
• Intensified year-round Behaviour Change Communication Campaign (Solid Body, Smart Mind) including ensuring delayed cord clamping in newborns.
• Testing of anemia using digital methods and point-of-care treatment.
• Mandatory provision of Iron and Folic Acid fortified foods in government-funded health programs.
• Addressing non-nutritional causes of anemia in endemic pockets, with a special focus on malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis.

Beneficiaries:

• Children, 6-59 months of age
• Children, 5-9 years of age
• Adolescent girls and boys, 10-19 years of age
• Women of reproductive age, 20-49 years of age
• Pregnant women
• Lactating mothers, 0-6 months

Institutions through which activities are carried out:

• Intra-Ministerial Coordination
• National Anemia Mukt Bharat Unit
• National Centre of Excellence and Advanced Research on Anemia Control (NCEAR-A)
• Convergence with other Ministries
• Strengthening Supply Chain and Logistics
• Anemia Mukt Bharat Dashboard and Digital Portal

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A girl with intellectual disability presents to the OPD with the following finding (image below). Cardiac evaluation shows a congenital endocardial cushion defect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Down's syndrome

The image shows simian crease. The clinical features of intellectual disability, congenital endocardial cushion defect point towards Down's syndrome

Down’s syndrome is an autosomal disorder. It was described by Langdon Down in 1866. It is also called trisomy 21 or mongolism. The clinical features of Down's syndrome seen in older children are: (Mnemonic: I C A PROBLEM Somewhere)

* Intellectual disability/Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly

* Congenital heart disease

* Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/Alzheimer's disease/Atlantoaxial instability/Atresia of the duodenum

* Protruding tongue

* Round face

* Occiput flat/Open wide fontanelle/Open mouth

* Brachycephalic/Brushfield's spots

* Low (depressed) nasal bridge

* Epicanthal fold/Ears low set and dysplastic

* Mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure)

* Simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes

Image: A child having features of Down’s syndrome

Image: Brushfield's spots

Simian crease is also seen in:

* Fetal alcohol syndrome

* Trisomy 13

* Cri du chat syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Thickened ventricular wall with normal diastolic function is a feature of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Athlete’s heart

Athlete’s heart is a physiological adaptation to intensive exercise, characterized by mild symmetrical left ventricular wall thickening with preserved systolic and normal diastolic function. It is a benign and reversible condition that must be differentiated from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Causes pathological ventricular hypertrophy with impaired diastolic relaxation (diastolic dysfunction) and may produce LV outflow tract obstruction.
• B. Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Characterized by severe diastolic dysfunction due to a stiff ventricle; wall thickness is usually normal or increased only in infiltrative diseases.
• C. Endomyocardial fibrosis: A type of restrictive cardiomyopathy causing marked diastolic dysfunction.
questions.learning: Athlete’s heart Athlete’s heart is a physiological adaptation to intensive exercise, characterized by mild symmetrical left ventricular wall thickening with preserved systolic and normal diastolic function.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is not associated with BRCA1/BRCA2 genes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Liver cancer

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes involved in the homologous recombination repair of double-stranded DNA breaks. Germline mutations in these genes significantly increase the risk of several hereditary cancers, most notably breast and ovarian cancer.

• A. Breast cancer ✅

• Strongly associated with both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations.
• BRCA1 is commonly associated with triple-negative breast cancer.

• B. Ovarian cancer ✅

• Both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations markedly increase the lifetime risk of high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

• C. Prostate cancer ✅

• Particularly associated with BRCA2 mutations.
• BRCA2 carriers have a higher risk of aggressive prostate cancer.

• D. Liver cancer ❌

• Not a recognized BRCA1/BRCA2-associated malignancy.
• Hepatocellular carcinoma is more commonly associated with HBV/HCV infection, cirrhosis, aflatoxin exposure, and alcohol.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents with acute onset colicky flank pain radiating to the groin. Non-contrast CT shows a ureteric calculus lodged at a site that is not a normal anatomical constriction of the ureter. Which of the following sites is most likely involved?
options: Crossing of ureter over iliac vessels at pelvic brim
Mid-ureter at level of L2 vertebra
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mid-ureter at level of L2 vertebra

There are three classical ureteric constrictions:

• Pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ)
• Crossing over iliac vessels at pelvic brim
• Vesico-ureteric junction (VUJ)

These are the most common sites where ureteric calculi get lodged

Non-constriction site: Mid-ureter at L2 vertebral level is NOT a normal anatomical narrowing

Clinical correlation:

• Stones outside these constrictions are less common but possible
• Pain typically radiates from flank to groin (loin-to-groin pattern)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman at 17 weeks of gestation presents with hypertension, with blood pressure readings of 140/94 mmHg initially and 144/90 mmHg four hours later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypertension in pregnancy is classified based on the timing of onset. Hypertension that is diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation is defined as chronic hypertension. Since this patient is at 17 weeks with sustained blood pressure readings above 140/90 mmHg, chronic hypertension is the most likely diagnosis. Gestational hypertension (Option A) and pre-eclampsia (Option D) are conditions that characteristically develop after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Pre-eclampsia also requires the presence of proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. Acute on chronic hypertension (Option C), often termed "superimposed pre-eclampsia," refers to the development of pre-eclampsia features in a patient with known chronic hypertension. Patients with chronic hypertension require close monitoring for fetal growth restriction and the later development of pre-eclampsia, as they are at significantly higher risk for these complications compared to the general obstetric population
questions.learning: Hypertension in pregnancy is classified based on the timing of onset. Hypertension that is diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation is defined as chronic hypertension.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is autosomal dominant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Achondroplasia

Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder.

It is caused by a mutation of the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR-3) gene.

The primary defect is abnormal chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate that causes development of short and thick bones.

Clinical features:

• Short limbs
• Normal trunk
• Large head
• Saddle nose
• Exaggerated lumbar lordosis
• Severe spinal deformity may lead to cord compression
questions.learning: Achondroplasia Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder. It is caused by a mutation of the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR-3) gene.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which form of anesthesia is most appropriate for dental procedures carried out in a daycare (outpatient) setting?
questions.explanation: For minor dental surgery in a daycare setting, Infiltration Anesthesia (Option D) is the preferred method. This involves injecting a local anesthetic directly into the tissue at the surgical site to block the terminal nerve branches. It is safe, effective, and allows the patient to remain fully conscious and mobile, facilitating immediate discharge. General anesthesia (Option A) is reserved for very complex surgeries, uncooperative children, or severe dental anxiety, but it carries higher risks and requires a longer recovery period. Spinal (Option B) and Epidural (Option C) anesthesia are used for procedures involving the lower half of the body (e.g., legs or lower abdomen) and have no anatomical application for dental work in the mouth. Infiltration anesthesia, often supplemented by a nerve block (like the inferior alveolar nerve block), remains the mainstay of pain control in clinical dentistry due to its localized effect and safety profile
questions.learning: For minor dental surgery in a daycare setting, Infiltration Anesthesia (Option D) is the preferred method. This involves injecting a local anesthetic directly into the tissue at the surgical site to block the terminal nerve branches.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in an immuno compromised patient from a low socioeconomic background who presents with low-grade evening fever, weight loss, and a soft, non- tender cervical swelling that shows a positive fluctuation test?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture describes a "cold abscess," which is a hallmark of Tubercular Lymphadenitis (Option B). The patient's immunocompromised status and lower-income background are significant risk factors for tuberculosis. "Mild nightly fever" and weight loss are classic constitutional symptoms of TB. A soft, non-tender, fluctuating mass in the neck without signs of acute inflammation (redness or heat) is the definition of a cold abscess, usually resulting from the liquefaction of caseous lymph nodes. A branchial cyst (Option A) is a congenital swelling located at the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid but lacks systemic symptoms. A thyroglossal cyst (Option C) is a midline mass that moves with tongue protrusion. A lipoma (Option D) is a painless, slow-growing fatty mass that is slip-sign positive but does not fluctuate. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or biopsy is required to confirm the presence of acid-fast bacilli or granulomatous inflammation
questions.learning: The clinical picture describes a "cold abscess," which is a hallmark of Tubercular Lymphadenitis (Option B). The patient's immunocompromised status and lower-income background are significant risk factors for tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The spectacles shown in the image are not used for the management of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypermetropia

The given image shows spectacles made of lenses with two different optical power. Thus, it is a pair of bifocal spectacles which is not used in hypermetropia or myopia.

Bifocal glasses have different corrective powers in the upper segment for distant vision and lower segment for near vision. Thus, they are useful in conditions where both distance and near vision are affected, like the following:

1. Presbyopia (option A): It is a definitive indication. It is used to correct age-related near and far vision defects.
2. Aphakia (option B): It provides both near and far vision correction when intra-ocular lens insertion is contraindicated.
3. Paediatric pseudophakia (option C): It is used to correct refractive errors or accommodative fluctuations post intra-ocular lens (IOL) insertion.
4. Non refractive accomodative esotropia

In hypermetropia there is defect in near vision only and hence a single vision glasses having uniform corrective power throught the entire surface is used instead of bifocal glasses.
questions.learning: Hypermetropia — The given image shows spectacles made of lenses with two different optical power. Thus, it is a pair of bifocal spectacles which is not used in hypermetropia or myopia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient receiving antitubercular therapy (ATT) develops visual disturbances. Which ATT drug is most likely responsible for this adverse effect?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the high-yield pharmacological principle detailed in Question 75. Among the first-line antitubercular drugs, Ethambutol is well-known for causing optic neuritis, leading to visual problems such as decreased acuity and red-green color blindness. Rifampicin (Option A) affects the liver and causes red fluid discoloration. Streptomycin (Option B) targets the eighth cranial nerve, causing hearing loss and balance issues. Pyrazinamide (Option D) is most associated with liver toxicity and joint pain due to high uric acid. The ocular toxicity of Ethambutol is often related to the total cumulative dose. It is vital for clinicians to perform regular visual screening for any patient on a long-term course of this medication. If a patient reports "blurred vision" or difficulty seeing traffic lights (red/green), the drug must be discontinued immediately to prevent permanent blindness. This specific side effect is a favorite topic on medical board exams due to its serious clinical implications

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following chart shows the hormonal variations in the menstrual cycle. Identify the true statement : (LH: luteinizing hormone, FSH: follicle-stimulating hormone)
options: The blue line represents FSH hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The blue line represents FSH hormone

The blue line represents follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle.

Other options :

* The pink line represents luteinizing hormone.

* The grey line represents estrogen.

* The purple line represents progesterone.

Phases of the menstrual cycle :

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

* A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.

* LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells.

* Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.

* FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.

* Progesterone levels are low.

Ovulation (day 14)

* Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length. Thus, in a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 22.

* A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge).

* Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.

* Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase).

* Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

* Progesterone levels are high.

* The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg.

* Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.

* If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

* The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.

Pearl PF0568: Hormonal Regulation of Menstrual Cycle

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Following image denote which side of placenta?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the fetal surface of the placenta, also known as the chorionic plate. This side is characterized by its smooth, shiny, and bluish-white appearance, covered by the transparent amnion. Critically, the umbilical cord is seen attaching directly to this surface, and large fetal vessels are visible radiating from the cord insertion. In contrast, the maternal surface (Options B and D), also known as the basal plate, is rough, dull, and dark red, divided into 15–20 cotyledons by septa. The decidual surface (Option C) refers specifically to the maternal tissue (decidua basalis) that remains attached to the maternal side of the placenta after delivery. Therefore, the presence of the umbilical cord and the smooth chorionic membrane makes it clear that this is the fetal side

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used in GERD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metoclopramide

Metoclopramide has both antiemetic and prokinetic action and is used in the treatment of GERD.

In GERD, the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) weakens or relaxes, allowing stomach acid to flow back into the esophagus, causing irritation and symptoms like heartburn and regurgitation. Metoclopramide is useful in this condition because it increases LES tone, preventing acid reflux, and enhances gastric emptying by promoting gastrointestinal motility. Additionally, it reduces nausea and vomiting by blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the central nervous system. These combined effects help alleviate the symptoms and discomfort associated with GERD.

Metoclopramide works in GERD by enhancing gastrointestinal motility through its antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors. In GIT, acetylcholine increases gastrointestinal motility and increases the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone. Therefore, D2 receptor inhibition augments ACh release and enhances GI motility and LES tone. Additionally, it exerts antiemetic effects by blocking D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the central nervous system. The combined actions help alleviate symptoms associated with GERD.

Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and antiemetic. It has the following pharmacological actions:

* Dopamine receptor antagonist

* Serotonin (5HT4) receptor agonist

* Serotonin (5HT3) antagonist

* Sensitization of muscarinic receptors on smooth muscle. This results in increased lower esophageal sphincter tone and stimulates gastric antral contractions.

Adverse effects of metoclopramide are mainly extrapyramidal effects, and these include acute dystonia, Parkinson-like symptoms (tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity), tardive dyskinesia, galactorrhea due to hyperprolactinemia, and methemoglobinemia in neonates.

Extrapyramidal symptoms can be treated by discontinuing metoclopramide and administering anticholinergics or antihistaminics.

Other options :

Option A: Ondansetron is a 5 HT3 receptor antagonist. It blocks impulses at the peripheral origin in GIT and does not suppress vomiting caused by motion sickness. It is most commonly indicated for the treatment of postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

Option C: Loperamide has μ opioid receptor activity and is an orally active antidiarrheal agent. The drug is more potent than morphine as an antidiarrheal agent and penetrates the CNS poorly. It is effective in patients with 5-fluorouracil-induced diarrhea and can be regarded as the treatment of choice. Loperamide is effective against traveler’s diarrhea and can be used alone or in combination. If clinical improvement in acute diarrhea does not occur within 48 hours, loperamide should be discontinued.

Option D - Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist that is structurally similar to meperidine. It is used in the treatment of acute, chronic, and traveller's diarrhea. Upon administration, it undergoes de-esterification to difenoxin, which is its active metabolite. Its side effects include constipation, toxic megacolon, paralytic ileus and can give rise to CNS depression in children.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under which provision of the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act are beneficiaries entitled to receive 70% of their wages for a period of three months?
questions.explanation: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Sickness Benefit provides cash compensation to insured workers during periods of certified illness. Eligible beneficiaries receive approximately 70% of their average daily wages for a maximum duration of 91 days (roughly 3 months) in two consecutive benefit periods. Medical benefit (Option B) refers to the direct provision of medical care and treatment to the worker and their family but does not involve cash wage compensation. Maternity benefit (Option C) provides full wages (100%) for 26 weeks for pregnancy. Dependent's benefit (Option D) involves a monthly pension for family members if the worker dies due to an employment-related injury. The 70% wage replacement for 3 months is the characteristic financial structure of the standard sickness cash benefit. This social security measure ensures that workers do not face total income loss due to temporary physical incapacity, provided they have met the contribution requirements
questions.learning: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Sickness Benefit provides cash compensation to insured workers during periods of certified illness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The predominant organ producing insulin-like growth factor I is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liver

Growth hormone acts on the liver to form small proteins called “somatomedins”

• Somatomedins increases bone growth in all aspect
• Effects are similar to insulin, hence referred to as insulin-like growth factor (IGF).
• Four types available:

• Most important is somatomedin C, specifically referred to as “insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
• Binds to carrier protein in blood
• Hence, longer duration of action than growth hormone.
• Half-life - about 20 Hrs (compared to growth hormone - 20 mins)
• Blood concentration of IGF-1, follows the levels of growth hormone.

• Growth effects of GH are mostly attributed to somatomedin (rather than its direct effect on bones & peripheral tissues)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the structure given below, what is the joint observed?
questions.explanation: The image points specifically to the pubic symphysis, which is the classic example of a secondary cartilaginous joint, also known as a symphysis. These joints are characterized by a fibrocartilaginous disc connecting the bony surfaces, which are themselves covered by a thin layer of hyaline cartilage. Unlike primary cartilaginous joints (Option B), which involve hyaline cartilage alone and usually ossify with age (like epiphyseal plates), secondary cartilaginous joints are permanent and typically located in the midline of the body. Syndesmosis (Option A) and fibrous joints (Option C) involve ligamentous or fibrous tissue connections, such as the sutures of the skull or the distal tibiofibular joint, but lack the fibrocartilage disc. The pubic symphysis allows for limited movement, which is particularly vital during childbirth to facilitate the passage of the fetus through the pelvic canal

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following are correct regarding normal placenta, except ______.
options: Placenta weight at term is 470 g
Extraplacental membranes and 2-vesseled umbilical cord present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extraplacental membranes and 2-vesseled umbilical cord present

Among the given options, Extraplacental membranes and 2-vesseled umbilical cord present (Option C) is the wrong statement.

At term, the normal placenta weighs 470 g (Option A), is round to oval with a 22-cm diameter (Option B) and has a central thickness of ≥2.5 cm (Option D). The placenta is composed of a placental disc, extraplacental membranes, and a three-vessel umbilical cord. Hence, option C is the wrong statement.

The normal human placenta is discoid, deciduate, and hemochorial.

The term deciduate means that the placenta is shed at the time of parturition. Hemochorial means that the maternal blood directly comes in contact with the fetal trophoblasts.

The placenta consists of two plates. The chorionic plate lies in the fetal surface. It is lined by the amniotic membrane and the umbilical cord is attached to this plate.

The basal plate is the maternal aspect and lies against the uterine wall. It is divided by clefts into portions termed as cotyledons.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic presented with abdominal pain, jaundice and weight loss. He has hypoglycemia and elevated alpha fetoprotein levels (600ng/ml) but has normal AST and ALT. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatocellular carcinoma

• Chronic alcoholic → chronic liver disease risk
• Abdominal pain + jaundice + weight loss → malignancy suspicion
• Hypoglycemia → paraneoplastic clue
• AFP = 600 ng/ml → tumor marker (normal: 10-25)
• Normal AST/ALT → not active hepatitis

Put together → Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)

Classic Triad of HCC:

• Weight loss
• Abdominal pain
• Liver mass

Other Paraneoplastic Features:

• Hypoglycemia
• Polycythemia (↑ EPO)
• Hypercalcemia

Imaging Hallmark:

• Arterial phase enhancement + venous washout (CT/MRI)

| Feature | HCC | Cirrhosis | Hepatitis | Cholangiocarcinoma

| ------- | --- | --------- | --------- | ------------------

| AFP | ↑↑ | Normal | Normal | Normal

| AST/ALT | Normal/slightly ↑ | Mild ↑ | ↑↑ | Mild ↑

| Hypoglycemia | Yes | No | No | No

| Cause | Cirrhosis | Alcohol, viral | Infection | Bile duct malignancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old nulligravida presents with third- degree uterine prolapse but has no cystocele or rectocele. What is the most appropriate management for her condition?
questions.explanation: For a young, nulligravida woman with significant uterine prolapse, the primary goal of management is to preserve the uterus and future fertility. Abdominal sling surgery (such as Shirodkar’s or Purandare’s abdominal cervicopexy) is the most appropriate choice. This procedure uses a synthetic or fascial sling to anchor the cervix to the anterior abdominal wall or sacrum, providing durable support without compromising the vaginal canal or uterine function. LeFort colpocleisis (Option A) involves closing the vagina and is reserved for elderly, sexually inactive women. The Fothergill operation (Option B) involves cervical amputation, which can cause infertility and cervical incompetence, making it less ideal for a nulligravida. While Shirodkar described a vaginal approach for cervical incompetence, the "abdominal sling" specifically refers to the corrective procedure for nulligravida prolapse. This approach addresses the underlying ligamentous laxity while maintaining the potential for childbearing
questions.learning: For a young, nulligravida woman with significant uterine prolapse, the primary goal of management is to preserve the uterus and future fertility. Abdominal sling surgery (such as Shirodkar’s or Purandare’s abdominal cervicopexy) is the most appropriate choice.

* Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about baroreceptors?
options: Located in the thick muscle layer
Afferent fibers pass via the glossopharyngeal nerve branch
Sensitive to changes in arterial pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Located in the thick muscle layer

Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors sensitive to changes in arterial pressure.

They are located in the adventitia of the carotid sinus and aortic arch, not in the thick muscle layer, thick muscle layer = tunica media, baroreceptors are located in the adventitia and elastic wall regions

Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors that detect stretch in arterial walls.

| Location | Nerve Supply

| -------- | ------------

| Carotid sinus | Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

| Aortic arch | Vagus nerve (CN X)

Pathway:

1️⃣ Increased BP stretches arterial wall

2️⃣ Baroreceptors increase firing

3️⃣ Signals sent to medulla (nucleus tractus solitarius)

4️⃣ Sympathetic activity decreases

5️⃣ Parasympathetic activity increases

Result: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure

Afferent impulses from the carotid sinus travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve (Hering’s nerve).

Thus, location in the thick muscle layer is incorrect.

| Reflex | Receptor Location | Stimulus | Afferent Nerve | Response

| ------ | ----------------- | -------- | -------------- | --------

| Baroreceptor reflex | Carotid sinus, Aortic arch | ↑ Blood pressure | CN IX (carotid), CN X (aortic) | ↓ HR, ↓ BP

| Bainbridge reflex | Right atrium | ↑ Venous return / atrial stretch | Vagus | ↑ Heart rate

| Bezold–Jarisch reflex | LV wall receptors | Ventricular stretch/ischemia | Vagal C fibers | Bradycardia, hypotension

| Cushing reflex | Brainstem | ↑ Intracranial pressure | CNS | Hypertension + bradycardia

| Chemoreceptor reflex | Carotid bodies | Hypoxia, hypercapnia | CN IX, X | ↑ respiration, ↑ BP

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn baby presents with irritability and cyanosis which subsides on crying. On examination, you are unable to pass a nasogastric tube and no mist formation is noted on the laryngeal mirror test. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oro pharyngeal airway

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of choanal atresia, the best next step would be to provide an oropharyngeal airway.

Choanal atresia is the persistence of the bucconasal membrane, unilateral is more common and may remain undiagnosed until adult life, bilateral atresia will present as a respiratory obstruction in the newborn. The initial clinical evaluation consists of placing a large laryngeal mirror under each nostril and checking for fogging, this is known as the laryngeal mirror test.

Diagnosis can be made by:

* Presence of mucoid discharge in the nose

* Absence of air bubbles in the nasal discharge

* Failure to pass a catheter from the nose to the pharynx

* Putting methylene blue dye into the nose and checking its passage to the pharynx

* Putting a radio-opaque dye into the nose and taking a lateral radiograph

* CT in the axial plane

Management: In bilateral atresia, emergency treatment is to provide an airway, which is done by McGovern's technique- (a feeding tube with a large hole that provides a good oral airway), this removes the need for tracheostomy. Definitive treatment is correcting the atresia either by transpalatal or transnasal approach, which is usually done at one and a half years of age.

Pearl PF1080: Choanal atresia

* It is due to the persistence of bucconasal membrane which separates primitive oropharynx from the primitive nasopharynx

* Unilateral > bilateral

* 30% of cases are bony and 70% are mixed

* Unilateral cases may be asymptomatic and present in adult life

* Bilateral cases are life-threatening and present with respiratory distress

* Associated with CHARGE syndrome

* C- Coloboma of the eye

* H- Heart defects

* A- Atresia of choana

* R- Retarded growth and development

* G- Genital anomalies

* E- Ear anomalies and hearing loss.

* CT scan is the best investigation

Image: Membranous, bilateral choanal atresia in a newborn

* McGoverns technique- A feeding nipple with a large hole provides a good oral airway

* Definitive treatment consists of correction of atresia by a trans-nasal or trans-palatal approach.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In obstetric practice, which factor is most commonly responsible for the development of consumptive coagulopathy, a condition characterized by rapid consumption of clotting factors exceeding their production?
questions.explanation: Consumptive coagulopathy, or Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), is a severe complication in pregnancy where systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leads to the depletion of platelets and clotting factors. While all the listed options can cause DIC, "placental abruption" (Option B) is the "predominant" or most common obstetric cause. When the placenta separates prematurely, thromboplastin and other tissue factors are released into the maternal circulation, triggering widespread clotting. Intrauterine death (Option A) can cause DIC, but usually only if the dead fetus remains in utero for more than 4 weeks. Amniotic fluid embolism (Option D) and sepsis (Option C) cause extremely severe DIC, but they are much rarer occurrences compared to placental abruption. In abruption, the extent of the coagulopathy often correlates with the size of the retroplacental clot. Management involves rapid delivery and the replacement of blood products (fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and platelets) to stabilize the patient's clotting capacity
questions.learning: Consumptive coagulopathy, or Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), is a severe complication in pregnancy where systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leads to the depletion of platelets and clotting factors.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maximum dose of PGF2 alpha in postpartum hemorrhage is ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 mg

The maximum dose of prostaglandin F2 alpha in postpartum hemorrhage is 2 mg.

Prostaglandins are paracrine/autocrine hormones and act locally at the site of production. Main sources for:

1. PGF2α  - Decidua and promotes myometrial contractility
2. PGE2 - fetal membranes (amnion) and induces labor and promotes cervical effacement and dilatation
3. PGI2 - Myometrium

Carboprost tromethamine (hemabate) is the 15-methyl derivative of prostaglandin F2 alpha. It is approved for the treatment of uterine atony at a dose of 0.25 mg IM. This dose can be repeated if necessary at 15- to 90-minute intervals up to a maximum of eight doses (2 mg).

It is the best drug to control PPH. ls also used an abortifacient in the second trimester.

Contraindications include asthmatic women and those with suspected amniotic fluid embolism, as they cause pulmonary airway and vascular constriction.
questions.learning: 2 mg The maximum dose of prostaglandin F2 alpha in postpartum hemorrhage is 2 mg. Prostaglandins are paracrine/autocrine hormones and act locally at the site of production.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which medication is preferred for treating migratory polyarthritis and joint pain in a patient with acute rheumatic fever?
questions.explanation: Migratory polyarthritis is the most common major manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF). The joints are extremely painful, but the inflammation responds dramatically and rapidly to salicylates. Aspirin (high-dose) remains the preferred drug for managing the arthritis and general inflammatory symptoms of ARF. Furosemide (Option A) and Digoxin (Option B) are used in the management of heart failure (carditis), but not for the primary treatment of joint pain. Amiodarone (Option D) is an anti-arrhythmic not used in the routine management of ARF. The response to aspirin is so specific that if the joint pain does not resolve within 48-72 hours, the diagnosis of ARF should be reconsidered. Once the acute phase is managed, the most critical intervention is long-term secondary prophylaxis with Benzathine Penicillin to prevent further streptococcal infections and progressive heart valve damage
questions.learning: Migratory polyarthritis is the most common major manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF). The joints are extremely painful, but the inflammation responds dramatically and rapidly to salicylates.

questions.text: What does number 9 in the given diagram related to hypertension denote?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adequately treated

The above diagram depicts the rule of halves, which is observed in hypertension, and "number 9" denotes adequately treated subjects.

The rule of halves depicts that only about half of the hypertensive subjects in the general population of most developed countries were aware of the condition and only half of those aware are being treated and only half of those being treated are considered to be adequately treated.

The numbers in the diagram denote the following:

* Whole community

* Normotensive subjects

* Undiagnosed hypertension

* Diagnosed hypertension

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Identify the imaging modality given below.

USG- Ultrasonography
MRI- Magnetic resonance imaging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG

The image shown in the question is the USG of the neck.

Sonographic examination of the neck shows the thyroid gland, muscles, blood vessels, bony structures or cartilages, and nerves. The thyroid of a healthy patient appears homogeneously echogenic with a uniform echotexture on USG. Lateral to the thyroid, the large blood vessels (the common carotid artery and more laterally, the internal jugular vein) can be identified. In the above image, hypoechoic areas are suggestive of the lumen of vessels seen in the neck i.e common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

Neck ultrasonography is the preferred modality for routine radiographic evaluation of the thyroid gland, as it offers the most accurate visualization of thyroid nodular disease. It also allows for the concomitant performance of percutaneous fine-needle aspiration biopsy of thyroid lesions.

Neck ultrasound can also be used to localize parathyroid disease.

Other options:

Option B: Fluoroscopy is an imaging modality that allows real-time X-ray viewing of a patient with high resolution. During this procedure, radiologists usually use contrast material (dye) to highlight the area being examined.

Below image shows the fluoroscopy of neck.

Option C: The below image shows the X-ray appearance of neck in AP view.

Option D: Relative to the neck musculature, the thyroid is hyperintense on MRI images.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Based on the family pedigree chart shown below, what is the most likely pattern of inheritance for this condition?
questions.explanation: The pedigree chart illustrates an Autosomal Dominant pattern of inheritance. Key diagnostic features visible in the chart include the presence of the trait in every generation (vertical transmission) and approximately equal numbers of affected males and females. Crucially, the chart shows male-to-male transmission (e.g., from father individual 1 to son individual 5), which definitively rules out X-linked inheritance (Option C and D) since fathers only pass their Y chromosome to their sons. Autosomal recessive inheritance (Option B) is unlikely because affected individuals 1 and 2 have an unaffected child (7); if the trait were recessive, both parents would be homozygous ('aa') and all their children would be affected. In an autosomal dominant condition, every affected person usually has at least one affected parent, and two affected parents can have an unaffected child if they are both heterozygotes ('Aa'). Common examples of this pattern include Huntington's disease, Marfan syndrome, and Achondroplasia. Analyzing these specific transmission links is the standard method for determining genetic risk in clinical practice

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following can be used for induction of anesthesia, maintenance and can be safely used in endotracheal intubation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sevoflurane

Among the given options, sevoflurane can be used for induction and maintenance of anesthesia. It can also be safely used in endotracheal intubation

Inhalation agents such as sevoflurane and halothane are useful in the induction of anesthesia, But sevoflurane due to its nonpungency and rapid onset makes it an excellent choice for smooth and rapid inhalation inductions in pediatric and adult patients. Sevoflurane has low blood solubility and partition coefficients resulting in more rapid emergence.

Sevoflurane also produces adequate muscle relaxation for intubation of children following an inhalation induction.

Other options:

Option A: Halothane can also be used for gaseous induction of anesthesia. Its disadvantage is long induction time owing to the high blood:gas partition coefficient. However, the incidence of halothane hepatitis and myocardial depression has reduced its use.

Option B: Desflurane produces laryngospasm when used for inhalational anesthesia and hence it is not used for induction. Laryngospasm is because of the pungent nature of the gas.

Option D: Isoflurane causes respiratory depression as well as upper respiratory irritation.

questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 35 year old male presented with rapidly progressing, symmetrical muscle weakness, starting in the legs. Which of the following is not a treatment option in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Steroids

Rapidly progressive, symmetrical ascending weakness suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

Effective treatments:

• IVIG (B) → first-line
• Plasmapheresis (C) → equally effective alternative
• Elective ventilatory support if respiratory muscle weakness or ↓ vital capacity

Corticosteroids (A) have no proven benefit in GBS and are not recommended.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman with urge urinary incontinence is started on a drug that relaxes detrusor smooth muscle independent of antimuscarinic action. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flavoxate

Flavoxate is a direct smooth muscle relaxant used in urge urinary incontinence. It relaxes the detrusor muscle independent of antimuscarinic (M3) receptor blockade, likely via phosphodiesterase inhibition and local anesthetic action. Hence, it reduces bladder spasms without typical anticholinergic side effects, making it distinct from standard antimuscarinic drugs.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Solifenacin: A selective M3 antimuscarinic that reduces detrusor contractions via receptor blockade.

B. Tolterodine: A nonselective antimuscarinic acting on bladder muscarinic receptors.

D. Darifenacin: Highly selective M3 receptor antagonist, not a direct smooth muscle relaxant.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The coding sequence present in the RNA molecule is CAAGGU. What will be the sequence in the template DNA strand from where it is transcribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ACCTTG

During transcription, the DNA sequence 5'ACCTTG3' serves as the template for synthesizing the RNA sequence 5'CAAGGU3'.

The template DNA strand is always complementary and antiparallel to the transcribed RNA strand. Given that the RNA sequence is:

5'- CAAGGU -3'

The complementary template DNA strand (which runs in the 3' → 5' direction) is:

3'- GTTCCA -5'

To match the 5' → 3' direction, we reverse it:

5'- ACCTTG -3'

Note: Unless otherwise specified, all sequences are written in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

According to Chargaff's rule in cellular DNA regardless of species:

* Adenine= Thymine, Guanine = Cytosine

* Sum of purine = Sum of pyrimidines i.e A+G=C+T.

When DNA is transcribed into RNA, the process involves complementary base pairing. Adenine (A) in DNA pairs with thymine (T), but in RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U). Similarly, cytosine (C) in DNA pairs with guanine (G) in both DNA and RNA. During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template and adds complementary RNA nucleotides accordingly.

Pearl PF0706: Differences between DNA & RNA Synthesis

RNA synthesis

DNA synthesis

Ribonucleotides are used

Deoxyribonucleotides are used

Uracil is the complementary base for Adenine

Thymine is the complementary base for Adenine

Primer is not involved as RNA polymerases have the ability to initiate synthesis de novo

Primer is necessary because DNA polymerases can only attach new DNA nucleotides to an existing strand of nucleotides

Only portions of the genome are vigorously transcribed or copied into RNA

The entire genome must be copied, once and only once during DNA replication

No highly active, efficient proofreading function

Highly active, efficient proofreading function is performed by DNA polymerase
questions.learning: ACCTTG During transcription, the DNA sequence 5'ACCTTG3' serves as the template for synthesizing the RNA sequence 5'CAAGGU3'. The template DNA strand is always complementary and antiparallel to the transcribed RNA strand.

questions.text: According to the MTP Act Amendment of 2021, at what gestational age range is the opinion of two registered medical practitioners required for termination of pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 20-24 weeks

Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act 2021

The 2021 amendment expanded access to abortion and modified the doctor approval requirements depending on gestational age.

| Gestational Age  | Doctor Requirement

| ---------------- | -------------------

| ≤20 weeks  | Opinion of 1 Registered Medical Practitioner

| 20–24 weeks  | Opinion of 2 Registered Medical Practitioners

| >24 weeks  | Allowed only for fetal abnormalities with approval of a State Medical Board

Thus, two doctors are specifically required for termination between 20 and 24 weeks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney? 1. It is the most common sporadic renal tumor 2. Associated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3 3. Arises from distal convoluted tubule 4. Cells show intracellular accumulation of PAS + Diastase sensitive substance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common sporadic renal tumor. It typically arises from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal tubule. Tumor cells appear “clear” due to intracellular accumulation of glycogen and lipids, which are PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive (glycogen).

Although ccRCC is classically associated with chromosome 3p deletion (VHL gene mutation), the key diagnostic features are:

• Most common RCC subtype
• Clear cytoplasm due to glycogen/lipid accumulation

Thus, statements 1 and 4 are correct.
questions.learning: 1, 4 Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common sporadic renal tumor. It typically arises from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal tubule.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea and breast development corresponding to Tanner stage IV. She has sparse pubic and axillary hair. On genital examination, a blind vaginal pouch is noted. Ultrasound reveals absence of the uterus and ovaries, and testosterone levels are within the normal male range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Complete AIS

Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) should be suspected in an adolescent with primary amenorrhea, normal breast development, sparse or absent pubic/axillary hair, a blind-ending vagina, absent uterus, and serum testosterone in the normal male range. It results from an X-linked mutation of the androgen receptor, causing complete resistance to androgens in a 46,XY individual.

Despite normal testicular production of testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH):

• AMH causes regression of the Müllerian ducts, resulting in absence of the uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes.
• Because tissues cannot respond to androgens, male internal genitalia (Wolffian derivatives) fail to develop, and female external genitalia are present.
• Peripheral aromatization of testosterone to estrogen leads to normal breast development, while pubic and axillary hair are sparse or absent because hair growth is androgen-dependent.

Why not the other options?

• B. Gonadal dysgenesis: Streak gonads cause poor breast development and a present uterus due to absent AMH.
• C. MRKH syndrome: 46,XX females with normal ovaries, normal pubic/axillary hair, and female-range testosterone.
• D. Turner syndrome: 45,X with short stature, streak ovaries, poor breast development, and a present uterus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A previously healthy child presented with acute-onset dyspnea. A chest X-ray shows unilateral hyperinflation of the lungs. What is true for this patient?
options: Focal area of decreased air entry will be suggestive of foreign body
In complete obstruction, ball and valve mechanism causes hyperinflation
The child has developed acute laryngotracheobronchitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Focal area of decreased air entry will be suggestive of foreign body

The above scenario is suggestive of a foreign body in the airway, most likely in the bronchi. In this condition, auscultation is likely to reveal a focal area of decreased air entry due to incomplete airway obstruction

It is more commonly seen in children below 4 years. The most foreign bodies in the airway are food items. The foreign bodies can be non-irritating types (plastic, glass, or metallic foreign bodies) and irritating types (vegetables, peanuts, beans, and seeds).

The clinical presentation depends upon the site of the obstruction.

Site of foreign bodies
Signs and symptoms

Larynx

• Complete obstruction causes asphyxia
• Incomplete obstruction causes croup, hoarseness, cough, stridor, and dyspnea.

Trachea
Dysphonia, dysphagia, dry cough, and biphasic stridor.

Bronchi

• May be asymptomatic.
• Asymmetric breath sound/air entry, coughing, and breathing.

Foreign bodies in bronchi are more likely to enter the right bronchus because it is wider and more in line with the tracheal lumen.

The initial evaluation is done with a plain X-ray chest in posteroanterior and lateral views (expiratory films are useful). It may reveal:

• The radio-opaque foreign body- size, shape, and location
• In complete airway obstruction- lobar or segmental atelectasis
• In incomplete airway obstruction- the ball valve mechanism is produced when a foreign body incompletely obstructs a bronchus allowing air to enter inside but not leave. This leads to the appearance of hyperinflation or obstructive emphysema of the affected area when an expiratory X-ray film is taken as the air is not allowed to escape.

Management of foreign body airway is as follows:

• Laryngeal foreign body- Heimlich maneuver should be attempted. If it fails, cricothyrotomy or emergency tracheostomy should be done
• Foreign bodies in the trachea and bronchi are removed through a rigid bronchoscope after adequate hydration and emptying of the stomach.
• Appropriate antibiotics are given to prevent secondary infection.

Option D: Laryngotracheobronchitis or croup is caused by the parainfluenza virus. It commonly affects children of age 6 months-3 years. The clinical features include barking cough, biphasic stridor, and low-grade fever. The chest X-ray shows a narrowing of the subglottic region known as the steeple sign.

The image given below shows the steeple sign seen in croup.
questions.learning: Focal area of decreased air entry will be suggestive of foreign body The above scenario is suggestive of a foreign body in the airway, most likely in the bronchi.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy with fever, weight loss, fatigue, and petechia spots came to the hospital. On examination, he was pale and had hepatosplenomegaly as well as sternal tenderness. The clinical scenario described above is most commonly associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

The above described clinical features point towards the diagnosis of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.

ALL is more common in childhood. The child had symptoms related to depression of marrow function including pallor, weight loss due to anemia, and fever secondary to infections. These infections are due to neutropenia and generalized lymphadenopathy, indicating the effect of neoplastic infiltration.

The above image points show lymphoblasts with condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli, scanty agranular cytoplasm which are characteristics of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Pearl PF0574: Morphological Characteristics of Blasts Cells in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia vs. Acute Myeloid Leukemia

Lymphoblasts
Myeloblasts

Blast population tends to be homogeneous
Blast population tends to be heterogeneous, with the exception of the undifferentiated form

Size is variable, mainly small
Size is variable, mainly large

Nucleus is central, mainly round; sometimes indented.

Nucleus tends to be eccentric, round, oval or angulated; sometimes convoluted, particularly in the form with a monocytic component

Chromatin is fine, with dispersed condensation
Very condensed in small lymphoblasts
Chromatin is fine, granular, delicately dispersed

Nucleoli absent in small lymphoblasts
Sometimes indistinct
Nucleoli almost always present, often large and prominent, double or triple

Cytoplasm is scanty, basophilic
Sometimes with a single long projection (‘hand-mirror cell’)
Cytoplasm is variable;
Abundant in monoblasts,
with protrusions in erythroblasts and megakaryoblasts

Granules are rarely present; Negative for peroxidase, esterases and toluidine blue
Granules present in forms with differentiation and positive with cytochemical stains

• Peroxidase in the neutrophil and esoinophil lineages
• Nonspecific esterase in the monocyte lineage

Auer rods are absent
Auer rods can be present;
Typically present in the hypergranular promyelocytic form

Vacuoles can be present
Vacuoles can be present;
Almost always present in forms with a monocytic component

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: "Vasopressin escape" in SIADH results due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Downregulation of aquaporin 2 production

Vasopressin escape in SIADH (Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion) results due to downregulation of aquaporin 2 production.

Prolonged exposure to elevated levels of vasopressin (ADH) leads eventually to downregulation of aquaporin-2 receptors. This prevents excessive reabsorption of water, despite high serum ADH levels and hence maintains euvolemia. This is known as vasopressin escape. This helps prevent excessive dilutional hyponatremia in SIADH.
questions.learning: Downregulation of aquaporin 2 production Vasopressin escape in SIADH (Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion) results due to downregulation of aquaporin 2 production.

questions.text: The thickness of lead apron to prevent radiation is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 0.5mm

The thickness of lead apron is 0.5mm. They will reduce the intensity of scattered X-rays by over 90% and shud be worn by all workers regularly associated with X-ray procedures.

Lead is the most common agent used in modern construction because of it's ability to provide radiation shielding. Lead can effectively attenuate certain kinds of radiation because of its high density and atomic number.
