questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child with AIDS presented with fever and productive cough. On auscultation, bronchial breath sounds and crepitations were heard in the right infra-scapular region. Chest X-ray showed right lower lobe consolidation. The CD4 count was 55 cells/mm3. What is the most common causative organism for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus pnuemoniae

The given clinical features of productive cough with fever, bronchial breath sounds and crepitations on auscultation along with lower lobe consolidation on chest X-ray point towards the diagnosis of lobar pneumonia.

The most common causative organism is Streptococcus pneumonia, irrespective of HIV status. In AIDS patients, opportunistic infection-causing bacterial pneumonia occurs at any clinical stage and at any CD4 cell count. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia would present with dry cough and interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray (option A).

Patients with pneumococcal (lobar) pneumonia present with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. On examination, involved lobes are dull to percussion, bronchial breath sounds, and crackles are heard on auscultation.

A chest radiograph reveals focal, segmental, or lobar consolidation of involved lobes.

Other options:

Option A:

Pneumocystis jiroveci causes pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm3.

PCP presents with fever, dry cough, and dyspnea. Inspiratory crackles are heard on auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral, symmetric, interstitial infiltration. Initially, infiltrates are perihilar, as the disease progress, it becomes diffuse.

The chest radiographs given below show ground-glass opacities in PCP

Option C:

Staphylococcus aureus causes bacterial pneumonia with features similar to pneumococcal pneumonia. The differentiating feature is that chest X-ray in Staph. aureus infection shows pneumatoceles (cavitation).

The X-ray shows pneumatoceles (air-filled cysts within lung parenchyma).

Option D: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia. Patients present with dry cough, fever, chills, malaise, and upper respiratory tract symptoms. On auscultation, wheezes or rales are heard. Chest X-ray shows peribronchial pneumonia with prominent bronchial markings, interstitial infiltration, and atelectasis.

The chest X-ray below shows patchy consolidation at the hilum and fanning to the periphery
questions.learning: Streptococcus pnuemoniae — The given clinical features of productive cough with fever, bronchial breath sounds and crepitations on auscultation along with lower lobe consolidation on chest X-ray point towards the diagnosis of lobar pneumonia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient complains of chest pain after waking up in the morning. Pain is more prevalent in the winter months. Which of the following best describes this patient?
options: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of myocardium
Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ach-induced coronary vasoconstriction

The above clinical scenario of a female patient with chest pain in the morning, worse in winter months, is consistent with the diagnosis of Prinzmetal angina. Prinzmetal angina occurs as a result of an abnormal response, causing Ach-induced coronary vasoconstriction. It may result in transient transmural ischemia. This type of angina is commonly seen in women under 50 years of age and is precipitated by smoking and cocaine use.

Prinzmetal angina occurs as a result of vasospasm of the epicardial coronary artery. It may result in transient transmural ischemia. The cause of this spasm is poorly understood and is suspected to be due to hypercontractility of cardiac smooth muscles. This type of angina is commonly seen in women under 50 years of age and is precipitated by smoking and cocaine use.

The vasospasm leads to transmural ischemia, which is seen on the ECG as transient ST-segment elevation, although there is no atherosclerosis present on angiography.

Depolarization of cardiac myocytes depends primarily on the influx of Ca2+ ions. Ca 2+ antagonists relax arterial smooth muscle, thereby decreasing arterial resistance, blood pressure, and cardiac afterload. Hence, calcium channel blockers such as long-acting nifedipine and amlodipine are employed along with nitrates to alleviate vasospasm.

Treatment: Nitrates and Calcium Channel blockers are used in Prinzmetal angina for endothelium-independent coronary vasodilatation. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in Prinzmetal angina.

Other options:

Option A: Fixed plaque obstruction describes Stable angina, which presents as effort-induced, relieved by rest, type of pain.

Option C: Subendocardial ischemia due to increased demand of the myocardium is the mechanism of unstable angina, which presents as pain that does not subside with rest.

Option D: Increased sympathomimetic drive in morning hours is not the key feature of Prinzmetal angina.

Pearl PF1920: Indications for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG)

Class I indications for CABG from the American College of Cardiology(ACC) and American Heart Association(AHA).

* Left main disease

* Three-vessel disease with or without proximal LAD disease

* Two vessel disease with proximal LAD disease

* Survivors of sudden cardiac death with presumed ischemia-mediated VT

Other indications for CABG include the following:

* Disabling angina

* Ongoing ischemia in the setting of a non–ST-segment elevation (MI) that is unresponsive to medical therapy

* Poor LV function but with viable, nonfunctioning myocardium above the anatomic defect that can be revascularized
questions.learning: Ach-induced coronary vasoconstriction — The above clinical scenario of a female patient with chest pain in the morning, worse in winter months, is consistent with the diagnosis of Prinzmetal angina.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A resident doctor sustained a needlestick injury while sampling blood of a patient who is HIV positive. A decision is taken to offer him post-exposure prophylaxis. Which one of the following would be the best recommendation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lamivudine + Tenofovir + Dolutegravir for 4 weeks

Triple therapy with tenofovir 300mg, lamivudine 300mg, and dolutegravir 50mg for 4 weeks is recommended for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

Steps to be undertaken after a needlestick injury are:

• Wash the wound and skin with water and soap. Do not scrub and avoid antiseptics.
• Assess exposed individual:

• Check baseline viral markers
• Monitor for acute seroconversion illness within 3-6 weeks after exposure
• If testing is positive, refer to ART center

• Assess exposure source and determine the risk of transmission
• Counseling and support
• Initiate PEP at the earliest - preferably < 2 hours and ideally < 72 hours
• 28-day prescription with drug information
• HIV test at 3 months after exposure
questions.learning: Lamivudine + Tenofovir + Dolutegravir for 4 weeks Triple therapy with tenofovir 300mg, lamivudine 300mg, and dolutegravir 50mg for 4 weeks is recommended for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which antibody is the first to appear and acts fastest during a primary (first) immune response to an infection?
questions.explanation: IgM is the initial antibody produced by naïve B cells upon the first exposure to a foreign antigen. Structurally, it exists as a pentamer, providing 10 distinct antigen-binding sites. This configuration results in very high avidity, allowing it to bind pathogens strongly even before affinity maturation has occurred. IgM is also highly efficient at activating the classical complement pathway to clear systemic infections rapidly. IgG (Option B) dominates the secondary immune response and appears later in the primary response once memory B cells are activated. IgE (Option C) is primarily involved in allergic reactions and the defense against parasitic infections rather than the early general response to bacteria or viruses. IgA (Option D) is the principal antibody in mucosal secretions like tears and breast milk, providing local rather than primary systemic immunity. Thus, IgM is the definitive first responder in primary immunity
questions.learning: IgM is the initial antibody produced by naïve B cells upon the first exposure to a foreign antigen. Structurally, it exists as a pentamer, providing 10 distinct antigen-binding sites.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not preferred in a child with bilateral SNHL?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

In bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), management focuses on amplification and auditory rehabilitation, not middle ear procedures.

·         SNHL involves inner ear (cochlea) or auditory nerve damage

·         Therefore, treatment should bypass or compensate for cochlear dysfunction

Appropriate management options:

·         Hearing aids → first-line in mild to moderate SNHL

·         Cochlear implant → severe to profound SNHL

·         Educational support → e.g., front-row seating, speech therapy

Why adenoidectomy with grommet insertion is NOT preferred:

·         Grommets treat conductive hearing loss (e.g., otitis media with effusion)

·         They act on the middle ear, not the cochlea

·         Hence, no benefit in SNHL

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrial matrix is the site for several major metabolic pathways, including the TCA (Krebs) cycle and beta-oxidation. Citrate synthase is a key TCA cycle enzyme located within the matrix that catalyzes the condensation of oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA to form citrate. Monoamine oxidase (Option B) is an enzyme located on the outer mitochondrial membrane. ATP synthase (Option C) is a complex structure embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, although its catalytic head projects into the matrix. Catalase (Option D) is primarily located in peroxisomes, where it breaks down hydrogen peroxide, not the mitochondria. Other matrix enzymes include pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and those of the urea cycle (CPS-I and ornithine transcarbamoylase). Sub-cellular localization of enzymes is essential for coordinating metabolic flux; the matrix provides the concentrated environment necessary for the efficient cycling of the TCA pathway and the generation of reduced electron carriers for the electron transport chain

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with abdominal discomfort and passage of motile segments in his stool after attending a party where he consumed multiple pork dishes. Over the next few weeks, he develops new-onset seizures and intermittent headaches. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cercosis

Understand that Taenia solium can cause two distinct diseases depending on the infective stage. Ingestion of cysticerci in undercooked pork leads to intestinal taeniasis, whereas ingestion of T. solium eggs (fecal–oral transmission or autoinfection) results in cysticercosis. Larval cysts in the brain cause neurocysticercosis, the most common parasitic cause of new-onset seizures in adults.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cysticercosis: ✔ Correct. New-onset seizures and headache are characteristic of neurocysticercosis, caused by larval cysts of T. solium.
• B. Abdominal taeniasis: Causes passage of motile proglottids and mild abdominal discomfort but does not cause seizures.
• C. Meningoencephalitis: May present with fever and altered sensorium but does not explain the history of tapeworm infection and passage of proglottids.
• D. Brain tumor: Can cause seizures but does not account for the parasitic exposure and intestinal tapeworm infection.

| Disease | Infective Stage | Clinical Manifestation

| ------- | --------------- | ----------------------

| Taeniasis | Cysticerci in undercooked pork | Intestinal infection, passage of proglottids

| Cysticercosis | Eggs of Taenia solium | Larval cysts in tissues (brain, eye, muscle); neurocysticercosis → seizures

Exam Tip:

• Eating pork → Taeniasis (adult worm).
• Swallowing eggs (fecal–oral/autoinfection) → Cysticercosis (larval disease).
• Neurocysticercosis is the leading parasitic cause of epilepsy worldwide.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the clinic with the lesion given in the image. He had a traumatic injury to the chest one year ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Keloid

The image showing a large area of scar tissue is suggestive of a keloid.

A keloid refers to excess accumulation of collagen at the scar site with growth of the scar tissue beyond the boundaries of the original wound. It does not regress. The patient's history of traumatic injury to the chest one year ago, followed by the development of an expanding scar, is suggestive of a keloid. The keloid is often glossy in appearance and rubbery in texture. They are composed of thick bundles of collagen.

Treatment of keloids usually involves intralesional injections of triamcinolone. Multiple doses are required at intervals over several weeks and may result in flattening but rarely does the wound narrow.

Option A: A hemangioma is a vascular tumor that arises from the endothelium. They typically present as red or pinkish macules or raised lesions.

Option B: Hypertrophic scars, unlike keloids, remain within the boundaries of the original wound and tend to regress over time. Since this scar has failed to regress over 1 year and has grown beyond the original wound margins, it is more likely to be a keloid.

Option D: Neurofibromas are benign tumors arising from Schwann cells. They usually present as soft, flesh-colored nodules, often in association with neurofibromatosis type 1, a genetic disorder. The patient's history of chest trauma and the appearance of the lesion make neurofibroma an unlikely diagnosis in this case.
questions.learning: Keloid — The image showing a large area of scar tissue is suggestive of a keloid. A keloid refers to excess accumulation of collagen at the scar site with growth of the scar tissue beyond the boundaries of the original wound.

questions.text: Which of the following is not used in the assessment of body fat?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breslow index

Breslow's staging is used for the staging of malignant melanoma, not for the assessment of body fat.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate next step in the management of a 40-year-old man who presents with generalized abdominal pain, has a known history of peptic ulcer disease, and exhibits abdominal rigidity on examination, in light of the findings shown on the abdominal X-ray?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the "classic triad" of hollow viscus perforation: history of peptic ulcer disease, sudden widespread abdominal pain with rigidity (peritonitis), and radiographic evidence of pneumoperitoneum (air under the diaphragm). This represents a surgical emergency. The appropriate next step is urgent surgical exploration (laparotomy or laparoscopy) to identify and repair the perforation. Antibiotics and NPO (Option A) are part of the initial resuscitation but are not definitive treatment. Upper GI endoscopy (Option B) is strictly contraindicated in suspected perforation because the air used to distend the bowel would worsen the pneumoperitoneum and spill more contents into the cavity. A CT abdomen (Option D) is highly sensitive for air but is unnecessary if the plain X-ray already confirms the diagnosis. Delay in surgical intervention significantly increases mortality from septic shock. Therefore, immediate surgical repair is the life-saving priority
questions.learning: The patient presents with the "classic triad" of hollow viscus perforation: history of peptic ulcer disease, sudden widespread abdominal pain with rigidity (peritonitis), and radiographic evidence of pneumoperitoneum (air under the diaphragm).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary PPH? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Placenta previa

Secondary postpartum hemorrhage (secondary PPH) is excessive vaginal bleeding occurring:

• After 24 hours postpartum
• Up to 6 weeks after delivery

Common causes include:

• Retained placental tissue or retained cotyledon
• Endometritis
• Placental polyp
• Subinvolution of the placental site

Placenta previa is a cause of antepartum hemorrhage, not secondary postpartum hemorrhage.

Important concepts:

• Retained products prevent proper uterine contraction and involution
• Infection causes uterine inflammation and delayed healing
• Placental polyp refers to retained placental tissue forming a vascular mass

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the active principle of the poison shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bhilawanol

The given image shows the seeds of Semecarpus anacardium, and its active principles are bhilawanol and semicarpol. Common names are marking nut, bhilwan, bibva, bhela, and oriental cashew.

The image shows black, heart-shaped seeds with hard rinds that identify them as seeds of S. anacardium. Within the fruit is a thick fleshy pericarp that yields the active principle, which is a brown oily resinous fluid called bhilawanol.

The juice when applied locally to the skin produces irritation, painful blisters, itching, and eczematous eruption. The seeds are used to produce an artificial bruise. Symptoms such as pain, fever, and painful passage of brownish urine may be seen.

A large dose taken orally can produce blisters in the mouth and throat, with gastroenteritis. It also produces dyspnea, cyanosis, tachycardia, coma, and death. The fatal period is 12 to 24 hours.

Medicolegal importance is the use of the juice by malingerers to fabricate wounds. Instilled in the eyes it can cause conjunctivitis or ophthalmia due to its local irritant effect.

Other options:

Option A: Ricin is the active principle of Ricinus communis. It is a toxalbumin or phytotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis by affecting the ribosomal RNA polymerase. The seeds are flat to oval-shaped and have dark brown markings (shown below). It is a chemical warfare agent.

Option C: Abrin is the active principle of Abrus precatorius. The seeds are egg-shaped, scarlet in color, and have a black spot at one end (shown below). On ingestion, it causes gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea, rectal bleeding, tachycardia, and circulatory collapse. Injecting the active substance can mimic viperine snakebite. Rarely, it may lead to tetanic convulsions.

The seeds of A. precatorius are decocted and mixed with datura, opium, onion, spirit, and water to form a paste. From this, small sharp needles called suis are made. They are used for hunting animals and even for homicide purposes.

Option D: Calotropin is one of the active principles of Calotropis. The toxic parts of the plant are the stem, branches, leaves, and milky white latex (Madar juice). When applied locally, it can mimic bruises, and form pustules and vesicles. In the eyes, it can lead to conjunctivitis. On ingestion, it causes abdominal pain, vomiting, mydriasis, and tetanic convulsions and can eventually lead to collapse and death.

It is shown in the image below.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman develops postpartum hemorrhage after a normal delivery, and surgical ligation of an artery is performed to control the bleeding. Following the procedure, she complains of pain beneath the gluteal region. Which artery was most likely ligated during the management of her condition?
questions.explanation: Ligation of the internal iliac (hypogastric) artery is a life-saving surgical procedure used to control intractable postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) when other measures have failed. The internal iliac artery provides the primary blood supply to the pelvic organs, including the uterus. However, it also gives rise to several extrapelvic branches, including the "superior and inferior gluteal arteries". Ligation of the main internal iliac trunk significantly reduces the pulse pressure in the uterus but can also result in ischemia or reduced perfusion to the gluteal muscles. This explains the patient's subsequent complaint of "pain under her gluteus muscle". Ligation of the uterine artery (Option A) specifically targets the uterus and would not affect the gluteal region. Options B and C are distal branches; while their ligation would cause localized pain, they are not standardly ligated for PPH. Understanding the pelvic vascular anatomy is crucial for surgeons, as internal iliac ligation is effective due to the rich collateral circulation that eventually restores pelvic perfusion
questions.learning: Ligation of the internal iliac (hypogastric) artery is a life-saving surgical procedure used to control intractable postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) when other measures have failed.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly diabetic patient presented with complaints of blurring of vision. He underwent a cataract surgery 1 month ago. The patient's fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed a flower-petal appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystoid macular edema

The given scenario of a diabetic patient with the blurring of vision and an FFA showing a flower petal pattern (petaloid appearance) is suggestive of cystoid macular edema (CME). It occurs due to the accumulation of dye in the macular region.

CME is defined as a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform (Henle's layer) and an inner nuclear layer of the retina. This results in the formation of cyst-like cavities around the foveola. It occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Common causes of CME include uveitis, previous cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa.

Patients may complain of blurring, distortion, and micropsia. In clinically established cases, the macula will show a 'honeycomb' appearance on ophthalmoscopy due to multiple cystoid spaces. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and foveal depression. In advanced cases, a lamellar macular hole may develop.

Treatment includes topical anti-prostaglandins (ketorolac), steroids, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (oral acetazolamide), and managing the causative factor.

Given below is the FFA image showing the classic flower-petal appearance, followed by an OCT image showing intraretinal cystoid spaces in CME:

Other options:

Option A: Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of the macular region neurosensory retina with/without retinal pigment epithelium detachment. Patients complain of sudden onset painless loss of vision, micropsia, and metamorphopsia. FFA shows two patterns of leakage, ink-blot pattern and smoke-stick pattern. OCT image of central serous retinopathy is seen below which neurosensory retinal detachment and accompanying small detachments of the retinal pigment epithelium.

Option B: Macular hole is a partial or full-thickness hole in the neurosensory retina of the foveal region. Causes include trauma, CME, or idiopathic. There is a decrease in vision, typically around 6/60 for full-thickness holes. FFA shows early foveal hyperfluorescene without a leak.

OCT image of the macular hole is seen below which shows a full-thickness hole in the foveal retina.

Option D: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is bilateral disease affecting people who are above 50 years of age. It can be exudative or non-exudative types. There can be a gradual or sudden loss of vision depending on the type of AMD. Drusens (yellowish-white elevated spots caused by extracellular deposits in the macular region) of various types can be noted. FFA shows punctate hyperfluorescence due to the drusen.

OCT and FFA image of drusens is shown below:

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following curves represents gamma-globin chain production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orange curve

In the given image, the Orange curve represents the gamma-globin chain production. Gamma globin chain is produced in the fetal period and drops to undetectable levels 6 months postpartum which is the pattern represented by the Orange curve.

Hemoglobin in blood has different variants throughout life, in different proportions. The type of hemoglobin essentially depends on the combination of globin chains. Adult hemoglobin is made of 2 alpha and 2 beta chains, whereas fetal hemoglobin is made of 2 alpha and 2 gamma-globin chains. Other combinations of chains can be found in embryonic hemoglobin.

Here,

• Gamma chain - Orange curve
• Alpha chain - Red curve
• Beta chain - Green curve
• Epsilon chain - Black curve
• Delta chain - Blue curve

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with a history of a road traffic accident. On examination his vitals are stable, but he could not speak. He had no other neurological findings, had normal handwriting skills, and could understand what was being asked of him to which he responds by nodding. Where could be the lesion for this clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Broca's area

Broca’s area is concerned with word formation and is the most likely area to be involved as only speech production is affected here and all other examinating findings are normal.

Broca’s area is in the inferior frontal lobe.

Broca area processes the information received from Wernicke area into a detailed and coordinated pattern for vocalization and then projects the pattern via a speech articulation area in the insula to the motor cortex. This then initiates the appropriate movements of the lips, tongue, and larynx to produce speech.

The probable sequence of events that occurs when a subject names a visual object is shown in the figure and flowchart.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with diabetes presents with progressively worsening pain in his calf. The pain predominantly affects the distal parts of the limb, such as the toes and feet, and is aggravated by movement and pressure. He reports that the pain intensifies when lying down or elevating the leg, but is relieved when he hangs the affected leg down, even preferring to sleep in a seated position for relief. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms are pathognomonic for Ischemic Rest Pain, a severe stage of peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Rest pain classically involves the distal foot and toes and is worsened by lying flat or elevating the limb, as gravity no longer assists the restricted arterial flow. The patient's preference to sleep in a seated position with the leg hanging down utilizes gravity to increase perfusion pressure, which provides characteristic relief. Sciatica (Option B) involves shooting pain down the back of the leg. Neurological claudication (Option C) is related to spinal stenosis and is relieved by leaning forward. Venous claudication (Option D) is worsened by standing or dependency (hanging the leg down) and relieved by elevation. Because this patient’s pain is specifically relieved by dependency and occurs at rest, it indicates critical limb ischemia. Therefore, "Rest pain" is the definitive clinical cause of his symptoms

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman diagnosed with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome presented to the casualty with severe abdominal pain. She was prescribed a drug that exerts a direct spasmolytic effect on the smooth muscles of the gastrointestinal tract. Which drug could it be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dicyclomine

Dicyclomine is a weak muscarinic receptor antagonist with non-specific direct spasmolytic effects on the smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract.

Other options:

Option B: Scopolamine exerts spasmolytic activity indirectly through its antimuscarinic action. It is not preferred due to its adverse effects like drowsiness, dryness, and blurred vision.

Option C and D: Galantamine and rivastigmine are central cholinesterase inhibitors and do not possess spasmolytic activity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An X ray was taken which showed dilated bowel loops as given in the image below. Identify the segment involved.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Jejunum

The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction where the involved segment is the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel) which is characteristic of jejunal involvement. The gas bubbles trapped between the valvulae connivente give a string of beads appearance.

Radiological features of bowel obstruction

• Small bowel - The involved dilated segments are straight and usually centrally located.
• Jejunum - It is characterized by the presence of valvulae connivente with gas bubbles trapped between them. This gives a string of beads/ ladder effect.
• Ileum - The distal ileal obstruction is usually described as featureless.
• Caecum - A rounded gas shadow in the right iliac fossa is suggestive of caecal obstruction.
• Large bowel - The presence of haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction. Haustral folds are irregular and do not cross the entire diameter of the bowel. These are absent in the caecum.

In intestinal obstruction, fluid levels appear as the obstruction progresses. When the fluid levels are prominent, it indicates that the obstruction is advanced. The number of fluid levels also increases if the lesion is more distal.

The most reliable criterion for the diagnosis of small bowel obstruction is the transition zone, seen on CT imaging. It identifies a definite point of obstruction. Dilated small bowel loops are seen proximal to the site of obstruction and collapsed loops are seen distal to the obstruction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency after he suddenly became unconscious while working in the field. On examination, his temperature was 105 degrees Fahrenheit and his skin turgor was decreased. Which of the following would not be seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sweating

The given clinical vignette in a patient with signs of dehydration and a body temperature of 105°F is highly suggestive of heatstroke. Sweating would not be seen in a patient with heatstroke.

The body has various mechanisms to maintain body temperature within a range of 36–37°C. When the body temperature is elevated by exposure to high environmental temperatures or physical exertion, the central control area in the medial preoptic and anterior hypothalamic nuclei is activated. This engages the autonomic pathways that promote sweating and cutaneous vasodilation, causing the heat to dissipate and bring the body to normal temperature.

Heatstroke occurs due to the failure of the heat regulation center of the hypothalamus. The person fails to lose heat by cutaneous circulation and sweating. It is likely to develop when the body temperature rises to a range of 105°F to 108°F. The predisposing factors include high temperature, increased humidity, minor infections, old age, and physical activity.

It is a medical emergency that leads to homeostatic imbalance. The symptoms include dizziness, abdominal distress, vomiting, delirium, and eventually leading to loss of consciousness. On examination, the skin is dry, hot, and flushed, with a complete absence of sweating (anhidrosis). Other signs seen in heat stroke are tachycardia, Kussmaul-type rapid deep breathing (tachypnea), hypotension, cardiac failure, dizziness, muscle cramping, confusion, and seizures.

Heatstroke can cause damage to multiple organ systems, including the brain, kidneys, and liver, which can lead to life-threatening complications. It is essential to initiate rapid cooling and supportive care measures to prevent permanent injury or death. The cooling methods used to treat heatstroke include:

• Cold water immersion: The patient is immersed in a tub of cold water, which is the most effective way to lower body temperature.
• Evaporative cooling: The patient's body is sprayed with water while fans blow air over the body to help facilitate evaporation and cooling.
• Applying cold packs: Applying ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin can help cool the body by targeting areas where large blood vessels are located close to the skin surface.
• Misting and fanning: Spraying the patient with cool water and using a fan to circulate air can help promote evaporative cooling.

Preventive measures for heatstroke include staying hydrated, taking regular breaks in shaded areas, and avoiding strenuous activities during the hottest part of the day.

Other Options

• Option A: Tachypnea - Rapid, deep breathing (Kussmaul breathing) can be seen in heatstroke as the body tries to eliminate excess heat through increased respiratory rate.
• Option B: Hypotension - Dehydration and vasodilation in an attempt to dissipate heat can result in hypotension in heatstroke patients.
• Option D: Red hot skin - Heatstroke patients often present with hot, flushed skin as a result of increased blood flow to the skin surface and the body's inability to dissipate heat effectively.
questions.learning: Sweating — The given clinical vignette in a patient with signs of dehydration and a body temperature of 105°F is highly suggestive of heatstroke. Sweating would not be seen in a patient with heatstroke.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: A 14-year boy came with chronic diarrhoea and malnutrition. The physician suspected celiac disease. Which of the following are correct in his diagnostic workup? 1. Presence of IgA antiendomysial antibody 2. Absence of reduced height of villi on intestinal biopsy 3. Increased lymphocytes in lamina propria in small intestine biopsy 4. Absence of tTG antibody in serum Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

In celiac disease, the classic diagnostic triad involves serology, biopsy findings, and clinical correlation:

• 1. Presence of IgA anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) ✔️: This is one of the most specific serological markers for celiac disease (along with tTG-IgA), and its presence strongly supports the diagnosis.
• 2. Absence of reduced height of villi on intestinal biopsy ✔️: In celiac disease, the small intestinal biopsy classically shows villous atrophy (blunting/flattening), which is a hallmark of the disease along with crypt hyperplasia. This forms part of the modified Marsh classification used to grade severity.
• 3. Increased intraepithelial and lamina propria lymphocytes in small intestine biopsy ✔️: Lymphocytic infiltration of the lamina propria (and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) is a classic histological feature of celiac disease, reflecting the immune-mediated damage to the mucosa.
• 4. Absence of tTG antibody (Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA) in serum ✘: This is actually the first-line, most sensitive serological test for celiac disease. Its absence would argue against, not support, the diagnosis — so this statement is incorrect for a case where celiac disease is being worked up and confirmed.

Summary of workup for celiac disease:

• Serology: tTG-IgA (first-line), EMA-IgA (highly specific, used for confirmation), with total IgA levels checked to rule out IgA deficiency
• Duodenal biopsy: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and lamina propria lymphocytic/plasma cell infiltration (Marsh classification)
• Clinical: Symptoms improve on gluten-free diet (supports diagnosis)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Feed forward control system is employed during the regulation of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Temperature

Feed forward control system is employed during regulation of temperature.

Feed forward control

There is a control system in our body when no stimulus is required but still the system anticipates and makes corrective changes.

Such a system is called Feed forward or Anticipatory or Adaptive Control.

Examples include

• Temperature control – Thermoregulatory responses are initiated by hypothalamus BEFORE the changes in environmental temperature have succeeded in changing the body’s core body temperature
• Cephalic phase of gastric secretion- Just thinking about food increases gastric acid production
• Thinking about exercise itself increases heart rate & respiratory rate
• Role of cerebellum in motor coordination

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presented with choking episodes after ingestion of a fish bone. The fishbone was impacted at the T4 level in the oesophagus. Which is the most likely site of obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The most likely site of obstruction in the case of a fishbone impacted at the T4 level is the arch of the aorta.

Normally, the oesophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* At the pharyngo-oesophageal junction (C6)—15 cm from the upper incisors.

* At the crossing of the arch of the aorta (T4)—25 cm from the upper incisors.

* Where it pierces the diaphragm (T10)—40 cm from the upper incisors.

Foreign bodies in the oesophagus can be held up at these constrictions.

Acute dysphagia is common with foreign body obstruction. They might also experience odynophagia, regurgitation of food, neck pain, or chest pain. Esophageal obstruction can cause complications such as esophageal perforation and lung aspiration.

When impaction of a foreign body occurs in an adult esophagus, it usually occurs in the presence of underlying structural abnormalities (such as a web or stricture), functional abnormalities resulting from abnormal esophageal peristalsis, or when the swallowed object is too large to navigate the anatomic constrictions of the normal esophagus. The two most common causes are eosinophilic oesophagitis and Schatzki rings. Esophageal webs, tracheo-oesophageal fistula/esophageal atresia (TOF/OA), and peptic strictures are conditions that predispose to food bolus obstructions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a complaint of choking due to peanut ingestion. On arrival, the child is found to be unresponsive. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chest compressions

In a child with foreign body airway obstruction (e.g., peanut) who becomes unresponsive, the next step is to start chest compressions (CPR).

• Once the child is unconscious, management shifts from choking maneuvers to CPR protocol
• Chest compressions help dislodge the foreign body by generating artificial airflow and also maintain circulation

Stepwise approach

• Conscious child (<1 yr): Back slaps + chest thrusts
• Conscious child (>1 yr): Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver)
• Unconscious child (any age):

→ Start chest compressions immediately

→ Open airway and look for visible object (remove if seen)

→ Attempt ventilation

Why not other options:

• A) Back slaps: Only for conscious infants
• B) Abdominal thrusts: Only for conscious children >1 yr
• C) Endotracheal intubation: Not the immediate first step; attempted after initiating CPR if trained
questions.learning: Chest compressions — In a child with foreign body airway obstruction (e.g., peanut) who becomes unresponsive, the next step is to start chest compressions (CPR). • Once the child is unconscious, management shifts from choking maneuvers to CPR protocol •…

Village Health Nutrition Day awareness program is conducted at Anganwadi centers once every month. questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which of the following is the best investigation for foreign body localization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT

CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization.

The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel. While chipping stone with an iron chisel, the chip of the iron chisel is more likely to enter the eye than the stone. A foreign body entering the eye may cause damage by:

* mechanical effects

* introduction of infection

* reacting with the intraocular tissues

Anteroposterior and lateral view X-rays are recommended for locating an IOFB as most foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Ultrasonographic localization can tell the position of even non-radiopaque foreign bodies. CT scan is the best method of IOFB localization.

MRI is contraindicated for metallic IOFB.MRI can be detrimental for a patient with a history of an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) after cutting stone with a hammer and chisel. It can cause further damage by producing movements of the foreign body if it is magnetic. The use of MRI is contraindicated for metallic (iron) foreign bodies and is not recommended as a screening procedure.

Management: A foreign body should always be removed unless:

* it is inert and probably sterile

* little damage has been done to vision

* the process of removal will destroy sight

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and cause atrophy.

Clinical features:

* Iris: first stained greenish and later turns reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.
questions.learning: CT CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization. The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient developed the following deformity, after overhead (weight-lifting) exercises. Which of the following muscle is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serratus anterior

The image shows winging of the scapula which is pulled upwards and towards the spine. This is due to paralysis of the serratus anterior which is supplied by the long thoracic nerve.

When the patient is asked to push against a wall with both hands, the medial border of the scapula on the affected side becomes prominent and this is known as ‘winging of the scapula.’

Scapular winging is almost always caused by damage to one of three nerves that control muscles in your arms, back, and neck:

* The long thoracic nerve, which controls the serratus anterior muscle

* The dorsal scapular nerve, which controls the rhomboid muscles

* The spinal accessory nerve, which controls the trapezius muscle

The muscles of the back and their innervation are:

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young girl had thigh swelling with discharging sinus from which a bony fragment came out. The parents were concerned about what it was and asked the doctor. What is the term used for it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sequestrum

A piece of dead bone is called sequestrum.

Sequestrum acts as the nidus of infection in chronic osteomyelitis.

Sequestrum is a piece of dead bone. It is formed when a fragment of bone gets separated from the healthy bone due to necrosis. It varies in size from a spicule to a large fragment. This sequestrum acts as a nidus for infection. It is the most common cause of non-healing in chronic osteomyelitis.

The involucrum is the dense new sclerotic bone surrounding the sequestrum. It is formed from deep layers of stripped periosteum.

Cloacae are the perforations in the involucrum. Pus and tiny spicules of bone may be discharged through them.

Sinus tract is formed when the abscess from the infected bone drains out through the skin.
questions.learning: Sequestrum — A piece of dead bone is called sequestrum. Sequestrum acts as the nidus of infection in chronic osteomyelitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is best method to survey the injection practices of health workers?
options: Direct observation with a structured checklist
In-depth interview with the healthcare provider
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Direct observation with a structured checklist

Direct observation with a structured checklist is the best method to survey the injection practices of health workers.

Checklist of practices for assessment or evaluation include:-

• In order not to harm the patient, each procedure should be administered with a new sterile single-use device, using the right medication, vaccine or fluid for infusion.
• In order not to expose the provider to any avoidable risk, in general, any needles used during a procedure should be placed in a puncture-proof closed container immediately after use without recapping. In addition, providers of these procedures should be fully vaccinated against Hepatitis-B.
•  In order that any waste produced during the performance of a procedure does not become a hazard for other people, used sharps waste and infectious non-sharps waste should be safely managed.
questions.learning: Direct observation with a structured checklist Direct observation with a structured checklist is the best method to survey the injection practices of health workers.

questions.text: A patient with a road traffic accident presented to the emergency room and requires a large amount of fluids to be transfused. Which of the following IV cannula is preferred?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Grey

Grey coloured IV cannula is required for this patient in order to transfuse large amount of fluids.

The ATLS 10th edition guidelines state that 2 cannulae of atleast 18G should be used to gain vascular access in trauma patients. In this scenario requiring large fluid transfusions, the grey (16G) cannula would be preferable to the green (18G) cannula due to the higher flow rate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a longitudinal observational and analytical study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort Study

Cohort study is an example of a longitudinal observational and analytical study.

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study. A well-designed cohort study is considered the most reliable means of showing an association between a cause or suspected risk factor and subsequent disease (or effect).

Types of epidemiological studies:

• Observational studies - allow nature to take its course, the investigator measures but does not intervene.

1. Descriptive studies - limited to the description of the occurrence of a disease in a population- (hypothesis formulation).
2. Analytical studies - go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables- (hypothesis testing).

• Ecological studies
• Cross-sectional studies
• Case-control studies
• Cohort studies

• Experimental studies or intervention studies involve an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease and are similar in design to experiments in other sciences- (hypothesis confirmation).

1. Randomized controlled trials
2. Field trials
3. Community trials

Other options:

Option A: Although case-control studies are inherently analytical, they are not longitudinal. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.

Option C: A randomized control trial is an experimental study in which an intervention is given to a group of patients participating in the study and compared to another group of patients with similar characteristics who are not given that intervention to be studied. It uses patients as the unit of study.

Option D: An ecological study is a type of analytical study that analyzes the health status and its relation with other variables. It is also called a correlational study, and it uses the population as a unit of study. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.
questions.learning: Cohort Study Cohort study is an example of a longitudinal observational and analytical study. A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs restrict the availability of thymidylate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-fluorouracil

5-FU acts during the S phase of the cell cycle inhibiting DNA synthesis by restricting the availability of thymidylate.

5-FU acts via two different pathways depending on its dose: G1- S-phase cell cycle arrest and apoptosis at a higher dose and G2-M-phase cell cycle arrest at a low dose.

5-FU:

* Converted in the body to the corresponding nucleotide 5-deoxyuridine monophosphate, which forms a covalent ternary complex with methyl-THFA and thymidylate synthase, resulting in the irreversible inhibition of thymidylate synthase.

* Failure of DNA synthesis occurs due to the non-availability of thymidylate.

* Inhibition of TS by 5-FU depends on THFA, infusion of leucovorin will enhance the efficacy of this drug. Cisplatin and oxaliplatin also synergize with this drug.

* Rapidly dividing cells are most commonly affected, but resting cells are also affected.

* Used as an anticancer drug for many solid cancers such as the colon, rectum, stomach, pancreas, liver, urinary bladder, head, and neck. Topical preparations are used in BCC and actinic keratosis.

* Toxicity includes myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Peripheral neuropathy may also occur.

Note:

Monoclonal antibodies recognize the extracellular domain of the EGFR, inhibit ligand-induced signaling, and can elicit an immune response. Cetuximab is a recombinant, chimeric human/mouse IgG1 antibody that binds to EGFR and prevents ligand-dependent signaling and receptor dimerization, thereby blocking cell growth and survival signals. It is used to treat patients with metastatic colon cancers and Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma(HNSCC)

Other options:

Option A: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and is used in the treatment of lymhomas.

Option B: Cisplatin induces its cytotoxic properties through binding to nuclear DNA and subsequent interference with normal transcription, and/or DNA replication mechanisms.

Option D: Methotrexate inhibits purine and pyrimidine synthesis, which accounts for its efficacy in the therapy of cancer as well as for some of its toxicities.  The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman with a known history of epilepsy requires treatment for a bacterial infection. To minimize the risk of seizure provocation, which antimicrobial agent would be the safest choice?
questions.explanation: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., Erythromycin, Azithromycin) generally have the lowest risk of central nervous system toxicity and are considered safe for patients with epilepsy. In contrast, several other antibiotic classes are known to lower the seizure threshold. Beta-lactams (Option A), particularly penicillins and carbapenems like Imipenem, act as GABA antagonists and can provoke seizures, especially in patients with pre-existing epilepsy or renal failure. Quinolones (Option B), such as ciprofloxacin, also inhibit GABA binding and can trigger convulsions. Isoniazid (Option D) interferes with the production of GABA (an inhibitory neurotransmitter) by depleting Vitamin B6, which is a known cause of drug-induced seizures. Therefore, for a patient with a known history of epilepsy, macrolides are the safest choice among the provided options to avoid precipitating a seizure event. Clinicians must always cross-check antibiotic choices with seizure risk in neurologically vulnerable patients
questions.learning: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., Erythromycin, Azithromycin) generally have the lowest risk of central nervous system toxicity and are considered safe for patients with epilepsy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is most responsible for the resting membrane potential (RMP):
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. K+

Resting membrane potential is primarily determined by potassium permeability across the cell membrane. High resting K⁺ conductance through leak channels allows outward diffusion, making the inside negative. The membrane potential closely approximates the K⁺ equilibrium potential. Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ have minimal resting permeability compared to K⁺.

High intracellular K⁺

↓

K⁺ diffuses out via leak channels

↓

Loss of positive charge from inside

↓

Cell interior becomes negative

↓

Electrical gradient opposes further K⁺ loss

↓

Equilibrium reached → Resting membrane potential
questions.learning: K+ Resting membrane potential is primarily determined by potassium permeability across the cell membrane. High resting K⁺ conductance through leak channels allows outward diffusion, making the inside negative.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A family consuming a diet mainly consisting of rice and pulses develops symptoms of muscle weakness and movement disorders. Which of the following should be given as a prophylactic measure in this situation?
questions.explanation: A diet consisting predominantly of polished rice and pulses is often deficient in thiamine (Vitamin B1). The thiamine is concentrated in the aleurone layer of the cereal, which is removed during the polishing process. Deficiency leads to beriberi; specifically, "dry beriberi" presents with muscle weakness, paresthesia, loss of reflexes, and peripheral neuritis. Calcium deficiency (Option A) would cause bone issues or tetany rather than isolated neurogenic weakness. Vitamin D deficiency (Option C) leads to rickets or osteomalacia. Iron deficiency (Option D) causes microcytic anemia, characterized by pallor and fatigue rather than the described neurological weakness pattern. Therefore, thiamine supplementation is the appropriate prophylactic measure to prevent the neuropathy associated with unsupplemented, polished grain diets
questions.learning: A diet consisting predominantly of polished rice and pulses is often deficient in thiamine (Vitamin B1). The thiamine is concentrated in the aleurone layer of the cereal, which is removed during the polishing process.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a field visit to assess the training of an ANM on safe immunization practices, you observe that she uses a syringe with needle, a vaccine vial, and a cotton swab. After completing the immunization, which of the following statements correctly describes the appropriate biomedical waste disposal?
options: The syringe with the needle should be disposed of in a black translucent container
The used vaccine vial should be discarded in a blue bag
A used cotton swab should be discarded in a red bag
The needle should be bent and thrown in a red bag
questions.explanation: According to the current Biomedical Waste Management (BMWM) rules, glass waste, such as used or expired vaccine vials and ampoules, must be discarded in blue-marked puncture-proof containers or blue bags for proper treatment or recycling. Sharps, including syringes with fixed needles, must be placed in white, translucent, puncture-proof containers. Bending or breaking needles (Option D) is strictly prohibited as it significantly increases the risk of needle-stick injuries. Contaminated cotton swabs (Option C) are classified as infectious waste and should be disposed of in yellow bags for incineration. Red bags are reserved for contaminated but recyclable plastic waste, such as IV sets, catheters, and syringes without needles. Black containers (Option A) are typically used for general non-infectious waste or specific chemical waste, not sharps. Therefore, the instruction to place the glass vaccine vial in a blue container is the only correct disposal statement provided
questions.learning: According to the current Biomedical Waste Management (BMWM) rules, glass waste, such as used or expired vaccine vials and ampoules, must be discarded in blue-marked puncture-proof containers or blue bags for proper treatment or recycling.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy complains of multiple episodes of acute severe pain in his fingers and toes which resolves on its own for the past 1 year. Which of the following conditions is he most likely suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sickle cell anemia

The features of multiple episodes of acute severe pain in fingers and toes with spontaneous resolution are suggestive of dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome), which usually occurs in sickle cell anemia.

The sickled RBCs have a sticking tendency towards the endothelium of the small venules. These abnormalities provoke unpredictable episodes of vaso-occlusion. Dactylitis is characterized by severe pain affecting the bones of the hands, feet, or both. It is often the first symptom of sickle cell anemia in children.

Treatment - Administration of patient-controlled analgesia or a frequent fixed dose of opioids with rescue doses for breakthrough pain are preferred with frequent monitoring during the initial 48-72 hrs to prevent unexpected death due to arrhythmias or pulmonary embolism.

Other manifestations include:

• Splenic autoinfarction - repeated splenic microinfarcts
• Acute splenic sequestration - venous obstruction, needing emergency transfusion/splenectomy
• Painful ischemic crises - vaso-occlusion in connective and musculoskeletal tissue
• Renal papillary necrosis leading to isosthenuria
• Cerebrovascular strokes
• Chronic lower leg ulcers
• Priapism in males

α-thalassemia (Option A) and β-thalassemia (Option B) are characterized by pallor, jaundice, growth failure, hepatosplenomegaly, characteristic thalassemic facies, and hair-on-end appearance of the skull.

Option D: Von Willebrand Disease is characterized by predominantly mucosal bleeding symptoms like excessive bruising and epistaxis.
questions.learning: Sickle cell anemia — The features of multiple episodes of acute severe pain in fingers and toes with spontaneous resolution are suggestive of dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome), which usually occurs in sickle cell anemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In ophthalmic procedures, a specific dye is used to enhance the visualization of structures within the anterior chamber of the eye. Which dye is employed for staining the anterior chamber?
questions.explanation: In modern ophthalmic microsurgery, Trypan blue is the standard dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens during cataract surgery (specifically for continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis). By providing a sharp contrast, it allows the surgeon to clearly see the edges of the capsule, which is especially vital in cases of dense ("white") cataracts where the red reflex is absent. It is also used to stain the donor corneal tissue in endothelial keratoplasty. Brilliant blue (Option B) is primarily used to stain the internal limiting membrane during vitreoretinal surgery. Fluorescein (Option C, often greenish when viewed with cobalt blue light) is used for assessing corneal ulcers and tear film. Lissamine green (Option D) is used to stain devitalized conjunctival cells in dry eye diagnostics. Trypan blue is non-toxic to the corneal endothelium when used appropriately. Its introduction has significantly improved the safety and predictability of complex cataract procedures by providing superior intraoperative visualization of clear ocular structures
questions.learning: In modern ophthalmic microsurgery, Trypan blue is the standard dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens during cataract surgery (specifically for continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Menkes disease (kinky hair syndrome) results from a defect in the metabolism of which substance?
questions.explanation: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7A gene, which encodes a copper-transporting protein. This mutation results in impaired copper absorption from the intestines and its defective distribution to various tissues. Consequently, patients suffer from severe copper deficiency, which impacts the function of essential copper-dependent enzymes like lysyl oxidase and tyrosinase. Clinical hallmarks include sparse, steely, or "kinky" hair, failure to thrive, and progressive neurological deterioration. Disturbance in zinc metabolism (Option A) leads to acrodermatitis enteropathica. Iron metabolism defects (Option C) cause conditions like hemochromatosis or sideroblastic anemia. Magnesium deficiency (Option D) is typically an electrolyte imbalance rather than a primary genetic metabolic syndrome. Because the underlying pathology of Menkes syndrome is specifically the inability of cells to transport copper effectively, copper is the responsible metabolic element
questions.learning: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7A gene, which encodes a copper-transporting protein. This mutation results in impaired copper absorption from the intestines and its defective distribution to various tissues.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who stopped consuming alcohol three days ago and subsequently developed irritability, disorientation, paranoid delusions, agitation, visual hallucinations, and altered consciousness?
questions.explanation: Delirium Tremens (DT) is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically occurring 48 to 96 hours (roughly 3 days) after the last drink. The clinical hallmarks perfectly match this scenario: clouding of consciousness (disorientation), autonomic hyperactivity (agitation, irritability), and prominent visual hallucinations (often described as "pink elephants" or insects). Paranoid delusions are also common. Wernicke's encephalopathy (Option B) is characterized by the triad of ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and confusion due to thiamine deficiency. Korsakoff psychosis (Option C) involves chronic amnesia and confabulation. Alcohol-induced psychosis (Option D) usually involves hallucinations in a clear sensorium, unlike the disorientation seen here. Because the symptoms are hyperacute, occur exactly on day 3 of cessation, and involve impaired consciousness with hallucinations, Delirium Tremens is the definitive diagnosis. It is a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Parathyroid gland post surgery is commonly transferred to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brachioradialis

The parathyroid is commonly transferred to the brachioradialis muscle post-surgery. This will facilitate easy removal if there is disease recurrence after surgery.

Parathyroidectomy is indicated in:

1. Symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT):
2. Asymptomatic primary HPT with:

• raise in serum calcium >1mg/dl of the normal range
• >400 mg urinary calcium in 24-hour urine test
• < -2.5 Z-score of bone mineral density
• Age <50yr and failed medical treatment

3. Severe cases of secondary HPT

Parathyroidectomy is performed in neck hyperextension (semi-Fowler position). The thyroid gland is mobilized, and the parathyroid gland with adenoma is identified and resected. The parathyroid tissue is transplanted to the non-dominant forearm.

Pockets are made in the belly of the brachioradialis muscle, and one to two pieces of parathyroid tissue measuring 1 mm each are placed into each pocket. A total of 12 to 14 pieces are transplanted. This is a type of heterotopic transplant.

Miami criteria (confirm the absence of another hyperactive parathyroid): A drop of parathyroid hormone intraoperatively, to more than half the maximum value at 10 minutes postresection is considered an adequate resection in a parathyroid adenoma. However, if there is no drop in PTH level, then a multi-gland disease is suspected and the surgery is converted to a bilateral neck exploration.

Complications of parathyroidectomy include:

1. Persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism
2. Hypoparathyroidism (presenting as hypocalcemia)
3. Hungry bone syndrome
4. Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
questions.learning: Brachioradialis — The parathyroid is commonly transferred to the brachioradialis muscle post-surgery. This will facilitate easy removal if there is disease recurrence after surgery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The rupture of penile urethra does not cause extravasation of blood into which of the following spaces?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ischiorectal fossa

Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial perineal pouch is a compartment of the perineum enclosed by the membranous layer of the perineal fascia that surrounds the scrotum or labia and penis or clitoris.

Anteriorly, the membranous layer of perineal fascia is continuous over the pubic symphysis and pubic bones. It is later continuous with the membranous layer of the anterior abdominal wall.  Thus, the fluid that accumulates in the perineal pouch extends to the lower anterior abdomen.

In the lower lateral abdominal wall, the abdominal fascia is attached to the deep fascia of the thigh, inferior to the inguinal ligament. Thus, on trauma at the penile urethra, urine does not extravasate into the anterior thigh.

The superficial perineal pouch is closed posteriorly by attaching the membranous layer of superficial fascia to the posterior margin of the urogenital diaphragm. Thus, commonly there is no extravasation into the deep perineal pouch and the ischiorectal fossa.

Also, the membranous layer of superficial fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami and forms the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle. Thus, the urine does not extravasate to the thigh.

But, the ischiorectal fossa would be a better answer because of the following reasons:

1. Bulbourethral glands that lie in the deep perineal space open their ducts into the spongy urethra, which is related to the superficial perineal space. Also, the muscles surrounding these glands were recently found to be a continuation of the deep transverse perinei and tail of the external urethral sphincter, both of which are components of the deep perineal space. Injury to the penile urethra can damage bulbourethral glands' ducts, which can lead to damage to the above-mentioned structures and may cause extravasation of urine into the deep perineal space.
2. Previously, the perineal membrane was thought to be a triangular membrane. However, recent studies show that it is contiguous anteriorly with the structures that support the urethra. Posteriorly, it is related to the support of the perineal body and lateral vaginal wall. So damage to the urethra might damage the anterior part of the perineal membrane which can make way for extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space.
3. Deep perineal pouch: It was believed initially that the urogenital diaphragm was formed by 3 layers: An inferior fascia (also called the perineal membrane), deep perineal space, and a superior fascia. The superior fascia formed the inferior border of the ischioanal fossa. The Colles fascia also separates the perineal membrane from the ischioanal fossa. So, extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space is possible but extravasation into the ischioanal fossa due to penile urethral injury is highly unlikely. Recent studies have shown that this might be a slightly more complex structure.
questions.learning: Ischiorectal fossa Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which type of intracranial hemorrhage is most likely shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: A subdural hematoma occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, leading to accumulation of venous blood between the dura mater and arachnoid mater. On NCCT, it appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity that can cross suture lines, a key distinguishing feature. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Extradural hemorrhage: Shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion and does not cross suture lines. (B) Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Appears as diffuse hyperdensity in sulci and basal cisterns, not a localized crescent-shaped collection. (D) Intraparenchymal hemorrhage: Seen as a hyperdense lesion within brain tissue, often with surrounding edema. Thus, based on standard imaging features, the correct diagnosis is subdural hematoma
questions.learning: A subdural hematoma occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, leading to accumulation of venous blood between the dura mater and arachnoid mater. On NCCT, it appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity that can cross suture lines, a key distinguishing feature.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the earliest symptom of alcohol withdrawal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tremors

Coarse tremors are the earliest symptom of alcohol withdrawal which develops around 6-8 hours post-cessation of drinking.

After 8-12 hours have passed, psychotic symptoms are seen like hallucinations which are predominantly auditory in nature.

Seizures are seen after 12-24 hours and can progress to delirium tremens at around 72 hours. Sometimes this progression is not seen and delirium tremens can be seen initially or be visible after a week of cessation.

Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, irritability, anxiety, arousal, sweating, tachycardia, facial flushing, mydriasis, tachycardia, and mild hypertension.

Treatment of Alcohol Withdrawal

* For patients showing withdrawal symptoms, Chlordiazepoxide 25-50 mg every 2-4 hours can be administered orally.

* For patients with Delirium tremens, 50-100 mg of chlordiazepoxide should be administered every 4 hours.  (Chlordiazepoxide oral preparations are only available)

* If oral administration of drugs is not possible, Intravenous lorazepam (0.1mg/kg) can be given.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the primary underlying mechanism of haemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: Complement-mediated destruction of CD59(–) red blood cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complement-mediated destruction of CD59(–) red blood cells

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by a PIGA gene mutation, resulting in defective synthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors. Consequently, red blood cells lack the complement regulatory proteins CD55 (Decay Accelerating Factor) and CD59 (Membrane Inhibitor of Reactive Lysis), making them susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

Why not the other options?

• A. ABO incompatibility ✗: Causes immune-mediated hemolysis due to mismatched blood transfusion, not PNH.
• B. Red cell fragmentation ✗: Seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) such as DIC, TTP, and HUS, producing schistocytes.
• D. Exotoxins produced by Clostridium perfringens ✗: Causes acute massive hemolysis due to α-toxin, unrelated to PNH.
