questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a PCSK9 inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Evolocumab

Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor.

PCSK9 refers to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9. They are mainly involved in the downregulation of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors in the liver.

Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits PCSK-9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin). Inhibition of PCSK-9 prevents the degradation of LDL receptors and thus increases LDL-cholesterol clearance by the liver. They are used in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) to decrease LDL levels.

Side effects of PCSK9 inhibitors are injection-site reactions, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection, and upper respiratory tract infection and it does not increase the risk of myopathy.

Other options:

Option B: Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption by enterocytes in the small intestine. It lowers the total and LDL-C levels.

Option C: Bempedoic acid inhibits adenosine triphosphate-citrate lyase (ACL) and results in decreased LDL in patients not responding to statin therapy.

Option D: Clofibrate binds to PPAR-alpha and causes stimulation of fatty acid oxidation and increased LPL synthesis. This results in reduced triglycerides, LDL and increased high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels. It causes myopathy when combined with statins and is associated with an increased risk of gallstone formation.
questions.learning: Evolocumab Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor. PCSK9 refers to proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A girl presented with complaints of irregular periods, acne, and increased facial hair growth.USG revealed multiple ovarian follicles. Which of the following would be increased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum testosterone

In the given clinical scenario history of irregular periods, acne, increased facial hair growth, and USG showing multiple ovarian follicles is suggestive of polycystic ovarian disease(PCOD). In PCOD, serum testosterone would be elevated.

Insulin induces LH to cause theca-cell hyperplasia and secrete androgens, testosterone, and epiandrostenedione which are converted to estrogen in the granulosa cells. Epi-androstenedione is converted in the peripheral fat to oestrone. This leads to rise in estrogen and inhibin levels. These in turn cause high LH surge. While the oestrone level increases, the oestradiol level remains normal which raises the Oestrone: Oestradiol ratio.

Endocrinological changes of PCOD:

* Elevated Estrone/E1 levels.

* LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls.

* Testosterone and epi-androstenedione levels rise.

* Testosterone elevated but < 200 ng/dL (normal range 20 - 70 ng/dL)

* Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests androgen-secreting ovarian tumor

* DHEA-S values may be normal or slightly elevated

* DHEA >700 ng/mL suggests adrenal tumour

* Serum SHBG is reduced.

* Triglyceride level >150 mg/dL-hyperlipidaemia HDL <50 mg/dL.

* Fasting blood glucose/fasting insulin <4.5 suggests insulin resistance

* Prolactin is mildly raised in 15% cases

* Fasting insulin is more than 10 mIU/L in PCOS in 50–70%cases

* Thyroid function tests may be abnormal (hypothyroidism)

* 17-a-hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase >300 ng/dL suggests adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

* Urinary cortisol <50 μg/24 h.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome

Important clinical features of PCOS are Menstrual abnormalities (70%) - oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, obesity, hirsutism, acne, and alopecia due to hyperandrogenism, acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance, and infertility.

Rotterdam criterion is used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS.

* Oligo/ amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility

* Hirsutism/ acne

* Ultrasound findings-

Investigations

* Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mm3

* 12 or more small follicles each 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally.

Hormonal studies

* USG is diagnostic of PCOS - it shows enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles in the periphery. It also rules out other pathologies like ovarian tumors, endometrial hyperplasia.

* Laparoscopy (therapeutic). It reveals bilateral enlarged ovarian cysts.

The ultrasound image below shows an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery.

Management of PCOD is individualized. Weight reduction and lifestyle changes are the first-line therapy for PCOD. Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. Hirsutism and acne are managed with OCP with cyproterone acetate and topical agents such as eflornithine, clindamycin lotion 1%, erythromycin gel 2%, and isotretinoin.

Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin and acarbose. Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical management includes laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary.

Note:

PCOS in association with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease presenting in reproductive age group is known as "X syndrome".
questions.learning: Serum testosterone — In the given clinical scenario history of irregular periods, acne, increased facial hair growth, and USG showing multiple ovarian follicles is suggestive of polycystic ovarian disease(PCOD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old lady underwent thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma. Postoperatively she developed muscle cramps, perioral and peripheral paresthesia, and carpopedal spasm. Which one of the following interventions is appropriate?
options: Nerve conduction velocity in both upper and lower limbs and administer methylcobalamin
EMG of both lower limbs and administer oral prednisolone
Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate
Measure serum bicarbonate and administer intravenous bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate

Hypocalcemia due to postoperative hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of thyroidectomy. It typically presents within 24–72 hours with perioral numbness, paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, tetany, and positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum ionized calcium, and symptomatic hypocalcemia requires immediate intravenous calcium gluconate.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nerve conduction velocity in both upper and lower limbs and administer methylcobalamin: Nerve conduction studies and methylcobalamin are indicated for peripheral neuropathy, not acute postoperative tetany.
• B. EMG of both lower limbs and administer oral prednisolone: EMG and prednisolone have no role in hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy.
• D. Measure serum bicarbonate and administer intravenous bicarbonate: Bicarbonate is used for metabolic acidosis, not for neuromuscular symptoms caused by hypocalcemia.
questions.learning: Measure serum ionized calcium and administer intravenous calcium gluconate Hypocalcemia due to postoperative hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of thyroidectomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following condition leads to the development of wing beating tremor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wilson's disease

Wing beating tremor is seen in Wilson's disease.

In Huntington's chorea, rapid jerky movements are seen and Sydenham's chorea is seen in Rheumatic disease. In Parkinsonism, the type of tremor is called resting tremor because they disappear on movement.

Wilsons disease:

The autosomal-recessive disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which encodes a membrane-bound, copper-transporting ATPase.

Clinical symptoms:

* Hepatitis and cirrhosis

* Behavioral disturbances

* Wing beating tremor( shown in the image below)

* Ophthalmic characteristics:

* Deposition of copper in the posterior capsule of the lens resulting in sunflower cataract

* KF ring

Diagnosis:

* Presence of KF rings

* Decreased serum ceruloplasmin (copper-containing enzyme/ferroxidase) levels

* Measured hepatic copper levels in liver biopsy

* Increased 24-hour urine copper excretion

The gold standard for diagnosis: Liver biopsy with quantitative copper assays

Treatment: Trientine and Zinc is the first choice of a drug regimen to be used for treating mild hepatic decompensation in Wilson’s disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman is found to have a short cervix and undergoes cervical cerclage. Which specific cerclage procedure is most likely to have been performed?
questions.explanation: A cervical cerclage is used to treat cervical insufficiency in women with a short or incompetent cervix. The Modified Shirodkar procedure is a variation that allows for a high placement of the suture (usually Mersilene tape) at the level of the internal os. This higher placement provides better structural support than the standard McDonald's cerclage (Option B), which is a purse-string suture placed lower at the cervicovaginal junction without dissection. The original Shirodkar technique (Option C) requires extensive bladder and rectal dissection to reach the internal os; the "modified" version is often technically simpler while still maintaining the high-placement advantage. Transabdominal cerclage is reserved for cases where vaginal approaches have failed. In this specific clinical context of significant shortening, the Modified Shirodkar is the most likely definitive procedure for high-level support
questions.learning: A cervical cerclage is used to treat cervical insufficiency in women with a short or incompetent cervix. The Modified Shirodkar procedure is a variation that allows for a high placement of the suture (usually Mersilene tape) at the level of the internal os.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Dynein protein is an example of?
questions.explanation: Dynein is a molecular motor protein that functions as a specialized intracellular transport protein. It "walks" along microtubules to move cargo, such as vesicles and organelles, within the cell. Notably, dynein moves cargo in the retrograde direction (from the periphery toward the cell center or the minus end of the microtubule). Another motor protein, kinesin, handles anterograde transport. Dynein also plays a crucial role in the movement of cilia and flagella (axonemal dynein) and in spindle assembly during mitosis. Option B is incorrect as dynein is cytoplasmic. Options C and D refer to different classes of skeletal or anchoring proteins like integrins or cadherins. Clinically, a defect in axonemal dynein results in Kartagener syndrome (Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia), characterized by a triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. These motor proteins are vital for maintaining cellular organization and facilitating the large-scale movement of materials required for neuronal function and respiratory clearance. AAns AAns AAns AAns AAns
questions.learning: Dynein is a molecular motor protein that functions as a specialized intracellular transport protein. It "walks" along microtubules to move cargo, such as vesicles and organelles, within the cell.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which treatment kit would you recommend for a 20‑year‑old woman presenting with vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain after recent sexual intercourse, following the syndromic management approach for sexually transmitted infections at a Suraksha clinic in the local primary health center?
questions.explanation: The syndromic management of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) uses color-coded kits to simplify treatment based on clinical presentations. For a woman presenting with the syndrome of lower abdominal pain accompanied by vaginal discharge, Kit 6 (the Yellow kit) is the correct recommendation. This kit is specifically designed to treat Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), which is the likely diagnosis in this scenario. It typically contains Cefixime, Doxycycline, and Metronidazole to cover common pathogens like Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and anaerobes. The Blue kit (Option A) is for vaginal discharge alone (Bacterial Vaginosis or Trichomoniasis). The Red kit (Option B) is for vaginal discharge specifically suspected as Candidiasis. The Black kit (Option C) is for inguinal buboes. Because the patient has symptoms suggesting an ascending infection (abdominal pain), the broader coverage provided by the Yellow kit is necessary. This standardized approach ensures that patients receive effective, immediate treatment at the primary care level, even without complex diagnostic laboratory testing

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For what population size is an urban Primary Health Centre (PHC) typically intended?
questions.explanation: Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) in India, the health infrastructure is tailored to the high density of city populations. An Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) is established to cater to a population of approximately 50,000 people. These centers serve as the first point of contact for the urban poor, particularly those living in slums or unauthorized colonies. This differs from rural norms, where a PHC covers 20,000 in hilly/tribal areas or 30,000 in plain areas. A population of 100,000 (Option B) is typically the benchmark for an Urban Community Health Centre (U-CHC), which provides more specialized services and indoor beds. Options C and D (250,000 and 200,000) do not correspond to the standard planning norms for primary health units in India. The U-PHC focuses on delivering essential services like immunization, maternal care, and screening for non-communicable diseases, ensuring that healthcare is accessible within a manageable distance for urban residents
questions.learning: Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) in India, the health infrastructure is tailored to the high density of city populations. An Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) is established to cater to a population of approximately 50,000 people.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with hematemesis and is found to have splenomegaly on examination. His history reveals that he underwent exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hematemesis (from esophageal varices) and splenomegaly in a young child, particularly with a history of neonatal umbilical vein manipulation (such as exchange transfusion or catheterization), is strongly suggestive of portal vein thrombosis. This is a common cause of pre-hepatic portal hypertension in children. Splenic vein thrombosis (Option A) can cause localized portal hypertension but is less common and doesn't explain the generalized portosystemic shunt as well as the history does. Budd-Chiari syndrome (Option C) involves hepatic vein obstruction and typically presents with hepatomegaly and ascites, which are not the primary features here. Liver cirrhosis (Option D) can cause portal hypertension but is rare in a 5-year-old without a known history of chronic liver disease or metabolic disorders. Thus, the neonatal history is the key to identifying portal vein thrombosis
questions.learning: The combination of hematemesis (from esophageal varices) and splenomegaly in a young child, particularly with a history of neonatal umbilical vein manipulation (such as exchange transfusion or catheterization), is strongly suggestive of portal vein thrombosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Papanicolaou stain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Eosin B

Eosin B is not a component of Papanicolaou stain.

Papanicolaou stain is the most popular stain used in the practice of histopathology. It is a polychrome stain containing multiple dyes to stain the various components of cells differentially. Papanicolaou stain includes both acidic and basic dyes:

• Hematoxylin is a basic dye and it stains the nucleus.
• Orange G is an acidic counterstain and it stains matured and keratinized cells.
• Eosin A is the second counterstain and it is a polychrome mixture of Eosin Y and Light green SF.
questions.learning: Eosin B Eosin B is not a component of Papanicolaou stain. Papanicolaou stain is the most popular stain used in the practice of histopathology.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following has the highest risk of causing invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Febrile neutropenia

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is a highly aggressive, angioinvasive fungal infection caused by Aspergillus fumigatus (most common).

Key Pathophysiology

• Neutrophils = primary defense against Aspergillus

• In neutropenia (<500/µL):

• No phagocytosis of hyphae
• Unchecked fungal proliferation
• Angioinvasion → thrombosis → hemorrhagic infarction

Pulmonary infarction → cavitation

Halo sign/ Air crescent sign

Key Findings:

• Halo sign (early) → Ground-glass opacity around nodule (hemorrhage)
• Air crescent sign (late) → Cavitation with air pocket

| Febrile neutropenia | Loss of neutrophil defense | Highest

| Bone marrow transplant | Severe immune compromise | +++

| Advanced AIDS | T-cell deficiency (less role here) | +

| COPD (severe) | Structural lung disease | +

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During endoscopy, a man is found to have the squamocolumnar junction positioned more proximally than usual. Which condition is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: In a sliding hiatus hernia, the gastroesophageal junction (the squamocolumnar junction or Z-line) and a portion of the stomach slide proximally into the thoracic cavity through the esophageal hiatus. This is the most common type of hiatus hernia and is strongly associated with GERD. A rolling (paraesophageal) hernia (Option C) involves a portion of the stomach protruding beside the esophagus, but the Z-line typically remains in its normal anatomical position. Achalasia cardia (Option A) involves a failure of the lower sphincter to relax, which does not displace the junction proximally. While chronic GERD (Option D) can lead to Barrett's esophagus (where the Z-line also appears proximal), the anatomical displacement of the junction itself is the definitive endoscopic finding of a sliding hernia. Sliding hernias are often managed medically unless severe reflux or complications occur. Identifying the location of the Z-line relative to the diaphragmatic pinch is the key to endoscopic diagnosis
questions.learning: In a sliding hiatus hernia, the gastroesophageal junction (the squamocolumnar junction or Z-line) and a portion of the stomach slide proximally into the thoracic cavity through the esophageal hiatus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 9-month-old boy presents with progressive pallor and abdominal distention. On investigations, hepatosplenomegaly and malar eminence is seen and his peripheral blood smear is as shown below. He has low Hb, Mentzer index is found to be less than 13. What diagnosis would this signify in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thalassemia

The clinical scenario, peripheral blood smear showing target cells and aniso-poikilocytes, along with the Mentzer index of less than 13 suggests Thalassemia.

Thalassemia syndromes:

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival. Disease severity is inversely correlated with the number of functioning globin chains.

Clinical features in thalassemia:

* Anemia

* Jaundice and pigment gallstones

* Skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, osteopenia/osteoporosis

* Iron overload

* Growth impairment

* Hepatosplenomegaly

* Endocrine abnormalities including hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus

* Heart failure and arrhythmias

Laboratory studies:

* Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases. These findings are non-specific.

* High RBC count

* Low reticulocyte count

* High LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coomb's test

* High transferrin saturation, normal serum iron levels, elevated ferritin levels

MCV/RBC count also known as Mentzer index can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio.

Mentzer index is:

* More than 13 in iron-deficiency anemia

* Less than 13 in thalassemia

Thalassemia syndromes and iron deficiency anemia (IDA) are the two most common etiologies of microcytic hypochromic anemia in children and adults. The reference standard to diagnose IDA is serum ferritin level. Since it is expensive and not widely available, an inexpensive & simpler way of evaluation is the Mentzer index.

Pearl PF0864: Thalassemia syndromes

Normally each individual carries 4 functional alpha chain genes and 2 functional beta chain genes. Alpha and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively.

* Alpha thalassemia: Gene deletion is the most common cause of reduced α-chain synthesis.

* Beta +- thalassemia: The most common cause is splicing mutation.

* Beta 0- thalassemia: Chain terminator mutations are the most common cause.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 37-year-old presented with fever. On examination, he had enlarged and ulcerated tonsils. His peripheral blood smear showed lymphocytosis. Monospot test was negative. Tonsillectomy was done and it showed large cells mixed with lymphocytes. The cells were positive for CD20, EBV LMP1, MUM1, CD 79a. Background cells were positive for CD3. The cells are negative for CD15. Your most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. EBV positive – DLBCL, NOS

The given clinical scenario suggests a likely diagnosis of EBV positive DLBCL, NOS (Epstein Barr virus-positive Diffuse Large B cell Lymphoma, Not otherwise specified).

The given slide shows sheets of large lymphoid cells with irregular vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli typical of DLBCL.

Approach to the question:

• In the given case, Monospot test negative rules out Infectious Mononucleosis and the identification of Reed-Sternberg cell and their variant is essential for the diagnosis of Hodgkin Lymphoma, which can also be ruled out.
• EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer is a localized lymphoproliferative disorder in immunocompromised patients. It is a self-limiting ulcer which reverts on treatment in Immunocompromised people. Histologically characterized by atypical large B cells with RS cell-like morphology. Hence, this is also ruled out.
• EBV positive DLBL(Diffuse Large B cell Lymphoma) occurs in patients more than 50 years of age and without a previous history of lymphoma. DLBCL typically presents as a rapidly enlarging mass at a nodal or extranodal site.
• Immunohistochemical studies indicate that EBV+ DLBCL, NOS is molecularly heterogeneous with a prominent background of T lymphocytes. The cells are positive for CD 20, CD 79a, IRF4/MUM1. EBV LMP-1(Latent membrane protein-1) is positive in about 2/3rdof cases, while EBNA-2 (Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen) is positive in the remaining 1/3rd of cases. It is negative for CD10 and BCL6.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is set to receive intermittent treatment with teriparatide. Which of the following complications does this drug predispose him to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Osteosarcoma

The use of teriparatide predisposes an individual to the development of osteosarcoma.

Teriparatide is a parathormone analog, which is given as subcutaneous injections. Pharmacokinetics and systemic actions of teriparatide on mineral metabolism are the same as for PTH. Its main target of action are the osteoblasts.

Teriparatide is administered by once-daily subcutaneous injection of 20 μg into the thigh or abdomen. The site of administration should be rotated, but the time at which the injection is made should be the same each day.

Teriparatide and abaloparatide (PTHrP analog) are the only anabolic agents currently available that increase new bone formation (option C). Candidates for treatment include women who have a history of osteoporotic fracture, who have multiple risk factors for fracture, or who failed or are intolerant of previous osteoporosis therapy. Men with primary or hypogonadal osteoporosis are also candidates for treatment with these agents.

Adverse effects include hypercalcemia, exacerbation of nephrolithiasis, and elevation of serum uric acid levels. The development of osteosarcoma has been a serious concern in patients treated with teriparatide. It comes with a black-box warning, and use should be limited to no more than 2 years and avoided in patients who are at increased baseline risk for osteosarcoma (including those with Paget disease of bone, unexplained elevations of alkaline phosphatase, open epiphyses, or prior radiation therapy involving the skeleton).

Other options :

Options A and B - Osteonecrosis of the jaw bone and subtrochanteric fractures are the adverse effects of bisphosphonates.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the term used for a disease that is not native to a country and is introduced from another country?
questions.explanation: In epidemiology, an exotic disease (Option D) is one that is not normally present in a given country or geographical region but is introduced from an external source (abroad). The 25-year-old male diagnosed at an Indian airport upon arrival represents an imported or exotic case. An endemic disease (Option A) is one that is constantly present in a specific population or region (e.g., malaria in parts of India). An epidemic (Option B) is a sudden, large-scale outbreak of a disease in a specific area. A zoonotic disease (Option C) is one that is transmitted from animals to humans, such as rabies or anthrax . Exotic diseases are a major focus of international health regulations and airport quarantine measures to prevent the domestic spread of "new" pathogens. Therefore, because the condition originated outside the country's borders, "exotic" is the correct epidemiological classification for this imported case

questions.text: What is the mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) threshold on Shakir’s tape that indicates severe acute malnutrition?
questions.explanation: cm Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a rapid and effective screening tool for assessing nutritional status in children aged 6 to 59 months. According to WHO standards and Shakir's tape classification, a MUAC of less than is the diagnostic criterion for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). This measurement corresponds to the "Red" zone on a standard tri-colored Shakir's tape. A MUAC between and (Option B) indicates Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM), represented by the "Yellow" zone. Measurements above (Option C and D) are considered normal and fall in the "Green" zone. MUAC is preferred in field settings because it is simple to use and correlates well with the risk of mortality. Children identified with SAM require urgent referral for therapeutic feeding and medical management. This screening is a core component of the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) protocol used by frontline health workers

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the next step in the management of an old patient who has undergone complete excision of glioblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Radiotherapy

Standard treatment post-surgical resection of glioblastoma includes radiotherapy in older patients. Radiation alone is effective as a single-modality therapy in the elderly owing to the survival benefit of radiation. Moreover, the combined-modality therapy of Chemoradiation has increased the risk of Neurotoxicity.

It is used in combination with temozolomide chemotherapy in younger individuals. Temozolomide is used as a first-line agent for the management of glioblastoma multiforme. It is used for newly diagnosed cases along with radiotherapy and also used for maintenance therapy. Bevacizumab, which is a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antibody may be used in the treatment of recurrent glioblastoma.

Glioblastoma is the most common adult primary intracranial neoplasm. It affects people usually in the sixth or seventh decade. These tumors may arise de novo or may result from a malignant transformation of lower-grade astrocytomas. Mutations of Isocitrate Dehydrogenase (IDH) and Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor gene (EGFR) are implicated in the pathogenesis of the same.

Clinically, patients usually present with headaches, seizures due to raised intracranial pressure or focal neurologic deficits depending upon the site involved.

Grossly, glioblastomas are found infiltrating the brain tissue and are poorly delineated. They have greyish tumor cells with central yellowish necrosis and multiple areas of hemorrhages. Microscopically, they are composed of poorly differentiated pleomorphic astrocytic cells with nuclear atypia and high mitotic activity. Necrosis and florid microvascular proliferation are characteristic. They exhibit pseudopalisading—dense arrangement of tumor cells lining up around the foci of tumor necrosis.

According to the WHO Classification of CNS diseases 2016, glioblastomas are classified as follows:

* Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype:

* About 90% of cases

* Primary or de novo glioblastoma

* Over 55 years of age

* Worst prognosis

* Glioblastoma, IDH-mutant:

* About 10% of cases

* Secondary glioblastoma, with a history of prior lower-grade diffuse glioma

* Arises in younger patients

* Poor prognosis

* Glioblastoma, NOS (not otherwise specified), where full IDH evaluation cannot be performed.

The given histological image shows foci of necrosis with pseudo-palisading of malignant nuclei and endothelial cell proliferation, which are characteristic of glioblastoma (previously called glioblastoma multiforme).
questions.learning: Radiotherapy Standard treatment post-surgical resection of glioblastoma includes radiotherapy in older patients. Radiation alone is effective as a single-modality therapy in the elderly owing to the survival benefit of radiation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the level of prevention when a person receives penicillin injections for the treatment of rheumatic heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary

Receiving penicillin injections for the treatment of rheumatic heart disease is Secondary prevention.

Secondary prevention includes early disease detection, and its target is healthy-appearing individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. This is defined as the action which halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.

Levels of Prevention :

1. Primordial prevention:

* Involves the prevention of the emergence or development of risk factors in countries or population groups in which they have not yet appeared.

* Examples include adult health problems like obesity and hypertension, which have an early onset due to lifestyles like smoking, eating patterns and physical exercise, which are discouraged from early childhood

* The main intervention in primordial prevention is through individual and mass education.

2. Primary prevention:

* These are defined as "action taken prior to the onset of disease, which removes the possibility that a disease will ever occur''

* It signifies intervention in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease or health problem

* Primary prevention is accomplished by measures promoting general health and well-being, and the quality of life of people by specific protective measures.

* They include two strategies:

* Population (mass) strategy: Where the target group is the whole population

* High-risk strategy: Where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease

* Examples: immunity, sanitation, and protection of food.

3. Secondary prevention :

* This is defined as "action which halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.".

* The specific interventions are early diagnoses like screening tests and adequate treatment.

* The main aim of secondary prevention is to arrest the disease process.

* Secondary prevention is largely the domain of clinical medicine and health programs initiated by governments.

* It is an imperfect tool in the control of the transmission of disease. It is often more expensive and less effective than primary prevention.

4. Tertiary prevention :

* Measures to reduce the duration of mental illness and family and community stresses to prevent further breakdown and disruption.

* Disability limitation belongs to tertiary prevention.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 56-year- old woman with a history of myocardial infarction two years ago who now presents with cough and breathlessness, given thoracocentesis findings of pleural fluid protein 3.2 g/dL, pleural fluid–to–serum protein ratio of 0.34, and pleural fluid–to–serum LDH ratio of 0.3?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is determined by applying Light’s criteria to the pleural fluid analysis. A transudative effusion is defined by a pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio and a pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio . This patient’s ratios (0.34 and 0.3 respectively) clearly indicate a transudate. Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) is the most common cause of transudative pleural effusion, consistent with her history of a myocardial infarction. Parapneumonic (Option A), malignant (Option B), and tubercular (Option D) effusions are all examples of exudates, which would show higher protein and LDH ratios, often with specific cellular findings like increased neutrophils (pneumonia) or very high ADA and lymphocytes (TB) . The turbid appearance (Option B) can occasionally be seen in transudates, but the biochemical ratios are the gold standard for classification. Management focuses on treating the underlying heart failure with diuretics and ACE inhibitors
questions.learning: The diagnosis is determined by applying Light’s criteria to the pleural fluid analysis. A transudative effusion is defined by a pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio and a pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH ratio .

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man has come with complaints of hair loss. Examination findings are given below. The most likely diagnosis in this man is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alopecia areata

The image above shows circumscribed, hairless, smooth patch. Short, easily extractable broken hairs, known as exclamation mark hairs, are seen at the margins of the bald patch. This is characteristic of alopecia areata.

It is characterized by a circumscribed, smooth patch of hair loss. Exclamation mark hairs are often seen at the margins of the bald patches during active phases of the disease. Follicular orifices may appear as yellow dots on dermoscopy.

Alopecia areata is a chronic, inflammatory, autoimmune disease that causes non-scarring hair loss.

Other options:

Option A: Tinea capitis (as shown in the images below): The appearance may vary from dull grey, broken‐off hairs with a little scaling to a severe, painful, inflammatory mass covering the entire scalp. Predominantly seen in children, however, adults can also be affected due to infection by T.tonsurans.

Option B: Kerion (T. verrucosum and T. mentagrophytes) is a severe inflammatory type that presents with an inflammatory mass with thick crusting and matting of hair with pus and sinus formation.

Option D: Androgenic alopecia is a disorder characterized by a reduction of hair fiber production by follicles and miniaturization. Dihydrotestosterone, an androgenic metabolite, is implicated in the etiology. It is of two types: male-pattern and female-pattern hair loss. Male-pattern hair loss causes frontal hairline recession and thinning of the vertex.  Female-pattern hair loss involves the mid-frontal scalp diffusely. There is no or minimal involvement of the temporal region.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A man falls into a deep sleep with one arm under his head. He finds he is not able to move this arm when he awakens. However, it tingles and pain sensation in the arm is still intact. What is the reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm?
options: B fibers are more susceptible to pressure than A fibers
A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A fibers
Motor nerves are more affected by sleep than sensory nerves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers

The reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm, A-fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers.

Sleeping for a long period with the arms under the head puts pressure on a nerve. It leads to the loss of conduction in large-diameter motor, touch, and pressure fibers, while pain sensation remains relatively intact. A-fibers (includes the motor fibers) are affected.

The susceptibility of the nerve fibers to pressure is A>B>C.

This is responsible for Saturday night or Sunday morning paralysis.

questions.text: A newborn presents with a progressively enlarging skin lesion, as shown in the image. According to the mother, the lesion has been increasing in size day by day. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
options: Immediate Biopsy due to Malignancy Risk
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows an infantile hemangioma, which is a benign vascular tumor common in neonates. These lesions typically go through a rapid proliferative phase during the first few months of life, as described by the mother, followed by slow, spontaneous involution over several years. The standard management for uncomplicated hemangiomas is simple observation. Regarding the distractors, excision or laser therapy (Option B) is reserved for complicated cases involving the airway, eyes, or severe ulceration. An immediate biopsy (Option C) is unnecessary as the diagnosis is clinical and the risk of malignancy is extremely low. Cryotherapy (Option D) is not a first-line treatment and can cause scarring. questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Patient presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of difficulty switching from one movement to another. He also reports having uncontrolled hand movements when trying to perform rapid alternating movements, particularly when asked to tap his fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dysdiadochokinesis

The patient has difficulty switching from one movement to another which is suggestive of Dysdiadochokinesia. It is the inability to perform rapid alternate movements.

It is a clinical manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction and is most evident when strength and sensation are intact. Focal lesions in the nervous system may produce highly asymmetric dysdiadochokinesia.

The following movement is the method to check for dysdiadochokinesis. The patient is showing normal movement, with no dysdiadochokinesis.

Other Options:

Option A: Resting tremor is an involuntary, rhythmic muscle movement that occurs when the affected body part is at rest and diminishes with voluntary movement. It is commonly associated with Parkinson's disease and basal ganglia dysfunction.

Option B: Intentional tremor is a slow, rhythmic tremor that occurs during purposeful movement and worsens as the target approaches. It is commonly seen in cerebellar disorders, such as multiple sclerosis or stroke.

Option D: Bradykinesia is the slowness of voluntary movements, often accompanied by reduced amplitude and difficulty initiating actions. It is a hallmark symptom of Parkinson’s disease and other basal ganglia disorders.

Pearl PF1419: Functions of cerebellum

Vestibulo cerebellum

• It is concerned with maintainence of balance and equilibirium.
• It is responsible for regulating the stability of head and body in space.
• It adjusts the tone of the trunk muscle.
• Controls the oculur movements and other postural reflexes.

Spino cerebellum

• Maintains the posture and helps in execution of gross movements.
• It controls the interplay between the agonist and antagonist group of muscles.
• It is essential for the control of rapid muscular activities like running and talking.

Cerebro cerebellum (Neocerebellum)

• Controls fine, highly precise and coordinated movements.
• It is involved in programming of voluntary and skilled movements
• It plays a major role in the timing of the motor activities and rapid progression from one movement to the next.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient was brought to the casualty after a road traffic accident with a suspected pelvic fracture. On examination, he is found to be in hypovolemic shock. What is the earliest treatment for the control of hemorrhage in this case?
options: Use bedsheets to compress the pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Use bedsheets to compress the pelvis

The earliest treatment to control hemorrhage in a case of suspected pelvic fracture is to use bedsheets to compress the pelvis similar to a compression binder.

The most likely source of bleeding in hemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma is abdominal or pelvic bleeding. A pelvic binder or a sheet should be applied around the true pelvis of all hemodynamically unstable patients and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded. It must be correctly positioned at the level of the greater trochanters. This is a potentially life-saving procedure that has to be done in the emergency department. Following this, they require an immediate pelvic radiograph. Mechanical testing of the pelvis should never be performed. A pelvic fracture should always be diagnosed radiographically.

In fractures of the pelvic ring, there is a risk of injury to the major vessels (internal iliac and external iliac vessels) and to the venous plexus around the sacroiliac joint. Bleeding from the venous plexus is the major cause of pelvic hemorrhage. Pelvic fractures can have a high mortality rate of more than 40% in some open pelvic fractures. Early mortality is mostly the result of hemorrhage.

Bleeding of venous origin can be controlled by compression either by binding/ external fixator or by extraperitoneal pelvic packing to compress the pelvic veins. Persistent bleeding after packing or bleeding of arterial origin may require angioembolisation. Severe pelvic injuries require a multidisciplinary team approach. An exploratory laparotomy may be considered if

• the source of the bleeding is in doubt
• FAST/CT results are positive, showing a significant amount of blood in the peritoneal cavity
• concurrent intra-abdominal injury cannot be excluded
questions.learning: Use bedsheets to compress the pelvis — The earliest treatment to control hemorrhage in a case of suspected pelvic fracture is to use bedsheets to compress the pelvis similar to a compression binder.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Purkinje cells

The cells marked in the above histological image are Purkinje cells.

Characteristics of Purkinje cells:

• Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
• The cells are evenly spaced and are arranged in a single layer.
• A dendrite arises from the neck of each flask-shaped cell, which passes upward to enter the molecular layer, which then branches extensively to form a dendritic tree.
• The axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer to enter the white matter.
• Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex.
• The initial segment of the axon receives synaptic contacts from basket cell axons.
• The main axon terminates in one of the cerebellar or vestibular nuclei.
• Purkinje cells are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Pathological significance:

• Negri bodies in rabies, are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells.
• Loss of Purkinje cells and granule cells is seen in ataxia-telangiectasia.
• In patients with subacute cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells. Some patients show circulating PCA1 antibody (antiYo) against Purkinje cells.
• Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia, and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Very high intraocular pressure, vertically oval mid-dilated pupil and shallow anterior chamber is seen in:
questions.explanation: The clinical features of very high intraocular pressure, a vertically oval mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber are pathognomonic for an attack of Acute Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (APACG). This condition is an ocular emergency caused by sudden obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by the iris, leading to a rapid spike in pressure. The vertically oval shape of the pupil is due to ischemic paralysis of the iris sphincter muscle at higher pressures. Primary open-angle glaucoma is typically asymptomatic with normal chamber depth and lacks these acute features. Malignant glaucoma, or aqueous misdirection, is a postoperative complication and presents with a shallowing of both the central and peripheral chambers. Pupillary block is the most common mechanism behind APACG but describes the process rather than the clinical syndrome. Immediate management of APACG involves pressure-lowering agents and a definitive peripheral iridotomy. Recognizing these signs is crucial to prevent irreversible optic nerve damage and permanent vision loss in the affected patient
questions.learning: The clinical features of very high intraocular pressure, a vertically oval mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber are pathognomonic for an attack of Acute Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (APACG).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the name of the staging system used for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA)?
questions.explanation: The Radkowski classification is the most widely utilized staging system for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumor found almost exclusively in adolescent males. The system stages the tumor based on its extension from the nasopharynx into the sinuses, pterygopalatine fossa, and intracranial compartments. TNM Staging (Option B) is the universal system for malignant cancers and is not applied to JNA. The Ann Arbor system (Option C) is used for lymphomas. Dukes criteria (Option D) is used for staging colorectal cancer. Staging JNA correctly using the Radkowski system is crucial for surgical planning, as these tumors are prone to massive hemorrhage. Management typically involves preoperative embolization to reduce blood flow, followed by either an endoscopic or open surgical approach depending on the stage of extension
questions.learning: The Radkowski classification is the most widely utilized staging system for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumor found almost exclusively in adolescent males.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following autoantibodies is most commonly associated with fetal heart block?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti-Ro antibody

Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are the autoantibodies most strongly associated with congenital heart block (CHB) in the fetus. These maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and can damage the fetal atrioventricular (AV) node, leading to irreversible congenital complete heart block. They are classically seen in mothers with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) or Sjögren syndrome, although they may also be present in asymptomatic women.

• Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are the most common cause of immune-mediated congenital heart block.
• Fetal manifestations include:

• Congenital complete heart block
• Fetal bradycardia
• Neonatal lupus syndrome

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-dsDNA antibody: Highly specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity, especially lupus nephritis, but is not associated with fetal heart block.
• C. Anti-Smith antibody: Highly specific for SLE, but has no association with congenital heart block.
• D. Anti-Jo antibody: Associated with polymyositis/dermatomyositis (antisynthetase syndrome), not neonatal lupus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The earliest sign seen in pregnancy on ultrasound is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gestational sac

The earliest sonographic sign of pregnancy is the visualization of the gestational sac which is seen as the double decidual sign.

The double decidual sac sign (DDSS) is a useful feature on early pregnancy ultrasound to confirm an early intrauterine pregnancy when the yolk sac or embryo is still not visualised. It consists of the decidua parietalis (lining the uterine cavity) and decidua capsularis (lining the gestational sac) and is seen as two concentric rings surrounding an anechoic gestational sac.

The double decidual sac sign differentiates normal pregnancy from the pseudo-gestational sac of an ectopic pregnancy. Pseudosac is irregular, usually centrally located in the uterus, has no double decidua sign, and the sac remains empty. The illustration below shows the difference:

Other options:

Option C: Roberts sign shows the presence of gas shadow within the chambers of the heart and in large vessels of the fetus. It is the earliest sign of intrauterine death, seen within 12 hours of death.

Option D: In a normal intrauterine pregnancy a gestational sac will be visible on TVS by 5 weeks of LMP and the embryonic poles can be visualized by 5.5 weeks. The fetal cardiac activity can be first visualized on TVS around 5.5-6 weeks, when the crown-rump length (CRL) is around 5mm.

Pearl PF1942: Radiological Signs in Obstetrics

Bagel Sign (USG)

It is seen in unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy. It is also known as the tubal ring sign or the blob sign. It refers to the appearance of an anechoic gestational sac in the adnexa surrounded by a hyperechoic ring.

Twin Peak Sign/ Lambda Sign (USG)

Chorionicity of the placenta is best diagnosed by ultrasound at 10–13 weeks of gestation. In dichorionic twins, there is a thick triangular projection of placental tissue between the two gestational sacs. This is known as the lambda sign or twin peak sign.

T Sign (USG)

The T sign which is seen in monochorionic diamniotic gestation is thin and T-shaped because there is no extension of placental tissue or chorion in between the amniotic membranes.

Double Decidual Sac Sign (USG)

It is seen in early intrauterine pregnancy as two concentric echogenic rings surrounding the gestational sac.

Lemon Sign (USG)

At the level of the lateral ventricles, there is inward bowing or scalloping of frontal bones (indicated by the arrow in the image below) giving rise to the lemon sign. It is suggestive of spina bifida. It is also characteristically associated with Chiari II Malformation.

Banana Sign (USG)

Anterior curvature of the cerebellum with effacement of the cisterna magna in the posterior fossa is seen as banana sign.

Spalding sign (USG)

It usually appears 7 days after intrauterine death and is caused by liquefaction of the brain matter and softening of the ligamentous structures supporting the vault, leading to irregular overlapping of the cranial bones on one another.

Frog Eye Sign (USG)

It is seen in anencephaly. Due to the absence of calvaria, the orbits appear more prominent. This is known as the "frog-eye sign".

Omphalocele (USG)

It is a congenital midline abdominal wall defect at the base of the umbilical cord insertion, with herniation of the solid abdominal viscera and/or bowel out of the fetal abdomen  (indicated with an asterisk). The extruded abdominal contents are covered in a sac.

Double Bubble Sign (USG)

Dilatation of stomach and first part of duodenum due to duodenal atresia.

Bunch of grapes sign or Snowstorm appearance (USG)

The appearance of multiple cystic spaces or lesions in a complete mole.

Ball sign (X-ray)

It is due to the crumpled up spine of the fetus seen in case of intrauterine death.

Robert’s sign (X-ray)

The presence of gas in the fetal great vessels in case of intrauterine fetal demise is known as Robert's sign.

Stuck twin sign (USG)

Smaller twin is held in a fixed position along the uterine wall due to the severe oligohydramnios. It is seen in twin-twin transfusion syndrome.

Butterfly sign (USG)

Normal appearance of the choroid plexuses on axial imaging of the fetal brain. An absence of this sign suggests holoprosencephaly.

Cloverleaf skull (USG)

Seen in craniosynostosis

Empty amnion sign (USG)

Visualization of an amniotic sac without concomitant visualization of an embryo. It is an indicator of pregnancy failure.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman who presented with complaints of fever and joint pain develops the following lesion on her nose after a few days of taking NSAIDs. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chikungunya

The given history of fever and joint pain along with centrofacial hyperpigmentation shown in the image point towards a diagnosis of chikungunya. Hyperpigmentation associated with chikungunya fever is macular and most commonly affects the nose and cheeks.

Nose pigmentation is striking in cases of Chikungunya fever and is termed as Chik sign. It appears as the fever subsides and persists for about 3-6 months.

Hyperpigmentation of the centrofacial face (nose and cheeks) mimics melasma and may be misdiagnosed if proper history is not taken.

Another close differential is fixed drug eruptions (FDE). FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It is characterized by well-defined brown, hyperpigmented plaques that may follow vesiculobullous lesions. They occur on lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and can cause a burning sensation. They usually present 30 min to 8 h after drug exposure and recur at the same location on re-exposure. NSAIDs, Paracetamol and Co‐trimoxazole are the most common drugs causing FDE.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient was intubated for surgery by a final-year resident. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. End-tidal CO2 concentration

The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography.

Capnography is a non-invasive method of measurement and graphical display of partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) in exhaled breath or the end-tidal CO2. Capnograph is the device used for measurement and capnogram is the CO2 waveform that is displayed. It is the most reliable indicator of endotracheal tube placement.

The proper placement of the endotracheal tube is indicated by a normal CO2 waveform for at least three breaths.

Other signs to confirm proper endotracheal intubation are:

Symmetrical chest rise, presence of equal bilateral breath sounds, absent breath sounds over the epigastrium, visible condensation in the ETT, large exhaled tidal volume, and appropriate compliance of the reservoir bag during manual ventilation.

Absent CO2 waveform tracing despite correct ETT intubation is seen in the following conditions:

• Severe bronchospasm,
• Equipment malfunction,
• Cardiac arrest, or hemodynamic collapse

Clinical relevance:

• Capnography does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation. Signs of endobronchial intubation include increased peak expiratory pressure, hypoxemia, increased airway pressures, asymmetric chest expansion and the absence of breath sounds over one lung, generally the left.
• In esophageal intubation, the capnograph can initially detect some CO2 in the stomach from swallowing expired air. But after a few breaths, this CO2  will be washed out and ETCO2 will become zero.
• The most sensitive and earliest indicator of malignant hyperthermia is a persistent increase in ETCO2.
questions.learning: End-tidal CO2 concentration — The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old chronic alcoholic male presents to the hospital with a history of abdominal pain, dehydration, weakness, and lethargy. Which of the following kidney segments is associated with maximum water reabsorption?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proximal convoluted tubule

The proximal convoluted tubule is the site of maximum water reabsorption about 67% of the filtered water.

The driving force for water reabsorption is a trans tubular osmotic gradient established by the reabsorption of solutes.

Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): Sodium is reabsorbed along with various inorganic and organic substances- chloride, bicarbonate, phosphate, lactate, glucose, and amino acids. In the early PCT, the main sodium channels used for reabsorption are Na+-glucose cotransporter (SGLT), Na+-H+ exchanger, Na+-amino acid cotransporter, Na+-phosphate cotransporter. In the distal PCT, the high chloride concentration in the lumen favors NaCl reabsorption, driven by the Cl− gradient.

Based on the ultrastructure proximal tubule is divided into three segments:

* S1 segment: 1st half of PCT

* S2 segment: 2nd half of PCT and 1st half of proximal straight tubule

* S3 segment: 2nd half of proximal straight tubule

The dilution of urine in water diuresis mainly occurs in the distal parts of the nephron. The proximal convoluted tubule absorbs water and solutes in equal proportions, while the descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to only water. As a result, the urine is concentrated as it enters the ascending limb.

The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water. There is reabsorption of solutes and thus, urine gets diluted. In the absence of vasopressin seen in water diuresis, the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct also remain impermeable to water, while sodium continues to get reabsorbed. Urine becomes hypo-osmolar to plasma. Thus, a large volume of dilute urine is excreted.

In chronic alcoholics, the production and release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, can be impaired. Alcohol inhibits the secretion of ADH from the pituitary gland. This leads to a decreased ability to concentrate urine and increases diuresis, resulting in excessive loss of water. Consequently, the kidneys reabsorb less water, causing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances. Over time, chronic suppression of ADH can lead to persistent polyuria and the risk of developing chronic dehydration and electrolyte disturbances, such as hyponatremia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme activities can be estimated in red blood cells to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutathione reductase

Glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells can be estimated to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency.

Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin. Its active forms are FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide). Glutathione reductase is a FAD-containing enzyme (flavoenzyme). Hence, riboflavin deficiency can be detected by measuring erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity. Red blood cell and urinary concentrations of riboflavin can also be estimated to detect a deficiency.

Deficiency of riboflavin can present as anemia, corneal vascularization, mucocutaneous lesions, and personality changes. Milk and other dairy products are important dietary sources.

Other options:

Option A - Transketolase contains thiamine diphosphate as a coenzyme. Estimation of erythrocyte apotransketolase (enzyme protein) after in vitro addition of thiamine diphosphate, can be used to assess thiamine nutritional status. Thiamine deficiency can result in peripheral neuritis, beriberi, and Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis.

Option C - Kynureninase is an enzyme that requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme. It converts 3-hydroxykynurenine, a tryptophan metabolite, to 3-hydroxyanthranilate. In vitamin B6 deficiency, this is impaired and results in the formation and subsequent urinary excretion of xanthurenate. This can be used for diagnosis.

Option D - Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase for which thiamine diphosphate acts as the cofactor. Therefore thiamine deficiency results in the accumulation of pyruvate. This leads to pyruvic and lactic acidosis, commonly seen in alcoholics.
questions.learning: Glutathione reductase Glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells can be estimated to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency. Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which disorder is characterized by the presence of a cherry-red spot on the retina?
questions.explanation: A cherry-red spot on the retina is a classic clinical finding observed in several metabolic storage disorders and vascular conditions. It occurs because the fovea remains transparent and reveals the underlying red choroid, while the surrounding ganglion cells are swollen and opaque due to the accumulation of storage material. Tay-Sachs disease is the most well-known lysosomal storage disorder associated with this sign, caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A. Fabry's disease (Option B) is more commonly associated with cornea verticillata rather than a cherry-red spot. Gaucher's disease (Option C) typically presents with hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain; while ocular findings exist, they rarely include a classic cherry-red spot. Von Gierke's disease (Option D) is a glycogen storage disease that primarily affects the liver and kidneys, not the retina. Besides storage diseases, a cherry-red spot is also a pathognomonic finding in Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO), which is an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate intervention to restore blood flow
questions.learning: A cherry-red spot on the retina is a classic clinical finding observed in several metabolic storage disorders and vascular conditions. It occurs because the fovea remains transparent and reveals the underlying red choroid, while the surrounding ganglion…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sinus that is labeled in the provided image.
questions.explanation: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities within the skull bones surrounding the nasal cavity. The arrow in the provided image points to the largest paranasal sinus, located within the body of the maxilla, inferior to the orbits. This is the maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore). The frontal sinuses (Option A) are located superior to the orbits within the frontal bone. The ethmoid sinuses (Option C) are a complex of small air cells located between the orbits and the upper nasal cavity. The pyriform sinus (Option B) is not a paranasal sinus; it is a recess in the laryngopharynx, making it an anatomical distractor. The maxillary sinus is clinically significant as it is frequently involved in sinusitis, and its close proximity to the roots of the upper molar teeth means that dental infections can sometimes spread to the sinus. Identifying these structures on imaging or diagrams is fundamental for diagnosing common otorhinolaryngological conditions and planning surgical drainage procedures
questions.learning: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities within the skull bones surrounding the nasal cavity. The arrow in the provided image points to the largest paranasal sinus, located within the body of the maxilla, inferior to the orbits.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A clinical assessment video shows a 7-year-old girl with continuous, slow, writhing involuntary movements involving the hands and fingers. What is the correct semiological term?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Athetosis

Athetosis is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by continuous, slow, sinuous, writhing involuntary movements, predominantly affecting the distal limbs (hands and fingers). These movements often worsen during voluntary activity and disappear during sleep.

The video description of continuous, slow, writhing movements of the hands and fingers is classic for athetosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hemiballismus: Characterized by violent, flinging, large-amplitude movements of one side of the body, usually due to a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.
• C. Chorea: Consists of rapid, irregular, jerky, dance-like movements that flow randomly from one body part to another.
• D. Myoclonus: Characterized by sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks, not slow writhing movements.
questions.learning: Athetosis Athetosis is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by continuous, slow, sinuous, writhing involuntary movements, predominantly affecting the distal limbs (hands and fingers).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3.5 kg term neonate born to a mother with eclampsia, did not cry at birth. Which of the following is the criteria for perinatal asphyxia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypotonia

Among the given options, the essential criterion for perinatal asphyxia is hypotonia.

Perinatal asphyxia is an insult to the fetus or newborn due to a lack of oxygen (hypoxia) and/or a lack of perfusion (ischemia) to the various organs. It is often associated with tissue lactic acidosis and hypercarbia.

Essential criteria for perinatal asphyxia:

• Umbilical arterial blood sample indicating prolonged metabolic or mixed acidemia (pH < 7.O).
• Apgar score of 0-3 persisting for >5 minutes.
• Neurological manifestations appearing in the immediate neonatal period Ex:- seizures, coma, hypotonia, or hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE).
• Neonatal multiorgan dysfunction.
questions.learning: Hypotonia Among the given options, the essential criterion for perinatal asphyxia is hypotonia. Perinatal asphyxia is an insult to the fetus or newborn due to a lack of oxygen (hypoxia) and/or a lack of perfusion (ischemia) to the various organs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical rib

The given X-ray shows cervical rib.

Patients with a cervical rib usually show a lump and tenderness in the supraclavicular fossa. The pallor and paresthesias are due to vascular and neural compressions respectively. A radiograph of the neck is useful in detecting a cervical rib.

However, the absence of a rib on the x-ray does not rule out the possibility of a cervical rib. CT and MRI are more sensitive.
questions.learning: Cervical rib — The given X-ray shows cervical rib. Patients with a cervical rib usually show a lump and tenderness in the supraclavicular fossa.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old community health officer in Jaipur, Dr. Priya Malhotra, is reviewing the healthcare statistics of her jurisdiction. She's observed an upward trend in vaccine-preventable diseases over the past few months. Concerned about this, she's keen on revisiting the immunization strategies to enhance vaccine coverage. She believes that understanding the most recent immunization patterns is pivotal. Which of the following data sources would best provide her with the latest trends of immunization in the community?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. District-level household survey

The District Level Household Survey (DLHS) is an important source of community-level data on maternal and child health indicators, including immunization coverage, making it useful for assessing recent vaccination trends and program performance.

Key features of DLHS:

• Provides district-level health indicators
• Evaluates reproductive and child health services
• Assesses immunization status, institutional deliveries, family planning, and healthcare utilization
• Helps in planning and monitoring public health programs

Why other options are incorrect:

• Census data → Conducted every 10 years; demographic rather than immunization-focused
• Rural survey → Not a standardized national source for immunization trends
• Sample Registration System (SRS) → Primarily provides birth rate, death rate, and infant mortality statistics
questions.learning: District-level household survey — The District Level Household Survey (DLHS) is an important source of community-level data on maternal and child health indicators, including immunization coverage, making it useful for assessing recent vaccination trends…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy with Down syndrome presents with features of superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome and is found to have a mediastinal mass. Bone marrow histopathology findings are available for evaluation. Based on the clinical presentation and histological features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Children with Down syndrome have a significantly increased risk of developing leukemia. Specifically, they have a 20-fold increased risk of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL). The clinical presentation of a mediastinal mass and SVC syndrome is highly characteristic of T-cell ALL, which often presents with a rapidly growing anterior mediastinal mass. The provided histology showing a dense population of small-to-medium lymphoblasts with scant cytoplasm and inconspicuous nucleoli confirms a diagnosis of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML, Option A) is also common in Down syndrome, particularly the megakaryoblastic subtype (M7) in children under 3 years old, but it typically does not present as a mediastinal mass. Aplastic anemia (Option B) would show a hypocellular marrow. Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (Option C) is a rare chronic myeloid disorder with different clinical features. In this 10-year-old patient, the combination of Down syndrome, a mediastinal mass, and lymphoid-predominant histology makes ALL the most definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Children with Down syndrome have a significantly increased risk of developing leukemia. Specifically, they have a 20-fold increased risk of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the first line therapy for aborting the acute attack of cluster headache?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 100% oxygen

Cluster Headache?

• A type of Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC)
• Characterized by:

• Severe unilateral orbital/temporal pain
• Associated autonomic symptoms:

• Lacrimation
• Nasal congestion
• Ptosis

Often called “suicide headache” due to intensity

Oxygen works by-

• Causes cerebral vasoconstriction
• Reduces trigeminal nerve activation
• Modulates hypothalamic activity

Result:

• Rapid pain relief within 10–15 minutes

| Drug | Role | Use in Cluster Headache

| ---- | ---- | -----------------------

| Oxygen | Vasoconstriction | First-line acute

| Sumatriptan | 5-HT agonist | Acute (2nd line)

| Lithium | Mood stabilizer |  Prophylaxis only

| Topiramate | AED |  Prophylaxis only

| Feature | Cluster | Migraine

| ------- | ------- | --------

| Behavior | Restless | Wants to lie down

| Autonomic signs | Prominent | Mild/absent

| Duration | Short (minutes–hours) | Long (hours–days)

| Oxygen response | Excellent | No role

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following staging systems is used in Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fisch staging system

The Fisch staging system is used in the case of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibromas.

Type
Details

1
Tumour limited to the nasopharyngeal cavity; bone destruction negligible or limited to the sphenopalatine foramen

2
Tumour invading the pterygopalatine fossa or the maxillary, ethmoid, or sphenoid sinus with bone destruction

3
A: Tumour invading the infratemporal fossa or orbital region without intracranial involvement
B: Tumour invading the infratemporal fossa or orbital region with intracranial extradural (parasellar) involvement

4
A: Intracranial intradural tumor without infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm
B: Intracranial intradural tumor with infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Other options:

Option A: Duke staging system is done in cases of colorectal cancer

Option C: Ann arbor staging system is used in Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

Option D: TNM staging system is used to classify malignancies. It is most commonly utilized in solid tumors and can help with prognostic cancer staging. The system evaluates the tumor size, regional lymph nodes, and distant metastases.
