questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following postmortem changes is shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marbling

The postmortem change shown above is marbling.

The blood in the vessels is hemolyzed, which stains the vessel walls and the adjacent tissues, giving rise to a marbled appearance. The marbling of the skin becomes prominent about 36–48 hours after death in summer and is distinctly appreciable in the superficial veins of the abdomen, shoulders, chest, and inguinal region.
questions.learning: Marbling — The postmortem change shown above is marbling. The blood in the vessels is hemolyzed, which stains the vessel walls and the adjacent tissues, giving rise to a marbled appearance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the preferred initial management for a patient presenting with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea?
options: Bed rest with head elevation and avoidance of straining activities
Immediate surgical repair without initial medical management
questions.explanation: Most traumatic CSF leaks, such as those following head injury or sinus surgery, resolve spontaneously without the need for immediate surgical intervention. The preferred initial approach is conservative medical management. This includes absolute bed rest with the head of the bed elevated at 30-40 degrees to lower intracranial pressure. The patient must strictly avoid activities that increase intracranial pressure (straining), such as nose blowing, coughing, or heavy lifting (Valsalva maneuvers), which can push air into the skull or prevent the dural tear from sealing. FESS (Option A) and other surgical repairs (Option D) are reserved for leaks that persist beyond 7-14 days of conservative care. Steroids (Option B) have no proven role in sealing a leak and may theoretically increase the risk of infection. Prophylactic antibiotics are also generally avoided to prevent the selection of resistant organisms should meningitis eventually occur
questions.learning: Most traumatic CSF leaks, such as those following head injury or sinus surgery, resolve spontaneously without the need for immediate surgical intervention.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following muscles primarily functions as an abductor of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) is the only muscle that functions as a true abductor of the vocal cords. By rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally, it opens the rima glottidis, which is essential for breathing. Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which supplies this muscle, can lead to vocal cord paralysis in an adducted position, potentially causing airway obstruction. Option A (Lateral cricoarytenoid) is a primary adductor, closing the vocal cords for speech and swallowing. Option C (Thyroarytenoid) and Option D (Vocalis) are involved in shortening and relaxing the vocal cords to change the pitch and quality of the voice. Because the PCA is the "safety muscle" of the larynx, its function is paramount during surgery on the thyroid or neck. Bilateral PCA paralysis is a medical emergency requiring tracheostomy or surgical lateralization of the cords to restore an adequate airway for the patient
questions.learning: The posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) is the only muscle that functions as a true abductor of the vocal cords. By rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally, it opens the rima glottidis, which is essential for breathing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Pacinian corpuscle is stimulated by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pressure

Pacinian corpuscle is stimulated by pressure.

Pacinian corpuscles are the largest cutaneous mechanoreceptors. They are present in the dermis of glabrous and hairy skin. They are composed of a nerve ending which is encapsulated by concentric layers of connective tissue that give it an onion-like appearance. These receptors respond to fast vibration and deep pressure and adapt very rapidly. The sensory nerves from cutaneous mechanoreceptors are myelinated Aα and Aβ fibers.

Image shows histology of Pacinian corpuscle.

Other mechanoreceptors:

• Meissner's corpuscles are present mainly in the dermis of non-hairy skin particularly in the fingertips, lips, and other locations where tactile discrimination is well developed. They have small receptive fields and can be used for two point discrimination. Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors that sense point discrimination, precise location, tapping, and flutter. These are encapsulated nerve endings of a large myelinated sensory nerve (Aβ type).

The image shows the histology of Meissner's corpuscle in the dermis.

• Merkel discs are seen in the epidermis of glabrous skin. They are slowly adapting receptors and have very small receptive fields. These receptors detect vertical indentations of the skin. They are expanded dendritic endings.
• Ruffini corpuscles are capsulated, enlarged, dendritic endings. They are located in the dermis of glabrous and hairy skin, and in joint capsules. They are slowly adapting receptors. Ruffini corpuscles detect stretch and joint rotation.

Pain and temperature sensations arise from receptors located on unmyelinated sensory neurons present throughout the glabrous skin, hairy skin, and deep tissue. Impulses from nociceptors are transmitted via thinly myelinated Aδ fibers and unmyelinated C fibers.

Activation of Aδ fibers is responsible for first pain (also called fast pain). It is a rapid response and helps in the discrimination of pain or the ability to localize the site and intensity of the noxious stimulus. It is mediated by the release of glutamate. An example is pinprick.

Activation of C fibers is responsible for delayed second pain(also called slow pain). It is a dull, intense, diffuse, and unpleasant feeling associated with a noxious stimulus. . Second pain is mediated by the release of a combination of glutamate and substance P. Example is visceral pain.

Types of nociceptors :

• Mechanical nociceptors respond to strong pressure (eg, from a sharp object).
• Thermal nociceptors are activated by skin temperatures above 45°C or by severe cold (<20°C).
• Chemically sensitive nociceptors respond to chemicals such as bradykinin, histamine, high acidity, and environmental irritants.
• Polymodal nociceptors respond to combinations of these stimuli.
questions.learning: Pressure Pacinian corpuscle is stimulated by pressure. Pacinian corpuscles are the largest cutaneous mechanoreceptors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain, numbness of both lower limbs and the right upper limb, and generalized malaise. On examination, his pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. All peripheral pulses are palpable. Laboratory evaluation shows: Normal renal function Urinalysis: proteinuria with RBCs but no casts Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Classical polyarteritis nodosa

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that causes multisystem ischemia without glomerulonephritis.

• Severe abdominal pain (mesenteric ischemia)
• Mononeuritis multiplex → limb numbness/neuropathy
• Hypertension due to renal artery involvement
• Constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise)

Renal findings:

• Renal ischemia → hypertension
• Proteinuria and hematuria without RBC casts
• No glomerulonephritis (distinguishes from microscopic polyangiitis and GPA)

Thus, systemic symptoms + neuropathy + abdominal pain + hypertension with preserved renal function strongly suggest classical PAN.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which test uses the graph given below to assess the viral load in a test sample ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Real time RTPCR

The image shows the Ct value(Cycle threshold) of Real-time RTPCR which can be used to assess the viral genetic load.

The image shows a graph with cycle number on the X-axis and relative fluorescence on the Y-axis. At 25.6 there is an exponential rise in the fluorescence which is the Ct value for the sample.

The cycle threshold (Ct) can be defined as the thermal cycle number at which the fluorescent signal exceeds that of the background and thus passes the threshold for positivity.

The first step for a real-time RTPCR is by extracting the viral RNA from the sample followed by purifying and concentrating it. They are then added to a mixture of primers, nucleotide bases, enzymes for the reaction, and fluorescently labeled probes (short stretches of nucleic acid which stick to the target ). The primers initially attach to the viral nucleic acid which is RNA and a complementary DNA strand is made using the nucleotides in the mixture. It is then subjected to repeated thermal cycles so that the copies of the viral targets are increased. The labeled probes stick to the viral genome and emit a fluorescent signal. An exponential rise occurs early when the viral load in the sample is high when compared to a less viral load.

A typical RT-PCR assay will have a maximum of 40 thermal cycles. The lower the Ct value the higher the quantity of viral genetic material in the sample.

A 3-point increase in Ct value is roughly equivalent to a 10-fold decrease in the quantity of viral genetic material. Low Ct values more likely indicate acute disease and high infectivity whereas high Ct values can be attributed to reduced viral load but might need clinical interpretation.

Note:

Ct values cannot be used to compare different types of assays nor does it provide information on the course of the illness. However, it can be used for clinical management in a hospital setting.
questions.learning: Real time RTPCR — The image shows the Ct value(Cycle threshold) of Real-time RTPCR which can be used to assess the viral genetic load. The image shows a graph with cycle number on the X-axis and relative fluorescence on the Y-axis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Inspiratory stridor is found in what kind of lesions:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supraglottic

Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi such as bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea like laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Stridor is an audible respiratory noise that gets produced by turbulent airflow through an obstructed upper airway. It is an inspiratory sound that may have an expiratory component. It is distinct from stertor which is a snoring-like noise produced from an obstructed nasopharynx or oropharynx.

The intensity and pitch of sounds originating from the respiratory system vary based on their site of origin within the respiratory tract and may be heard with or without a stethoscope. Usually, the pitch of the sound increases, and the intensity decreases as one goes lower into the respiratory tract.
questions.learning: Supraglottic Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a 15-year history of smoking one pack per day presents with hemoptysis. Chest X-ray reveals a 3 cm mass in the upper lobe near the lung apex. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: For a peripheral lung mass, specifically one located in the upper lobe near the apex (Pancoast tumor region or peripheral nodule), a CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy is the most appropriate next step to obtain a tissue diagnosis. This method provides high diagnostic yield for peripheral lesions that are difficult to reach via internal airways. Bronchoscopy (Option A) is better suited for central masses that are visible within the larger bronchial trees; peripheral masses are often beyond the reach of standard fiberoptic bronchoscopes. Sputum cytology (Option C) has a low sensitivity for diagnosing lung cancer and is rarely the definitive next step for a 3 cm mass. Sputum for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) (Option D) is used to rule out tuberculosis (TB); while TB is a differential for a lung mass, the smoking history and mass characteristics strongly mandate ruling out malignancy first via biopsy. Therefore, CT-guided biopsy provides the necessary pathology to guide subsequent cancer staging and treatment
questions.learning: For a peripheral lung mass, specifically one located in the upper lobe near the apex (Pancoast tumor region or peripheral nodule), a CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy is the most appropriate next step to obtain a tissue diagnosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to ______________ ?
options: Sodium influx via voltage gated sodium channels
Influx of both sodium and calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium currents only

The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to calcium currents only. It occurs due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.

The action potential of the SA node differs from that of the atria, ventricles, and Purkinje fibres in the following ways: (1) In the absence of neural input, the SA node demonstrates automaticity and the ability to produce its own action potentials. (2) It has an unstable resting membrane potential. (3) It has no sustained plateau.

The resting membrane potential (RMP) of the SA node is -55 to -60 millivolts. Phases of this potential are:

• Phase 0 (Upstroke wave)-  This is due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.
• Phase 3 (Downstroke wave)- This is due to the efflux of K+ leading to repolarization. (Option C)
• Phase 4 (Prepotential)- Because of ongoing K+ efflux, hyperpolarization sets in. This makes the channel more permeable to Na+ ions and since these Na+ channels are activated during hyperpolarization they are referred to as funny currents (Ih/ If). They form the first half of the pre-potential. The second half of the prepotential is completed by the opening of the voltage-gated T-(transient) type Ca2+ channel. The slope of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.
questions.learning: Calcium currents only — The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to calcium currents only. It occurs due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following is not true according to case-control study?
questions.explanation: A case-control study is a retrospective observational study design. It begins by identifying individuals who already have the outcome/disease (cases) and comparing them to those without it (controls). Therefore, it moves backward from the effect to the cause (Option A). Because researchers start with existing cases, this design is the most efficient and preferred method for studying rare diseases (Option B). The standard measure of association calculated in a case-control study is the Odds Ratio (Option C). The statement "Cause to effect" (Option D) is NOT true for case-control studies; instead, it describes a cohort study, which follows an exposed group over time to see who develops the disease. Understanding these directional differences is critical for selecting the appropriate study design for an epidemiologic investigation and interpreting its results correctly
questions.learning: A case-control study is a retrospective observational study design. It begins by identifying individuals who already have the outcome/disease (cases) and comparing them to those without it (controls).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use presents with recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back and significant weight loss. He reports steatorrhea for the past 6 months. Imaging shows pancreatic calcifications and a dilated pancreatic duct measuring 9 mm with multiple intraductal calculi. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive surgical management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Puestow procedure

This patient has chronic pancreatitis with:

• Dilated pancreatic duct (>7 mm)
• Intraductal calculi
• Pain and exocrine insufficiency

The preferred surgical treatment in such cases is a drainage procedure, specifically longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow procedure).

• “Large duct disease” (duct >7 mm) → drainage procedure
• “Small duct disease” → resection procedures

Why Puestow procedure:

• Longitudinal opening of pancreatic duct
• Anastomosis with jejunum
• Relieves ductal hypertension → pain relief

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Whipple is indicated for malignancy or head-dominant disease without ductal dilatation

B. Distal pancreatectomy is for disease limited to tail

D. Total pancreatectomy leads to brittle diabetes and is rarely first-line

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During your rural posting, you are asked to educate a small, uneducated village about the importance of routine antenatal care for pregnant mothers. You want to deliver some statistical data to emphasize its importance. Which of the following is the best way to do so?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pictogram

Pictogram is the best method of presenting data among people, who cannot understand orthodox charts.

In this method, small pictures or symbols are used to present the data. Fractions of the picture are used to represent numbers smaller than the value of a whole symbol. Basically, pictograms are a form of bar charts.

Other options

Option B- Line diagrams are mainly used to show the trend of events in a given period of time. For example trend of dengue cases in Asia during 2018-21.

Option C- Histogram is a pictorial diagram of a frequency distribution that consists of a series of blocks. The frequencies are given along the vertical axis and class intervals on the horizontal axis. The area of each block obtained is proportional to frequency.

Option D- Frequency polygon is the diagrammatical representation of frequency distribution obtained by joining the midpoints of the histogram blocks.

Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following is a histogram of cholesterol levels from the Framingham Heart Study.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.
questions.learning: Pictogram Pictogram is the best method of presenting data among people, who cannot understand orthodox charts. In this method, small pictures or symbols are used to present the data.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A software engineer presents to the outpatient department with easy fatiguability. He gives a history of sitting in front of the computer for 12 - 14 hours. He consumes a lot of junk food with very less fruits and vegetables. Hb is 9gm/dl and MCV 120 fl. What is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folic acid deficiency

The given laboratory values showing anemia and increased MCV are suggestive of megaloblastic anemia. This could be due to cyanocobalamin deficiency or folic acid deficiency. The history of inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables points towards folic acid deficiency.

Dietary sources of Vit-B12 are animal products such as meat, fish, milk, and eggs. Dietary sources of folic acid are green vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, asparagus, and broccoli.

Megaloblastic anemia can occur due to Vit-B12 or folic acid deficiency. Inadequate intake, intrinsic factor deficiency, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, malabsorption, ileal resection, alcoholism, anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, infancy, disseminated cancer, markedly increased hematopoiesis, folic acid antagonists are some of the causes.

Patient can present with anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, constipation, glossitis, angular cheilosis, reversible melanin skin hyperpigmentation, paresthesias, muscle weakness, dementia, or psychotic disturbances.

In megaloblastic anemia, DNA synthesis is impaired that leading to ineffective hematopoiesis and distinctive morphologic changes.

Peripheral blood examination shows oval macrocytes, usually with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis. MCV is usually >100 fL. The normal value of MCV is between 80-100 fL. Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated. The reticulocyte count is low. Neutrophils are larger than normal and show nuclear hypersegmentation with five or more nuclear lobules.

Marrow is markedly hypercellular. Megaloblastic changes are seen at all stages of erythroid development. There is nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony, where nuclear maturation is slower than cytoplasmic maturation. Granulocytic precursors are seen in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms. Megakaryocytes may be abnormally large with bizarre, multilobate nuclei.

Peripheral blood smear showing hypersegmented neutrophil:

Other options:

Option A - In cyanocobalamin deficiency, MCV will be increased. But the dietary sources of cyanocobalamin are mainly of animal products. In the given clinical scenario there is inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables. Hence, this is not the answer.

Option C - In iron deficiency anemia, MCV will be decreased.

Option D - In hereditary spherocytosis, MCV will be normal.
questions.learning: Folic acid deficiency — The given laboratory values showing anemia and increased MCV are suggestive of megaloblastic anemia. This could be due to cyanocobalamin deficiency or folic acid deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing are correct? 1. Reduces bacterial load 2. Maximum pressure is -125mm of Hg 3. Promotes granulation tissue 4. Reduces size of wound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3 and 4

All statements about Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) dressing are correct.

| Statement | Explanation

| --------- | -----------

| Reduces bacterial load | Continuous suction removes exudate, debris, and bacteria, lowering infection risk.

| Maximum pressure −125 mmHg | Standard optimal negative pressure used in VAC therapy is around −125 mmHg.

| Promotes granulation tissue | Negative pressure increases blood flow and angiogenesis, stimulating granulation tissue formation.

| Reduces size of wound | VAC causes macrodeformation, pulling wound edges together and decreasing wound size.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-week-old neonate is brought with fever, poor feeding, and irritability. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained on lumbar puncture appears cloudy, with a total cell count of 500 cells/ mm³ predominantly neutrophils. Culture of the CSF reveals an organism that is resistant to bacitracin. Based on these findings, which organism is the most likely cause of meningitis in this infant?
questions.explanation: In a 2-week-old neonate, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis is Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS). The CSF profile (high neutrophils, cloudy appearance) confirms acute bacterial infection. The key microbiological differentiator is bacitracin resistance; GBS is characteristically resistant to bacitracin, whereas Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) (Option B) is highly sensitive. Pneumococcus (Option A) and Meningococci (Option D) are common causes of meningitis in older children and adults but are less frequent than GBS in the first month of life. GBS is typically acquired from the maternal urogenital tract during labor. Management involves immediate, high-dose intravenous antibiotics (typically ampicillin and gentamicin). Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis has significantly reduced the incidence of early-onset disease, but late-onset meningitis (appearing after the first week) remains a significant neonatal challenge
questions.learning: In a 2-week-old neonate, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis is Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS). The CSF profile (high neutrophils, cloudy appearance) confirms acute bacterial infection.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A dead body is discovered with multiple injuries consistent with a violent assault. Examination reveals one bruise on the right side of the neck and three linear bruises on the left side, along with curved, semilunar abrasions beneath the angle of the jaw and a fractured hyoid bone. Additional injuries are noted on the left thigh, back, scapula, pelvis, and shoulder, with associated fractures. Based on these findings, what is the most likely cause of death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Throttling

Throttling (manual strangulation) is characterized by finger and thumb pressure marks on the neck, along with internal injuries such as hyoid bone fracture.

• Asymmetrical bruises on neck:

• Single bruise on one side (thumb)
• Multiple bruises on opposite side (fingers)

• Semilunar (crescent-shaped) abrasions:

• Caused by fingernails

• Fractured hyoid bone:

• Strong indicator of manual strangulation

Associated findings:

• Signs of struggle/assault:

• Injuries on thigh, back, scapula, pelvis, shoulder

• May have congestion, petechiae, cyanosis

Why not others:

• Ligature strangulation: Continuous ligature mark, not finger marks
• Gagging: No neck compression signs
• Mugging: Non-specific trauma, lacks classical neck findings

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following steps is not included in STEP approach of WHO?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Therapeutic assessment

Therapeutic assessment is not included in the STEP approach of WHO.

STEP approach of WHO is a survey methodology developed to assess risk factors of non-communicable diseases(NCD). It helps the countries to establish an NCD surveillance system. The steps include the following:

• Questionnaires contain questions about behavioral risk factors like tobacco use, alcohol use, diet, and physical activity.
• Physical measurements contain blood pressure, height, weight, and waist size
• Biochemical measurements contain blood glucose, blood lipids, urinary sodium, and creatinine.

Note: Mental health and suicide are included in optional behavioral risk factors (step 1). Hence, psychological assessment is also included in the STEP approach.

Surveillance is defined as systematic and continuous data analysis and taking appropriate preventive actions according to the results obtained. Identification of cases that are missed and not notified is known as sentinel surveillance. It is used in communicable diseases such as HIV, malaria, etc. The study population for HIV sentinel surveillance are sex workers, IV drug abusers, transgender people, migrant workers, truck drivers, etc.
questions.learning: Therapeutic assessment — Therapeutic assessment is not included in the STEP approach of WHO. STEP approach of WHO is a survey methodology developed to assess risk factors of non-communicable diseases(NCD).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which type of epithelium lines the inner surface of the fallopian tube?
questions.explanation: The fallopian tubes (uterine tubes) are lined with a specialized mucosa designed to facilitate the transport of gametes and the early embryo. This lining consists of simple ciliated columnar epithelium. These ciliated cells work in coordination with secretory (peg) cells; the cilia beat rhythmically toward the uterus to help move the secondary oocyte and subsequently the zygote. Simple columnar epithelium without cilia (Option A) is typical of the gastrointestinal tract. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (Option B) is the "respiratory epithelium" found in the trachea and large bronchi. Cuboidal epithelium with microvilli (Option D) is characteristic of the proximal convoluted tubules in the kidney. The presence of cilia is the defining feature of the fallopian tube epithelium required for reproductive function. Therefore, because these cells are single-layered, tall, and possess active cilia, ciliated columnar epithelium is the accurate histological classification
questions.learning: The fallopian tubes (uterine tubes) are lined with a specialized mucosa designed to facilitate the transport of gametes and the early embryo. This lining consists of simple ciliated columnar epithelium.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary PPH?

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with diarrhea is eager to drink, but the skin pinch returns slowly. According to IMNCI guidelines, into which category does this child fall?
questions.explanation: Under the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines, the classification of dehydration is based on specific clinical signs. A child who is eager to drink (thirsty) and has a skin pinch that goes back slowly (less than 2 seconds) meets the criteria for "Some Dehydration", which is coded as the Yellow category. The Pink category (Option A) is for "Severe Dehydration," characterized by lethargy, inability to drink, and a skin pinch that goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds). The Green category (Option C) is for "No Dehydration," where the child has none of these signs. Management for the Yellow category involves "Plan B" rehydration—providing oral rehydration solution (ORS) in the health facility over a 4-hour period while monitoring the child’s progress. This standardized color-coded system allows health workers to rapidly identify the severity of illness and initiate life-saving treatment protocols in resource-limited settings
questions.learning: Under the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines, the classification of dehydration is based on specific clinical signs.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate initial treatment for an infertile woman diagnosed with bilateral cornual block on Hysterosalpingography? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hysteroscopic Cannulation

Cornual (proximal tubal) block on hysterosalpingography (HSG) may be due to:

• Tubal spasm
• Mucus plugs
• Debris
• True proximal tubal obstruction

The initial management is hysteroscopic or transcervical tubal cannulation, which:

• Confirms true obstruction
• Can restore tubal patency
• Is minimally invasive

Why other options are incorrect:

• IVF is reserved when tubal recanalization fails or severe tubal disease exists
• Salpingectomy is mainly indicated for hydrosalpinx or damaged tubes before IVF
• Salpingostomy is used for distal tubal obstruction, not proximal cornual block

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The viruses of the filoviridae family like Ebola and Marburg resemble which of the following morphologies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

Viruses belonging to the filoviridae family, such as Ebola and Marburg, resemble the morphology shown in image 3.

Image 1- Influenza virus -  Influenza viruses have a linear, segmented, single-stranded RNA.

Image 2- Adenovirus contains double-stranded DNA. They have an icosahedral symmetry with structures known as fibers extruding from the vertices.

Image 3 - Ebola viruses are filamentous viruses with nonsegmented single-stranded RNA as genetic material.

Image 4 - Corona virus belonging to the family  are shaped viruses with nonsegmented single-stranded RNA. Corona virus has petal/club-shaped peplomers radiating like sunrays.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In the National Malaria Control Programme, Indoor Residual Spray (IRS) is the primary method of vector control in rural settings. Which one of the following is the insecticide of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synthetic pyrethroid

Indoor Residual Spray (IRS) is a key vector control strategy under the National Malaria Control/Elimination Programme. IRS involves spraying the inside walls and ceilings of houses with long-acting insecticides to kill mosquitoes resting indoors after feeding. Synthetic pyrethroids are currently the insecticides of choice for IRS in most areas because of their high efficacy and safety profile.

• Examples: Deltamethrin, Alpha-cypermethrin, Lambda-cyhalothrin
• Advantages:

• Highly effective against Anopheles mosquitoes
• Long residual action
• Lower mammalian toxicity
• Widely used due to increasing resistance to DDT

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. DDT: Previously the mainstay of IRS but its use has declined due to widespread insecticide resistance in malaria vectors.
• B. Malathion: An organophosphate used mainly where resistance to other insecticides exists or for specific vector control programs; not the current insecticide of choice.
• D. Temephos: A larvicide, used to control mosquito larvae in water bodies, not for indoor residual spraying.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a lesion involving the right lateral lemniscus presents with hearing difficulty. Which of the following is the most likely clinical finding?
options: Complete hearing loss in the right ear
Complete hearing loss in the left ear
Partial hearing loss in both ears
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Partial hearing loss in both ears

The central auditory pathway is bilaterally represented from the level of the cochlear nuclei onward:

• Cochlea → Cochlear nuclei → bilateral crossing (trapezoid body) → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex
• Because decussation occurs early (predominantly at the trapezoid body, with contributions continuing at multiple levels), each cochlear nucleus projects to both the ipsilateral and contralateral lateral lemniscus/superior olivary complex. This means each ear's signal is represented in both hemispheres beyond the brainstem entry point.

Clinical significance:

• Peripheral lesions (cochlea, auditory nerve, cochlear nucleus itself) → unilateral, often complete hearing loss, since these are pre-decussation and represent only one ear.
• Central lesions (lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body, auditory cortex) → partial, bilateral hearing loss — true "cortical deafness" or complete central deafness is rare and requires bilateral lesions.

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Complete hearing loss in the right ear, B. Complete hearing loss in the left ear: Complete unilateral deafness implies a peripheral (pre-crossing) lesion — cochlea, auditory nerve, or cochlear nucleus — not a lateral lemniscus lesion.
• D. No significant hearing deficit: A lesion at this level does produce a measurable deficit, just not complete or purely unilateral.
questions.learning: Partial hearing loss in both ears — The central auditory pathway is bilaterally represented from the level of the cochlear nuclei onward: • Cochlea → Cochlear nuclei → bilateral crossing (trapezoid body) → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus →…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old male was diagnosed with achalasia cardia. High-resolution manometry revealed massive, simultaneous, high-pressure contractions of the distal oesophagus. According to the Chicago classification, the patient has which type of achalasia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type III

The given features are suggestive of type III achalasia cardia.

Type III achalasia cardia is characterised by massive, simultaneous, high-pressure contractions of the distal esophagus.

Achalasia cardia occurs due to the loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of GIT. During swallowing, the food bolus normally triggers a primary peristaltic wave, which is responsible for carrying the bolus to the stomach, accompanied by the relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to allow esophageal emptying into the stomach.

Achalasia is characterized by a disruption of this normal process. Failure of relaxation of the LES causes an elevated median integrated relaxation pressure and a complete failure of peristalsis. The esophagus becomes progressively more tortuous, leading to a megaesophagus.
questions.learning: Type III — The given features are suggestive of type III achalasia cardia. Type III achalasia cardia is characterised by massive, simultaneous, high-pressure contractions of the distal esophagus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The co-factor for glutathione peroxidase is __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Selenium

Selenium act as a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase.

Glutathione peroxidases:

* Also known as selenoproteins

* Selenium-containing glutathione peroxidases help transform hydrogen peroxide to harmless water (anti–oxidant action)

* Selenium deficiency results in Impaired function of glutathione peroxidases. As a result, destructive hydrogen peroxide breaks down into even more dangerous hydroxyl radical which damages cell membranes and cell DNA leading to serious disease

Selenium:

Selenium is an important trace element that is a part of the 21st amino acid selenocysteine.

There are many selenium-containing enzymes such as :

* Glutathione peroxidase

* De-iodinase

* Thioredoxin reductase

Selenium is also an intracellular antioxidant that complements the role of Vitamin E. Dietary sources of selenium include seafood, muscle meat, and some cereals.

Note:

Keshan Disease: Endemic cardiomyopathy.
Population affected: Primarily children and young women.
Location: Occurs in areas of China with low dietary selenium intake.
Cause: Linked to selenium deficiency in the diet.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with a history of smoking and diagnosed hypertension presents to the outpatient department for a routine health evaluation. As part of cardiovascular risk assessment, a device is used to evaluate vascular health and arterial status. The device is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding its functions and capabilities is NOT correct?
options: Based on infrared emitted from RBC's
Check thickness of artery and vein
questions.explanation: The device shown is a Doppler ultrasound machine, which is a cornerstone for evaluating vascular health. The statement that it is "based on infrared emitted from RBC's" (Option A) is NOT accurate. Doppler technology is based on the Doppler shift principle, where high-frequency ultrasound waves (sound, not light/infrared) reflect off moving red blood cells to determine the velocity and direction of blood flow. The other statements are accurate: the device checks blood flow (Option B) to identify stenosis or occlusion; it can localize calcified plaques (Option C) which appear as bright echogenic areas with shadowing; and it can check the thickness of the vessel walls (Option D), such as measuring the carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) as a marker of atherosclerosis. Doppler ultrasound is a non-invasive, safe, and highly effective tool for assessing cardiovascular risk in hypertensive patients and smokers. Understanding the fundamental physics of ultrasound versus infrared is essential for clinical practice
questions.learning: The device shown is a Doppler ultrasound machine, which is a cornerstone for evaluating vascular health. The statement that it is "based on infrared emitted from RBC's" (Option A) is NOT accurate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is restitution in the events of labour?
options: Head rotated by 1/8th of a circle
Head rotating due to untwisting of the neck
The shoulder undergoing rotation by 1/8th of circle
The movement by which the head is born
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Head rotating due to untwisting of the neck

During a normal vaginal delivery, the fetal head undergoes a series of movements called the cardinal movements of labour.

The sequence is:

1. Engagement
2. Descent
3. Flexion
4. Internal rotation
5. Extension
6. Restitution
7. External rotation

| Feature | Restitution | External Rotation

| ------- | ----------- | -----------------

| Cause | Untwisting of neck | Shoulder rotation

| Degree of rotation | \~45° (1/8 circle) | Further rotation

| Occurs when | Immediately after head delivery | After restitution

| Purpose | Align head with shoulders | Align shoulders with pelvis

A) Head rotated by 1/8th of a circle

Although restitution involves 1/8th rotation, the definition emphasizes that it occurs due to untwisting of the neck.

C) Shoulder undergoing rotation by 1/8th circle

This describes internal rotation of the shoulders, not restitution.

D) Movement by which the head is born

This refers to extension, not restitution.

“ReSTitution = Straightening of the neck.”
questions.learning: Head rotating due to untwisting of the neck During a normal vaginal delivery, the fetal head undergoes a series of movements called the cardinal movements of labour.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant was brought to the OPD with complaints of poor feeding and irritability. On examination, neck rigidity was present. Her sister has been on antitubercular therapy for 2 months. What are the CSF analysis findings expected in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymphocytosis, low sugar, high protein

The given clinical scenario, along with a neck stiffness and contact with patient of tuberculosis is suggestive of TB meningitis. The CSF picture is lymphocytosis, with low sugar and high protein

Tuberculous meningitis is the most severe form of tuberculosis.

Predisposing factors

* Young age

* Household contact

* Recent measles

* Protein-energy malnutrition

After the initial infection, the disease presents with vague symptoms accompanied by intermittent bacillemia. These feed the meninges forming Rich's foci. When the body's immunity is lowered during stress or coinfections, these ruptures cause widespread meningitis

Clinical Features

* Prodromal phase: irregular fever, anorexia, irritability and occasional vomiting. These could last 1 to 4 weeks

* The second stage has the nervous system involvement, with seizures, focal deficits and meningeal signs.

* The third stage is one of coma and sequelae like Hydrocephalus (communicating or obstructive), decerebrate posturing, cranial nerve palsies, optic atrophy, extrapyramidal signs, and focal deficits.

Diagnosis:

* CSP typically shows raised pressure, lymphocytic predominance, high protein, and low sugar

* Imaging can show exudates and if present, features of the sequelae

* The diagnosis is confirmed detection of tubercular bacilli in CSF. This can be by culture or cartridge-based tests like Gene Xpert

Treatment includes antitubercular treatment with two months of four drug-intensive therapy(HRZE) and 10 months of two-drug (maintenance) therapy  Sometimes, intravenous is dexamethasone is followed by oral administered for 8-12 weeks. This is to prevent sequelae of TB.. Patients with severe hydrocephalus may require shunts or ventriculostomy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised A woman presented in her 8th week of pregnancy seeking MTP. What is the appropriate dosage of Misoprostol administered by the mucosal route?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 800 mcg

The dosage of Misoprostol administered by mucosal route in this case, is 800 mcg.

Mucosal misoprostol administration has increased efficacy and minimizes gastrointestinal side effects and is now preferred over the prior oral administration. The mucosal route includes buccal, sublingual, and vaginal.

Medical management protocol for induced abortion for < 12 weeks of gestation (As per WHO 2018 guideline):

* Combined Regimen (Recommended): 200 mg of oral Mifepristone followed 1-2 days later by 800 mcg of buccal, vaginal or sublingual Misoprostol

* Misoprostol-only regimen (Alternative): 800 μg misoprostol administered vaginally, sublingually, or buccally.

Outpatient medical abortion is an acceptable option for pregnancies with a menstrual age < 63 days (9 weeks)

Various regimens for medical termination of pregnancy

First trimester

* Mifepristone/Misoprostol Combined Regimen (Recommended)

* Misoprostol-only regimen (Alternative)

Second Trimester

* Mifepristone/Misoprostol Combined Regimen (Recommended): 200 mg of oral Mifepristone followed 1-2 days later by 400 mcg of buccal, vaginal or sublingual Misoprostol every 3 hours

* Misoprostol Alone(Alternative): 400 mcg of buccal, vaginal or sublingual Misoprostol every 3 hours

* Dinoprostone- 20 mg vaginal suppository every 4 hr

* Concentrated Oxytocin- 50 units of oxytocin in 500 mL of normal saline infused in an incremental fashion through 150, 200, 250, and finally 300 units of oxytocin each in 500 mL of normal saline

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: 800 mcg The dosage of Misoprostol administered by mucosal route in this case, is 800 mcg. Mucosal misoprostol administration has increased efficacy and minimizes gastrointestinal side effects and is now preferred over the prior oral administration.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A young female patient presents with ptosis which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. What is the most probable cause?
options: Decreased calcium influx at presynaptic membrane
Increased sodium influx at postsynaptic membrane
Antibody against Ach receptor at postsynaptic membrane
Increased endplate potential at postsynaptic membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antibody against Ach receptor at postsynaptic membrane

The most probable cause in the given case is myasthenia gravis, which is due to antibodies against the Ach receptor at the postsynaptic membrane.

Intermittent ptosis is considered one of the earliest signs of myasthenia gravis. Pyridostigmine is the preferred treatment for symptomatic patients at this stage of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterised by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the postsynaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Hence, the goal is to increase the duration of action of acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase. The most commonly used anticholinesterase drug is pyridostigmine.

Females are more commonly affected than males. It occurs in individuals of all ages, but the highest incidence is seen in women during their twenties and thirties, and in men during their fifties and sixties.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles, particularly the lids and extraocular muscles, are involved early in the course – diplopia, ptosis.

* Facial weakness – snarling expression when smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of the palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis – acute exacerbation of muscle weakness, especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles, resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, neuromyelitis optica, Systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test – application of an ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases the activity of acetylcholinesterase; this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission).

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* A repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test – improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Symptomatic treatment: Anticholinesterase agents – Pyridostigmine is the initial therapy of choice.

* Chronic immunomodulating therapy: Glucocorticoids (prednisone) and immunosuppressive drugs (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine) are implemented in patients significantly symptomatic on pyridostigmine.

* Rapid immunomodulating treatment: IVIG and therapeutic plasma exchange —Used to tide over severe illness (myasthenic crisis) and as 'bridge' therapy before surgery or starting chronic immunomodulating treatment.

* Surgical approach: Thymectomy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a non-recurring indication of a previous lower segment cesarean section now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Attempt a normal vaginal delivery

In a woman with a non-recurring indication of lower segment cesarean sections who now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position, the next step of management would be to try to attempt a vaginal delivery.

Occipitoposterior position is an abnormal position of the vertex and can undergo normal labor in favorable circumstances.

In a majority of cases, the occiput rotates through 3/8th of the circle, and the baby is born in the occipitoanterior position. Hence, when the diagnosis of occipitoposterior position is made, labor is allowed to proceed normally when there are good uterine contractions and a favorable pelvis.

The occipitoposterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint or directly over the sacrum. It is the most common fetal malposition. It is an abnormal position seen in the vertex presentation, not an abnormal presentation.

* Occipitoposterior position is commonly seen in the android pelvis/deflexed head.

* The engaging diameter of this position is sub-occipitofrontal.

* The most common type in the occipitoposterior position is right OP.

* A persistent occipitoposterior position results from a failure of internal rotation prior to birth.

Examination findings of OP position:

* Inspection: The abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening).

* Pelvic grips:

* The head is not engaged.

* The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt.

* Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in direct OP position, they are heard in the midline.

Features of occipitoposterior position include infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds localized to the flank. The fetal parts are more prominently felt near the midline.

Other options

Option A: Indications of cesarean section in occipitoposterior position:

* Arrest of labor

* Inadequate uterine contraction

* Fetal distress

* Other obstetrical indications

Option C: External cephalic version (ECV) is done in non-cephalic presentations like breech and transverse lie, to bring the favorable cephalic pole to the lower pole of the uterus. The ideal time to do the external cephalic version is 37 weeks.

Option D: Vaccum-assisted delivery is used to help with prolonged labor, fetal distress, maternal exhaustion, or ineffective pushing and fetal malposition.

Pearl PF1974: Fetal Skull Dimensions

Note:

Shortest diameters of fetal skull: Bimastoid - 7.5 cm (doesn't engage) < Bitemporal - 8 cm

Longest diameter of fetal skull: Mentovertical 14 cm > Submentovertical / occipitofrontal - 11.5cm
questions.learning: Attempt a normal vaginal delivery — In a woman with a non-recurring indication of lower segment cesarean sections who now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position, the next step of management would be to try to attempt a vaginal delivery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complained of acute painful diminution of vision in the left eye for the past 2 days. On ophthalmic examination, circumcorneal congestion and irregularly shaped pupil were noted as shown below, with the left eye visual acuity at 6/60 and the right eye at 6/12. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute anterior uveitis

Given the patient's symptoms—acute pain, decreased vision in the left eye, circumcorneal congestion, irregularly shaped pupil and keratic precipitates, as shown in the image—the most likely diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis. This condition, also known as iritis, involves inflammation of the iris and anterior chamber.

Key features of acute anterior uveitis include unilateral eye pain, circumcorneal redness, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity. The pupil may appear irregular or constricted, and keratic precipitates (KP) on the corneal endothelium are pathognomonic for this condition. Inflammation leads to pseudo-rubeosis iridis and aqueous flare, a hazy appearance in the anterior chamber due to inflammatory exudate.

Anterior uveitis involves inflammation of the uvea, which can cause sluggish pupillary reactions and a "muddy" appearance of the iris. Aqueous flare is often the earliest sign seen during slit-lamp examination, alongside Koeppe and Busacca nodules and potential posterior synechiae formation.

Management focuses on reducing inflammation and managing symptoms, typically using topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics like homatropine or atropine to relieve pain and prevent synechiae. Monitoring intraocular pressure is also essential, as cycloplegics are contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma due to the risk of exacerbating the condition.

Other options:

Option A: Angle-closure glaucoma involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure due to blockage of the anterior chamber angle. It is characterized by severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated pupil, with diffuse redness rather than the circumcorneal congestion seen in uveitis.

Option C: Acute conjunctivitis typically presents with diffuse redness, discharge, and mild irritation, without significant pupil changes or severe vision loss.

Option D: Episcleritis features sectoral or diffuse redness with mild tenderness but does not cause severe pain, irregular pupil, or substantial visual changes seen in anterior uveitis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about grey rami communicants except:
options: Present medial to white rami communicants
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preganglionic

Gray rami communicants are branches that connect the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral ganglia) to the spinal nerves and carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers to the body wall.

• Unmyelinated fibers
• Contain postganglionic sympathetic fibers
• Connect the sympathetic chain ganglion to the spinal nerve
• Present at all spinal levels (C1–Co)
• Located medial to the white rami communicants

| Feature | White rami | Gray rami

| ------- | ---------- | ---------

| Fiber type | Myelinated | Unmyelinated

| Fibers carried | Preganglionic sympathetic | Postganglionic sympathetic

| Levels present | T1–L2 only | All spinal levels

| Direction | Spinal nerve → sympathetic trunk | Sympathetic trunk → spinal nerve

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with the findings as shown in the image below. What is the most likely voice abnormality that would be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhinolalia clausa

The image shown above is indicative of adenoid hypertrophy. Patients with this condition would present with rhinolalia clausa.

Adenoid hypertrophy occurs in response to allergens or infections. It is more common in children. Affected children typically present with symptoms of nasal obstruction, sinusitis, and rhinolalia clausa (loss of nasal tone of voice).

They may also experience aprosexia (inability to concentrate) leading to declining academic performance. These children have characteristic adenoid facies marked by a dull expression, open mouth, hitched-up upper lip, pinched-in nose, high arched palate, and crowded upper teeth.

Other options:

* Rhinolalia aperta is hypernasality seen in Velopharyngeal insufficiency etc.

* Muffled and thick speech, often called “hot potato voice” is seen in peritonsillar abscess or quinsy.

* Staccato voice is broken speech and is seen in multiple sclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient is having the following hand movements. In which of the following conditions would this be seen?
questions.explanation: The image depicts asterixis, commonly known as "flapping tremors". This is a negative myoclonus characterized by a loss of muscle tone when the patient extends their wrists and fingers. Asterixis is a hallmark sign of metabolic encephalopathy. It is most classically seen in Hypercarbia (excess CO2 in the blood, often from COPD or respiratory failure) and Hepatic Encephalopathy (liver failure). It can also occur in uremia (renal failure). Thyrotoxicosis (Option A) causes a fine, fast tremor, not a slow flap. Hemiballismus (Option C) involves violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the limbs. Hypoxia (Option D) causes confusion and cyanosis but is not the primary cause of flapping tremors. Recognizing asterixis at the bedside is a vital clinical clue for identifying systemic metabolic derangement. Treatment focuses on the underlying cause, such as non-invasive ventilation for hypercarbia or lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy
questions.learning: The image depicts asterixis, commonly known as "flapping tremors". This is a negative myoclonus characterized by a loss of muscle tone when the patient extends their wrists and fingers.

questions.text: During a field visit to monitor the training of an ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwife) on safe immunization practices, you observe that she has used a syringe with a needle, a vaccine vial, and a cotton swab. After completing the immunization, which of the following statements regarding biomedical waste disposal is correct?
options: Syringe with needle should be disposed of in a black translucent container
Used cotton swab should be discarded in a red bag
Used vaccine vial should be discarded in a blue bag
Needle should be bent and thrown in a red bag
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Used vaccine vial should be discarded in a blue bag

As per Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, glassware waste such as used or discarded vaccine vials and ampoules (except those contaminated with cytotoxic drugs) must be placed in a blue container or cardboard box with blue marking, followed by proper disinfection (autoclaving, microwaving, hydroclaving) and safe recycling.

Other options:

Option A: Syringes with fixed needles and sharps must be discarded in a white (translucent, puncture-proof, tamper-proof, leak-proof) container, not in black containers.
Option B: Cotton swabs contaminated with blood/body fluids fall under yellow bag waste (human anatomical/soiled waste).
Option D: Needles are to be directly placed in a white puncture-proof container, not in red bags.

questions.text: Gamma radiation is used for sterilization of ____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Syringes, needles and catheters

Gamma radiation is used for the sterilization of articles such as syringes, needles, catheters, and gloves.

Gamma particles show maximum penetration and since there is no increase in temperature during the process it is called as cold sterilisation.

* When a nucleus disintegrates, it will emit radiation either as photons (X or gamma rays) or as high velocity particles.

* Gamma rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation (EMR) similar to X-rays, however, distinguished from the latter by the fact that they are emitted from an excited nucleus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common site for a peripheral arterial aneurysm? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Popliteal

The popliteal artery is the most common site for peripheral arterial aneurysms. Popliteal aneurysms account for approximately 70% of all peripheral aneurysms and are classically diagnosed in males in their seventh decade of life. They are bilateral in about 50% of cases. An important clinical consideration is that one-third of patients with popliteal aneurysms also have abdominal aortic aneurysms, necessitating abdominal examination in these patients.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Cat scratch disease is caused by?
questions.explanation: Cat scratch disease (CSD) is an infectious condition characterized by regional lymphadenopathy following a cat scratch or bite. It is caused specifically by Bartonella henselae, a small, gram-negative intracellular bacterium. Bartonella quintana (Option B) is the cause of trench fever, typically transmitted by lice. Bartonella bacilliformis (Option C) causes Carrion's disease (Oroya fever/Verruga peruana). Borrelia burgdorferi (Option D) is the causative agent of Lyme disease, which is transmitted by ticks. CSD is a self-limiting illness in most immunocompetent individuals, though it can cause more severe systemic or neurological disease in immuno compromised patients. Diagnosis is often made clinically and supported by serology or PCR. Therefore, B. henselae is the definitive causative organism associated with feline transmission and regional adenitis
questions.learning: Cat scratch disease (CSD) is an infectious condition characterized by regional lymphadenopathy following a cat scratch or bite. It is caused specifically by Bartonella henselae, a small, gram-negative intracellular bacterium.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A worker employed in a groundnut processing unit develops features of food poisoning after eating groundnuts that had been stored for a long duration. What is the most probable cause of this illness?
questions.explanation: Aflatoxins are potent mycotoxins produced by the molds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, which commonly contaminate "groundnuts" (peanuts), maize, and other crops stored in damp conditions. Acute ingestion of high levels of aflatoxin can cause severe toxic hepatitis, while chronic exposure is one of the strongest risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma. Beta oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) (Option A) is the neurotoxin found in Lathyrus sativus (Khesari dal) that causes neurolathyrism. Option B is an environmental pollutant. Sanguinarine (Option C) is the toxin found in Argemone mexicana (prickly poppy) seeds; when mixed with mustard oil, it causes Epidemic Dropsy. In the context of "stored groundnuts," aflatoxin is the most probable epidemiological culprit. Public health efforts focus on proper agricultural storage and the monitoring of moisture levels to prevent the fungal growth that produces these dangerous toxins
questions.learning: Aflatoxins are potent mycotoxins produced by the molds Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, which commonly contaminate "groundnuts" (peanuts), maize, and other crops stored in damp conditions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient wakes up unable to extend the wrist after sleeping with the arm hanging over the back of a chair. This condition is most likely caused by what underlying mechanism or injury?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus. This results in "wrist drop" due to the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. According to Seddon's classification of nerve injuries, this type of temporary compression causes "neuropraxia"—a localized conduction block without any structural damage to the axon or its sheath. Recovery from neuropraxia is typically spontaneous and occurs within days to weeks. Axonotmesis (Option C) involves axonal damage with an intact sheath, requiring longer recovery. Neurotmesis (Option A) is a complete severance of the nerve and sheath, which does not recover without surgery. Neurolysis (Option B) is a surgical procedure to release a nerve from adhesions, not a type of injury. Conservative management including wrist splinting and physical therapy is usually sufficient for Saturday night palsy
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus. This results in "wrist drop" due to the inability to extend the wrist and fingers.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Arrange the following in sequential order with regards to the steps of collection of samples for pap smear testing:

1. Use posterior vaginal wall retractor
2. Take the sample
3. Make smear on a slide
4. Fix the smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 4

The correct sequence of the procedure involved in the collection of a sample for a pap smear is 1, 2, 3, 4.

The Pap/Papanicolaou smear is used for screening cervical neoplasia.

Procedure:

• The patient is put in a dorsal position & the labia are separated.
• Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced/posterior vaginal wall retractor is used
• The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula.
• Endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush.
• Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides.
• The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol.
• Stained with Pap stain or Short stain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All are used in recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering) except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isomerases

Recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering) involves cutting, modifying, and joining DNA molecules to produce recombinant DNA. This process requires enzymes that cut DNA, join DNA fragments, or modify DNA ends. Enzymes used in recombinant DNA technology:

1. Phosphatases

• Example: Alkaline phosphatase
• Removes 5′ phosphate groups from DNA ends.
• Prevents self-ligation of plasmid vectors, improving insertion of foreign DNA.

2. CRISPR–Cas9

• A gene-editing system derived from bacterial defense mechanisms.
• Cas9 nuclease cuts DNA at specific sequences guided by RNA.
• Used for precise genome editing.

3. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (Terminal transferase)

• Adds nucleotides to the 3′ end of DNA without a template.
• Used in DNA labeling and cloning techniques.

Not used in recombinant DNA technology: Isomerases

• Catalyze rearrangement of molecules within the same molecule (e.g., glucose-6-phosphate ↔ fructose-6-phosphate).
• Function mainly in metabolic pathways, not in DNA cutting or joining.
questions.learning: Isomerases Recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering) involves cutting, modifying, and joining DNA molecules to produce recombinant DNA. This process requires enzymes that cut DNA, join DNA fragments, or modify DNA ends.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old lady comes with complaints of erythematous scaly rash, loose stools, and cognitive dysfunction. The rash involved her forearm, neck, and face. She seems to have difficulty remembering things from the recent past. Her electrolytes are within normal range. She admits to having shifted to a corn-based diet due to economic reasons. Which of the following would improve her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral Nicotinamide supplementation

The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

Other options:

Option B: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency leads to conditions like beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which are characterized by symptoms such as muscle weakness, peripheral neuropathy, cardiovascular issues, and confusion. While cognitive dysfunction can result from thiamine deficiency, rash and loose stools do not fit with thiamine deficiency. Therefore, thiamine would not address the full spectrum of this patient’s symptoms.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, which is associated with symptoms like bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain, and fatigue. Scurvy is not associated with a rash like the one described, nor does it typically cause cognitive dysfunction or diarrhea. Hence, high-dose vitamin C would not improve this patient’s symptoms.

Option D: Corn-based diets are low in niacin and tryptophan, leading to pellagra over time, especially if the diet is not balanced with other niacin-rich foods. While stopping the corn-based diet could prevent further niacin deficiency, it will not immediately address the existing deficiency and symptoms like rash, diarrhea, and cognitive dysfunction. The patient would still need niacin supplementation to resolve the current symptoms.
questions.learning: Oral Nicotinamide supplementation — The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Match the following postmortem findings and their time of appearance:

A. Adipocere formation
1. 24 hrs

B. Relaxation of urethral sphincter
2. 2-3 days

C. Marbling of veins
3. 4-5 days

D. Liquefaction of tissues
4. 5-10 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4

The correct match is A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4.

Adipocere formation starts in 4-5 days.
Relaxation of urethral sphincter by 2-3 days.
Marbling of veins starts in 24 hours.
Liquefaction of tissues by 5-10 days.

In postmortem marbling, blood in the vessels is haemolysed to sulfmeth-hemoglobin, which stains the vessel walls and the adjacent tissues, giving rise to a marbled appearance. The marbling of the skin begins by about 24 hours and becomes prominent in 36–48 hours after death. The image below shows postmortem marbling which is distinctly appreciable in the superficial veins of the abdomen, shoulders, chest, and inguinal region.

Urethral sphincter relaxation is of two types;- Primary and Secondary. Primary relaxation occurs before rigor mortis sets in. Secondary relaxation occurs at the time of decomposition i.e. around 2-3 days.

Adipocere formation, also called corpse wax, grave wax, or mortuary wax is a late sign of death. A wax-like organic substance is formed by the anaerobic hydrolysis or hydrogenation of fat in tissues by bacteria like Clostridium welchii. It has a greyish-white appearance with a distinctive offensive or sweetish smell. In a country like India, adipocere formation begins within 4-5 days and takes several weeks to complete.

Liquefaction or colliquative changes begin 5 days after death and become prominent in 10 days. Soft tissues change into semisolid masses which are black and get separated from bones and fall off.

Note: The first visible sign of putrefaction is greenish (due to sulfmeth-hemoglobin) discolouration of the anterior abdominal wall, usually in the right iliac fossa.
questions.learning: A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4 — The correct match is A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4. Adipocere formation starts in 4-5 days.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department unconscious. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis shows: pH 7.1, PCO₂ 23 mmHg, PO₂ 98 mmHg, HCO₃ 16 mEq/L. What does this ABG indicate about the patient’s acid-base status?
questions.explanation: The ABG analysis reveals a pH of 7.1, which indicates significant academia. The bicarbonate (HCO3) level of 16 mEq/L is low (normal is 22–26 mEq/L), which is the primary cause of the low pH, thus defining metabolic acidosis. The low PCO2 of 23 mmHg (normal is 35–45 mmHg) indicates that the patient is hyperventilating to blow off carbon dioxide as a secondary "respiratory compensation" for the metabolic acid load. In respiratory acidosis (Option C), the pH would be low but the PCO2 would be high. In metabolic alkalosis (Option B) or respiratory alkalosis (Option D), the pH would be elevated above 7.45. Common causes for this severe metabolic acidosis in an unconscious patient include diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), lactic acidosis (from shock or sepsis), or toxic ingestions like aspirin or ethylene glycol
questions.learning: The ABG analysis reveals a pH of 7.1, which indicates significant academia. The bicarbonate (HCO3) level of 16 mEq/L is low (normal is 22–26 mEq/L), which is the primary cause of the low pH, thus defining metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following murmur increases on standing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HOCM

The murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM) increases with standing, as there is a reduction in preload. In conditions of reduced preload, there is lesser end diastolic volume in the left ventricle, leading to a narrower outflow tract, and a louder murmur is heard.

The murmur heard in HOCM is a mid-systolic murmur, which is loudest along the left sternal border. It increases in conditions of decreased preload and afterload (standing, valsalva, vagal maneuvers) or conditions of increased contractility (inotropic stimulation) and decreases when preload and afterload are increased (squatting, vasopressors).

Most murmurs decrease in intensity with reduced preload and afterload except HOCM and mitral valve prolapse (MVP).
