questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The principle of linear accelerators is used in the production of _____?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. X-rays

X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from LINAC (Linear Accelerator).

A LINAC is used in radiation therapy to deliver high-energy X-rays or electrons to target specific areas of the body, typically to treat cancerous tissues. It uses microwave technology to accelerate charged particles (such as electrons) at a high speed and then directs them into a target (usually a heavy metal) to produce X-rays. These X-rays are then carefully directed at the patient's body to deliver therapeutic radiation doses to the tumor while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissues.

Gamma rays: They are also a form of electromagnetic radiation used in medical imaging and radiation therapy, but linear accelerators are primarily associated with the production of X-rays for medical purposes, and gamma rays are usually produced in different ways.

Sources of radiation exposure:

* Natural:

* Cosmic rays

* Environmental - terrestrial and atmospheric

* Radioactive isotopes - of potassium (K-40) and carbon (C-14)

* Man-made:

* Medical and dental - X-rays, radioisotopes

* Occupational exposure

* Nuclear - radioactive fallout.
questions.learning: X-rays X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from LINAC (Linear Accelerator).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the management of Non–ST Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) is incorrect?
options: An immediate loading dose of aspirin should be administered.
ACC/AHA guidelines recommend a P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor) as a class I recommendation.
Glycoprotein IIB/IIIA inhibitors are useful adjuncts.
Fibrinolytic therapy is useful in acute coronary syndrome without ST-segment elevation.
questions.explanation: In the management of NSTEMI, the pathophysiology involves a partially occlusive thrombus. Fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) therapy (Option D) is strictly contraindicated and considered "incorrect" in this setting because clinical trials have shown it provides no benefit and significantly increases the risk of intracranial hemorrhage without improving coronary flow. In contrast, thrombolytics are only indicated for STEMI. All other statements are correct: an immediate loading dose of aspirin (Option A) is standard to inhibit platelets. P2Y12 inhibitors (Option B) are a Class I recommendation for dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). Glycoprotein IIB/IIIA inhibitors (Option C) are valuable adjuncts during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for high-risk patients. Therefore, the recommendation for fibrinolysis is the only inaccurate clinical guideline listed for NSTEMI care
questions.learning: In the management of NSTEMI, the pathophysiology involves a partially occlusive thrombus. Fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) therapy (Option D) is strictly contraindicated and considered "incorrect" in this setting because clinical trials have shown it provides…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient developed a loss of sensations over the root of the penis following open hernia surgery. Which of the following nerves would you implicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ilioinguinal nerve

Loss of sensation in the root of the penis and adjacent part of the scrotum is suggestive of an injury to the ilioinguinal nerve. It is most commonly injured within the inguinal canal in open hernia repair due to traction or thermal injury.

Other options:

Option A: The iliohypogastric nerve carries the sensory supply from the suprapubic area. Injury to this nerve in the right iliac fossa rarely causes sensory disturbances, as the suprapubic area has a rich nerve supply from other sources too. If the nerve is severed above the anterior superior iliac spine, it can lead to the weakened posterior wall of the inguinal canal resulting in a direct inguinal hernia. The iliohypogastric nerve can also get injured following appendicectomy.

Option C: Injury to the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve results in loss of sensation in the skin of the scrotum of males, and loss of sensation of the mons pubis and labia majora in females.

Injury to the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve causes hypoesthesia over the anterior thigh below the inguinal ligament.

Option D: The medial cutaneous nerve of thigh is a sensory branch of the femoral nerve. Injury to this nerve leads to loss of sensations over the areas supplied by this nerve, which include anterior-medial aspect of the thigh and knee.
questions.learning: Ilioinguinal nerve Loss of sensation in the root of the penis and adjacent part of the scrotum is suggestive of an injury to the ilioinguinal nerve. It is most commonly injured within the inguinal canal in open hernia repair due to traction or thermal injury.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Pterygium can lead to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Astigmatism

Pterygium is a fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva extending onto the cornea that can distort corneal curvature, leading to astigmatism.

Mechanism:

• Progressive growth over cornea → mechanical traction and flattening (especially horizontal meridian)
• Causes irregular or with-the-rule astigmatism → decreased visual acuity

Why not others:

• Eye pain: Usually asymptomatic or mild irritation, not significant pain
• Macular edema: Posterior segment pathology, unrelated to pterygium
• Purulent discharge: Seen in bacterial conjunctivitis, not pterygium

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: While observing anesthesia equipment in the operating theater, a specific vaporizer is in use. Which of the following gases is it most likely designed to contain?
questions.explanation: Anesthesia equipment uses a universal color-coding system to prevent medication errors. A vaporizer with a blue color-coded dial or housing is designed exclusively for Desflurane (Option A). Desflurane requires a specialized heated and pressurized vaporizer (like the Tec 6) due to its extremely high vapor pressure and boiling point near room temperature. Halothane (Option B) is color-coded red. Sevoflurane (Option C) is color-coded yellow. Isoflurane (Option D) is color-coded purple. Identifying these colors is a fundamental safety skill for anesthetists. Since the vaporizer in the image is marked with the blue distinctive color of Desflurane, that is the gas it comprises. This visual identification ensures that the correct agent is matched to its corresponding calibrated delivery device
questions.learning: Anesthesia equipment uses a universal color-coding system to prevent medication errors. A vaporizer with a blue color-coded dial or housing is designed exclusively for Desflurane (Option A).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An elderly patient is brought to the emergency department with acute episodes of severe breathlessness. Laboratory testing detects target sequences of the RdRp gene, E gene, N gene, and ORF1. Which diagnostic test was performed in this case?
questions.explanation: The detection of specific viral genetic sequences—the "RdRp gene, E gene, N gene, and ORF1"—is the standard molecular diagnostic profile for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19). The gold standard test for detecting these viral RNA targets is the "Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR)". RT-PCR converts the viral RNA into DNA and then amplifies specific target regions to detectable levels. CLIA (Option A) and ELISA (Option B) are serological/immunoassays used to detect "antigens or antibodies" in the blood, not specific genetic sequences. CBNAAT (Option C), while a molecular test, is primarily used in India for the rapid diagnosis of Tuberculosis. During the pandemic, the simultaneous detection of multiple genes like RdRp and E increased the specificity of the RT-PCR test. For an elderly patient with acute respiratory distress, rapid and accurate genetic testing via RT-PCR was essential for guiding isolation and clinical management protocols
questions.learning: The detection of specific viral genetic sequences—the "RdRp gene, E gene, N gene, and ORF1"—is the standard molecular diagnostic profile for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of fetal biophysical profile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contraction stress test

The contraction stress test is not a component of the biophysical profile.

Biophysical profile is a multi-parametric screening test to assess uteroplacental insufficiency. It consists of five components and the observations are made for 30 minutes.

Parameters
Minimal Normal Criteria

Non-stress Test (NST)
≥2 accelerations within 20-40 minutes.

Fetal breathing movements
≥ 1 episode of rhythmic breathing lasting > 30 seconds.

Gross body movements
≥ 3 discrete body/limb movements

Fetal muscle tone
≥ 1 episode of active extension(limb or trunk) with return of flexion.

Amniotic fluid volume
A pocket of amniotic fluid that measures at least 2 cm in two perpendicular planes (2 ×2 cm pocket)

Each parameter has a maximum score of 2 and a minimum score of 0. So the total maximum score will be 10. A score of 4 or less indicates fetal acidemia.

Interpretation and management of BPP scores:

BPP score
Interpretation
Management

10
Normal, nonasphyxiated fetus
Repeat test weekly

8 with normal AFV
Normal, nonasphyxiated fetus
Repeat test weekly

8 with decreased AFV
Suspicion of chronic fetal asphyxia

If ≥36 weeks, delivery is done

6
Possible fetal asphyxia

If AFV is abnormal-Deliver>36 weeks.

If AFV is normal- deliver≥ 37 weeks.

4
Probable fetal asphyxia

If ≥32 weeks, deliver

0-2
Almost certain fetal asphyxia
Delivery

The modified biophysical score has only 2 components i.e NST and amniotic fluid index (AFI). It is considered abnormal (nonreassuring) when the NST is non-reactive and/or the AFI is <5.

Note: The contraction stress test (oxytocin challenge test) is an invasive method to assess fetal well-being during pregnancy. When there is an alteration in FHR in response to uterine contractions, it suggests fetal hypoxia.
questions.learning: Contraction stress test — The contraction stress test is not a component of the biophysical profile. Biophysical profile is a multi-parametric screening test to assess uteroplacental insufficiency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child in your unit is admitted with acute bronchiolitis. Which of the following is the most common etiological agent responsible for this condition during infancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory syncytial virus

Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases.

Acute bronchiolitis refers to airway inflammation and obstruction of the lower respiratory tract. Commonly, symptoms of bronchiolitis begin with rhinitis or congestion and cough and may progress to signs of increasing respiratory distress (tachypnea, wheezing, and accessory muscle use). Management is mainly conservative.
questions.learning: Respiratory syncytial virus Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the fungus depicted in the provided image, which has been stained using India ink dye.
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic negative stain using India ink, which is the gold standard for identifying Cryptococcus neoformans. The India ink particles are too large to penetrate the fungus's thick, polysaccharide capsule. As a result, the capsule appears as a clear, luminous halo surrounding the round yeast cell against a dark, blackened background. Aspergillus (Option A) is a filamentous mold showing septate hyphae. Candida (Option B) typically appears as budding yeasts with pseudohyphae and does not possess a capsule. Penicillium (Option D) is another mold characterized by its "brush-like" conidiophores. Cryptococcus is a significant opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with HIV, often causing life-threatening meningitis. The identification of an encapsulated yeast in CSF or culture using India ink is a critical diagnostic step. Therefore, the presence of the clear halo in a negative stain definitively identifies Cryptococcus
questions.learning: The image displays a classic negative stain using India ink, which is the gold standard for identifying Cryptococcus neoformans. The India ink particles are too large to penetrate the fungus's thick, polysaccharide capsule.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids can form oxaloacetate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspartate

The amino acid Aspartate can be converted into oxaloacetate through a series of enzymatic reactions.

Oxaloacetate is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle (also known as the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle), a key metabolic pathway in cells that generates energy through the oxidation of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

Aspartate can be transaminated (an amino group transferred) to form oxaloacetate, which plays a crucial role in linking various metabolic pathways, including the citric acid cycle and gluconeogenesis (the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources).

Anaplerotic process is the replenishment of the intermediates of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle to replace the catalytic processes and to ensure the continuation of the cycle.

Transamination of aspartate to form oxaloacetate is one of these reactions.

Other anaplerotic reactions:

* Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, which is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

* Glutamate and glutamine to α-ketoglutarate, a reaction catalyzed by glutamate dehydrogenase and glutaminase, respectively

* Compounds that produce propionyl CoA can be then carboxylated and isomerized to succinyl CoA.

* Pyruvate can be carboxylated to malate.

Entry level in TCA cycle

Amino Acids

Alpha keto-glutarate

• Arginine
• Histidine
• Glutamine
• Proline
• Glutamate

Succinyl CoA

• Valine
• Isoleucine
• Methionine

Fumarate

• Phenylalanine
• Tyrosine

Oxaloacetate

• Aspartate
• Asparagine

Pyruvate

• Serine
• Threonine
• Alanine
• Cysteine
• Glycine
• Hydroxyproline

• Lysine
• Tryptophan

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which statement correctly explains the key features of the Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics curve?
options: Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration
Km doesn't vary with the enzyme concentration
Km is indirectly proportional to substrate concentration
Km has no relation to substrate concentration
questions.explanation: The Michaelis constant (Km) is a fundamental parameter in enzyme kinetics that reflects the affinity of an enzyme for its substrate. By definition, Km is equal to the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is exactly half of the maximum velocity (Vmax). A critical characteristic of Km is that it is an intrinsic property of the enzyme-substrate pair; therefore, it does not change regardless of the amount of enzyme present in the system. Statements A, C, and D are incorrect because Km is defined at a specific substrate concentration but is not proportional or inversely proportional to it as a variable; rather, Km is a constant used to describe the enzyme's behavior. While Vmax increases with higher enzyme concentration, Km remains stable. Consequently, understanding that Km is independent of enzyme concentration is vital for analyzing how different enzymes interact with their substrates in metabolic pathways

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient department after falling on his outstretched arm while riding his bicycle. Clinical examination findings are shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Malunion of a supracondylar fracture of humerus
questions.explanation: The image displays a Gunstock deformity (Cubitus varus), which is the most common late complication of a Supracondylar fracture. It results from a malunion of the fracture, specifically when the distal fragment heals with a medial tilt or rotation. While an acute supracondylar fracture (Option A and B) is the initial injury, the "deformity" seen weeks or months later in the OPD is the result of improper healing (malunion). Proximal humerus fractures (Option D) involve the shoulder and would not cause an elbow-specific angulation. While cubitus varus is primarily a cosmetic deformity with minimal functional impact on the elbow joint itself, it can lead to secondary issues like ulnar nerve instability or late-onset posterolateral rotatory instability. If the deformity is severe and causes patient distress, it can be corrected surgically via a lateral closing wedge osteotomy (French osteotomy). Recognizing this classic "gunstock" appearance is vital for identifying the long-term outcomes of pediatric elbow trauma
questions.learning: The image displays a Gunstock deformity (Cubitus varus), which is the most common late complication of a Supracondylar fracture. It results from a malunion of the fracture, specifically when the distal fragment heals with a medial tilt or rotation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents with intermittent flank pain, a sense of fullness, and hematuria. CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis reveals a left renal lesion containing fat-density areas along with a neovascular mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of fat density (characterized by Hounsfield units typically between -20 and -100) within a renal mass on a CT scan is virtually pathognomonic for a Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML). AML is a benign triphasic tumor composed of dysplastic blood vessels (angio-), smooth muscle (-myo-), and adipose tissue (-lipoma). While Renal Cell Carcinoma (Option A) is the most common renal malignancy and can cause flank pain and hematuria, it very rarely contains visible macrofat. Renal oncocytoma (Option B) typically shows a central stellate scar and lacks fat density. A renal cyst (Option D) appears as a simple, fluid-filled, well-circumscribed lesion with water density, not fat or vascularity. AMLs are often associated with Tuberous Sclerosis. Given the specific radiological finding of fat density, which appears as black pockets on the CT image, Renal Angiomyolipoma is the most accurate diagnosis for this patient
questions.learning: The presence of fat density (characterized by Hounsfield units typically between -20 and -100) within a renal mass on a CT scan is virtually pathognomonic for a Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is NOT used as a first line therapy for ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors

First-line treatment of ADHD includes stimulant medications and certain non-stimulants with proven efficacy on attention and impulse control.

• Stimulants are first line:
• Methylphenidate and its derivatives
• Amphetamines (e.g., dextroamphetamine)
• Non-stimulant first-line alternative:
• Atomoxetine (selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor)
• Alpha-2 agonists (guanfacine, clonidine) may be used

Why option D is incorrect:

• Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are not standard first-line therapy for ADHD
questions.learning: Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors First-line treatment of ADHD includes stimulant medications and certain non-stimulants with proven efficacy on attention and impulse control. • Stimulants are first line: • Methylphenidate and its…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with lytic lesions on the skull is suspected of a diagnosis of Langerhan cell histiocytosis. Which of the following is a characteristic finding on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Birbeck granules

The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance. It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy.

The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH.

Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules are seen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a and langerin (CD207) markers.

The image below shows histopathological image of Langerhan cells with folded nuclei.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system.

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

• Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease)
• Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)- The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad.
• Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH.
questions.learning: Birbeck granules — The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day-old male neonate presents with abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium since birth, without fever. Rectal examination causes a forceful expulsion of stool. A barium enema shows characteristic findings. What is the gold standard test for confirming the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The neonate displays classic signs of Hirschsprung Disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distension, and the "blast sign" (forceful stool expulsion) on PR exam . The barium enema showing a transition zone between the narrow aganglionic segment and the dilated normal segment supports this. While manometry (Option D) can show failure of the internal sphincter to relax, the gold standard for definitive diagnosis is a rectal biopsy (Option C). The biopsy must demonstrate the complete absence of ganglion cells in the Meissner and Auerbach plexuses and the presence of hypertrophied nerve fibers. Ultrasonography (Option A) and MRI (Option B) are non-specific and do not provide the microscopic evidence required for diagnosis. Therefore, histopathological confirmation via suction or full-thickness rectal biopsy remains the definitive clinical standard before proceeding with corrective surgery (pull-through procedure)
questions.learning: The neonate displays classic signs of Hirschsprung Disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distension, and the "blast sign" (forceful stool expulsion) on PR exam .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman attends a routine antenatal visit at 28 weeks of gestation. She has a history of obesity but no prior diagnosis of diabetes. Her fasting plasma glucose is 104 mg/ dL, and her 2-hour plasma glucose level following a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is 167 mg/dL. Based on these results, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start lifestyle modifications and repeat OGTT at 32 weeks gestation.
Diagnose her with pre-existing diabetes and initiate insulin therapy.
Diagnose her with GDM and initiate dietary modifications with close monitoring of blood glucose levels.
Monitor her closely without intervention since her glucose levels are borderline.
questions.explanation: According to standard diagnostic criteria, Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if the fasting plasma glucose is mg/dL or the 2-hour post-OGTT level is mg/dL. This patient meets both criteria ( mg/dL and mg/dL), confirming a diagnosis of GDM. The immediate next step is dietary and lifestyle modifications combined with frequent blood glucose monitoring to ensure levels stay within the target range. Regarding the distractors, repeating the test (Option A) is unnecessary as the diagnosis is already established. Pre-existing diabetes (Option B) requires much higher thresholds (fasting mg/dL) and history before conception. Simply monitoring without intervention (Option D) is inappropriate, as uncontrolled GDM increases the risk of macrosomia and other fetal complications. Thus, the establishment of a management plan for GDM is required
questions.learning: According to standard diagnostic criteria, Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if the fasting plasma glucose is mg/dL or the 2-hour post-OGTT level is mg/dL.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was brought to casualty following a road accident. The patient is unconscious; the following image shows the CT scan. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subdural hematoma (SDH)

The plain computed tomography (CT) scan shows a concave-convex shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of subdural hematoma.

An acute SDH is the result of the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. It is usually due to the rupture of bridging veins running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses. The level of consciousness is usually impaired at presentation and may deteriorate further as the hematoma expands. Elderly and alcoholic patients are at a higher risk of acute SDH formation after head trauma due to brain atrophy. On CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion.

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

* Thickness >1 cm

* Midline shift >5 mm

* Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score drops by two or more points from the time of injury to hospitalization.

Chronic subdural hematoma results from a hematoma that expands over days or weeks by osmosis, ultimately producing symptoms of raised ICP or focal deficits. On a CT scan, diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface would be seen as shown in the image below.

Pearl PF0339: Intracranial Hemorrhage (ICH)

Extradural hemorrhage (EDH):

* Source: Arterial bleed

* MC- Middle meningeal artery

* Cause- Trauma

* Clinical features: Lucid interval is characteristic

* CT – Lentiform opacity

* Treatment: A large or rapidly evolving EDH requires surgical evacuation

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH)

* Source: Venous bleed

* Bridging dural veins

* Causes: Trauma, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol abuse, shaken baby syndrome

* Clinical features

* Acute SDH: may be associated with lucid interval

* Chronic SDH: drowsiness, headache

* CT- crescentic opacity

* Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)

* Source: Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – Trauma

* 2nd MC – Rupture of berry aneurysm

* MC sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery

* Clinical features: Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness +/- FND

* Investigations:

* Non-contrast CT brain,

* CSF xanthochromia (peaks in 2 days and subsides in 2 weeks)

* Treatment:

* Clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm,

* Triple H therapy – hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution to prevent vasospasm

Intraparenchymal hemorrhage- (MC type of ICH)

* Source- Arterial bleed

* Causes:

* MC – hypertension

* Trauma, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, bleeding disorders, neoplasms, vascular malformations

* MC sites:

* Putamen (basal ganglia)

* Thalamus

* Cerebellum

* Pons

* Treatment:

* Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP or fresh platelets as required

* Surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoms >3 cm in size
questions.learning: Subdural hematoma (SDH) — The plain computed tomography (CT) scan shows a concave-convex shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of subdural hematoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to occur during a normal pregnancy? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elevated systolic blood pressure

Normal pregnancy is associated with major cardiovascular adaptations to meet increased maternal and fetal metabolic demands. Physiologic cardiovascular changes in pregnancy:

• Increased heart rate
• Increased cardiac output
• Increased blood volume
• Decreased systemic vascular resistance

Because systemic vascular resistance falls due to progesterone-mediated vasodilation and placental circulation, blood pressure usually:

• Decreases slightly during mid-pregnancy
• Returns toward baseline near term

Therefore, elevated systolic blood pressure is not a normal finding in pregnancy and may suggest hypertensive disorders such as gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.
questions.learning: Elevated systolic blood pressure Normal pregnancy is associated with major cardiovascular adaptations to meet increased maternal and fetal metabolic demands.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve of the second branchial arch is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Facial nerve

The facial nerve is the nerve of the 2nd pharyngeal arch.

Each pharyngeal arch is characterized by its own muscular components. The muscular components of each arch have their own cranial nerve. Wherever the muscle cells migrate, they carry their nerve component with them.

The neurons of the 5th, 7th, 9th, and 10th cranial sensory ganglia that supply the pharyngeal arch structures are derived from ectodermal placodes (epipharyngeal placodes) and from the neural crest cells.
questions.learning: Facial nerve — The facial nerve is the nerve of the 2nd pharyngeal arch. Each pharyngeal arch is characterized by its own muscular components.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the vitamin which when deficient can lead to neonatal seizures.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyridoxine

Pyridoxine deficiency can cause refractory seizures in the neonatal period and infancy.

Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P5P) is the active form of pyridoxine and functions as a cofactor for enzymes involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, amino acid metabolism, and glycogen metabolism. Intracellular P5P deficiency in the brain can lead to a seizure disorder that does not respond to typical anticonvulsant medications but shows a response to pyridoxine.

Antiquitin deficiency is the most common cause of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (due to mutations in the ALDH7A1 alleles)

They primarily present with generalized seizures in the early days of life. The seizures can be of various types, recurrent focal motor seizures, generalized tonic seizures, and myoclonus. Additional manifestations may include dystonia, respiratory distress, abdominal distention with vomiting, hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia.

Increased α-aminoadipic semialdehyde and pipecolic acid levels are observed in the CSF, plasma, and urine. Treatment with vitamin B6 (50-100 mg/day) shows significant improvement in seizures. Life-long therapy is needed.

Other options:

Option B: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency causes beriberi.

Option C: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency causes glossitis, cheilosis, keratitis, and corneal vascularization.

Option D: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) deficiency causes burning feet syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What are the imaging modality being used and the diagnosis in the given image below of the kidneys?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI of Polycystic kidney disease

As the bones and vertebrae appear white in a CT image while in an MRI the bones are seen as black, this is an MRI image. The given image is of an MRI with multiple cysts in the kidney and is suggestive of Polycystic kidney disease, mostly ADPKD( Adult polycystic kidney disease).

ADPKD is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with mutations in the PKD1(chromosome 16) and PKD2 genes (chromosome 4).

The disease does not usually manifest before 30 years of age, and in some patients, it is never diagnosed. The progression of renal failure in this disease is faster in males.

Hypertension is the most common presentation. Renal manifestations of ADPKD include:

* Flank/loin pain -  either due to hemorrhage inside cysts or due to renal stones (most commonly uric acid stones)

* Irregular upper quadrant renal mass

* Hematuria

* Renal failure (seen in 10-15% of the patients who receive hemodialysis)

It is associated with a number of extrarenal manifestations like polycystic liver disease, where cysts are usually asymptomatic but symptoms may occur due to mass effect of cysts, intracranial berry aneurysms are seen in approximately 10% of patients with ADPKD and mitral valve prolapse, the most common valvular abnormality observed in patients with ADPKD can be diagnosed by echocardiography.

Intravenous pyelography shows a characteristic spider leg pattern, as a result of narrowed and stretched calyces and elongated, compressed renal pelvis.

Treatment includes management of hypertension using ACE inhibitors like lisinopril or angiotensin receptor blockers like telmisartan. Narcotic analgesics should be limited to episodes of acute pain. V2 receptor antagonists like Tolvaptan have been observed to slow the decline in renal function over a 3 year period.

USG-guided CT aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic; surgical unroofing of multiple or large cysts may alleviate symptoms of pain. Nephrectomy is indicated for symptomatic patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

Note:

Horseshoe kidney is a common congenital anomaly in which there is a fusion of the inferior poles of both kidneys. It is common in patients with Turner's syndrome. Stone disease and hydronephrosis can occur as complications due to blockage of the ureteropelvic junction.

The image shown below shows the appearance of the horseshoe kidney on a CT scan.
questions.learning: MRI of Polycystic kidney disease As the bones and vertebrae appear white in a CT image while in an MRI the bones are seen as black, this is an MRI image.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Consider the following about hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and choose the correct statements.

1. TACE is used for multinodular lesions.
2. Lenvatinib is used for lesions less than 3 cm.
3. The incidence of HCC is increasing.
4. NASH and NAFLD are risk factors for HCC.

TACE- Transarterial chemoembolization
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4

The correct statements about hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are 1,3 and 4. Lenvatinib is used in the advanced stages of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

HCC is the most common cause of primary liver cancer. It is more commonly seen in males and the peak age group is between 65-70 years. The main risk factor for HCC is cirrhosis and associated chronic liver damage due to chronic infection by hepatitis B or C virus (HBV or HCV) infection, alcohol abuse, metabolic syndrome, or hemochromatosis.

The incidence of HCC is increasing (statement 3) worldwide. This is contributed by the increase in HCV and HBV infections, along with lifestyle disorders like obesity. Obesity is associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This progresses on to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) causing cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Thus, NASH and NAFLD are risk factors of HCC (statement 4).

Barcelona-Clinic-Liver Cancer (BCLC) Classification is the commonly used staging system. It stages the tumors as follows:

• Very early HCC - Single, well-differentiated tumor <2cm
• Early HCC - Single tumor or a maximum of 3 nodules <3cm in diameter
• Intermediate HCC - Any other size or number confined to the liver
• Advanced HCC - Presence of cancer-related symptoms or tumors with macrovascular invasion (of any type, including branch, hepatic, or portal vein), lymph node involvement, or extrahepatic spread
• End-stage disease - Severe liver dysfunction with impaired quality of life

Treatment

Very early HCC is treated by ablation. Early HCC with a single nodule is resected but when there are multiple nodules over 3 cm, ablation or transplantation are considered.

Intermediate stage HCC is treated by chemoembolization. Transarterial chemoembolization(TACE) is used for multinodular lesions (statement 1).

Advanced stages of the disease with macrovascular invasion are treated with systemic therapies. Lenvatinib and sorafenib are first-line drugs. Supportive care is given at the terminal stage of the disease.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 The correct statements about hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are 1,3 and 4. Lenvatinib is used in the advanced stages of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A healthcare worker sustains a needle-stick injury from a syringe used on a confirmed HIV-positive patient. To definitively determine whether she has acquired HIV infection, which diagnostic test should be used?
questions.explanation: Western blot is the gold standard confirmatory test for definitive diagnosis of HIV infection. It detects specific antibodies against individual HIV proteins (gp120, gp41, p24), and a positive result definitively confirms HIV infection. It is used as a confirmatory test after a reactive ELISA result. Why other options are wrong: (A) p24 antigen is incorrect because p24 antigen detection is useful during the early window period before antibody development. It is a marker of early/acute infection but is not used as a definitive confirmatory diagnostic test for established HIV infection. (B) PCR is incorrect because although PCR detects HIV RNA/DNA with high sensitivity and is useful in window period and infants, it is not the standard definitive confirmatory test used in routine clinical practice for diagnosing HIV infection following needle-stick injury. (C) HIV ELISA is incorrect because ELISA is a screening test, not confirmatory. It has high sensitivity but lower specificity, meaning false positives can occur. It always requires confirmation by Western blot before definitive diagnosis is established
questions.learning: Western blot is the gold standard confirmatory test for definitive diagnosis of HIV infection. It detects specific antibodies against individual HIV proteins (gp120, gp41, p24), and a positive result definitively confirms HIV infection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which type of complication is most commonly associated with advanced diabetic retinopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tractional retinal detachment

In advanced diabetic retinopathy (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR), the most common complication is tractional retinal detachment (TRD).

• Chronic retinal ischemia → VEGF release
• Formation of neovascularization (on disc and elsewhere)
• These vessels are associated with fibrovascular proliferation
• Contraction of these membranes → pulls the retina → tractional detachment

Why not others:

• Rhegmatogenous RD:

• Caused by retinal tear + vitreous fluid entry
• Not the primary mechanism in diabetic retinopathy

• Exudative RD:

• Due to fluid accumulation without traction/tear (e.g., tumors, inflammation)
• Not typical of diabetes

• No retinal detachment:

• Incorrect, as TRD is a well-known late complication
questions.learning: Tractional retinal detachment — In advanced diabetic retinopathy (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR), the most common complication is tractional retinal detachment (TRD). • Chronic retinal ischemia → VEGF release • Formation of neovascularization (on…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acid classifications are correctly matched? 1. Uncharged amino acid – Cysteine 2. Nonpolar amino acid – Proline 3. Basic amino acid – Histidine 4. Basic amino acid – Lysine Choose the correct combination:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

Amino acids are classified based on the chemical properties of their side chains (R groups) into nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic, and basic amino acids. Correct classification is fundamental for understanding protein structure and function.

Correct matches:

• 1. Cysteine → Polar uncharged amino acid ✓
• 2. Proline → Nonpolar amino acid ✓
• 3. Histidine → Basic amino acid ✓ (weakly basic; partially protonated at physiological pH)
• 4. Lysine → Basic amino acid ✓

Why are all correct?

• Cysteine contains a sulfhydryl (-SH) group, making it polar but uncharged and capable of forming disulfide bonds.
• Proline is a cyclic nonpolar amino acid that introduces bends in protein chains.
• Histidine contains an imidazole ring and is classified as a basic amino acid.
• Lysine has a positively charged ε-amino group and is a strongly basic amino acid.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4 Amino acids are classified based on the chemical properties of their side chains (R groups) into nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic, and basic amino acids.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of chest pain at rest for 6 hours and ECG suggestive of Myocardial Ischemia. Which among the following is used for diagnosis? LDH - Lactate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LDH1

Measurement of LDH1 is suggestive of MI as it is seen predominantly in the heart.

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)

* Normally, serum levels of LDH2 are greater than those of LDH1; but, in MI, LDH1 is more than LDH2. This is called flipping of the LDH ratio.

*

LDH: A tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H isoform (Heart) and M isoform (Muscle)

* LDH-1: Heart.

* LDH-2: Blood.

* LDH-3: Brain, kidney, lungs, spleen, pancreas.

* LDH-4: Liver and skeletal muscle.

* LDH-5: Liver and skeletal muscle.

* MI diagnosis: LDH no longer recommended.

The other cardiac biomarkers are:

Troponin T and Troponin I

* These are the proteins that mediate calcium-mediated contraction of the cardiac and skeletal muscles.

* They are highly specific for MI.

* Troponin I is more important than troponin T.

* Troponins will remain elevated longer than creatine kinase (CK), for up to 14 days.

* This makes troponins a superior marker for diagnosing MI in the recent past (late diagnosis).

* Reinfarction: It is now clear that cardiac troponin (cTn) increases rapidly, even if it is from an abnormal baseline in patients with reinfarction.

* If the cTn concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction, the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement

Creatine kinase (CK).

* It is less sensitive and specific than troponins.

* For initial diagnosis of acute MI, cTn is preferred over CK

Myoglobin

* It is the earliest enzyme to increase after MI.

* Myoglobin is a protein found in the skeletal and cardiac muscles, which binds oxygen.

* It is a very sensitive indicator of muscle injury.

* However, it is not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle.

* The rise in myoglobin can help to determine the size of infarction.
questions.learning: LDH1 Measurement of LDH1 is suggestive of MI as it is seen predominantly in the heart. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) * Normally, serum levels of LDH2 are greater than those of LDH1; but, in MI, LDH1 is more than LDH2.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man who has recently returned from India presents with abdominal cramps and multiple episodes of watery diarrhea after consuming street food. Based on this clinical scenario, which antidiarrheal drug would be most appropriate for treatment?
questions.explanation: The patient has acute watery diarrhea after consuming street food, which is typical of traveler’s diarrhea. In uncomplicated cases (no blood in stool, no high fever), the primary goal is symptomatic relief, and loperamide is commonly used. Loperamide is an opioid receptor agonist that acts on the intestinal wall to reduce gut motility, allowing increased absorption of water and electrolytes. This leads to reduced stool frequency and improved consistency, providing rapid relief. It is widely used in mild to moderate traveler’s diarrhea and is often the first-line symptomatic treatment in exam scenarios. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Octreotide → Used for severe secretory diarrhea (e.g., VIPoma), not routine cases (C) Rifaximin → Antibiotic; used in moderate cases, but not primary symptomatic drug (D) Bismuth subsalicylate → Mild effect; less effective than loperamide
questions.learning: The patient has acute watery diarrhea after consuming street food, which is typical of traveler’s diarrhea. In uncomplicated cases (no blood in stool, no high fever), the primary goal is symptomatic relief, and loperamide is commonly used.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a sagittal section of the brain, the green- highlighted area represents the paracentral lobule. Damage to this region would affect which neurological structures or functions?
questions.explanation: The paracentral lobule is located on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere and represents the continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri. According to the motor and sensory homunculus, this specific region is responsible for the motor and sensory functions of the lower limb (leg and foot) and the perineum (including bladder and bowel control). Therefore, a lesion in this area, such as a stroke involving the anterior cerebral artery, typically results in contralateral lower limb paralysis and sensory loss, often accompanied by urinary incontinence. The scapular region, neck, trunk, and shoulder (Options A and B) are represented more superiorly and laterally on the convexity of the brain. The face and neck (Option D) are represented even further laterally, near the lateral sulcus. Precise knowledge of this functional topography is essential for localizing strokes or tumors based on the patient's specific pattern of sensory and motor deficits
questions.learning: The paracentral lobule is located on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere and represents the continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old male was brought to the emergency room following a road traffic accident. On examination, his GCS was E2M2V3. He had no fractures and no hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure. Non-contrast CT was performed and was found to be normal. The likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury

The given clinical scenario of an RTA with no imaging abnormality along with a disproportionate clinical manifestation suggests diffuse axonal injury.

It is caused due to stretching of axons in subcortical white matter due to sudden deceleration injuries. It is usually associated with mild nonspecific changes in NCCT. It is visualized on T2 MRI characterized by multiple lesions showing microbleeds or linear hypointensities. It may also show disruption of white matter tracts on tractography.

Other options

Post-concussion syndrome usually follows mild traumatic brain injury. It does not have a severe clinical status as seen in this patient.

Extradural hemorrhage is produced usually results secondary to trauma to head. The bleeding is usually arterial and blood collects between outer dura and inner table of the skull. It can very well be visualized on CT.

A cerebral herniation is defined as a shift of cerebral tissue in an adjacent space. Intracranial brain herniation can be classified into 3 types - subfalcine, transtentorial and tonsillar. A distinct clinical picture can be produced as a result of compression of neurovascular structures by the herniating part. CT is the imaging modality of choice because it can be done rapidly.
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury — The given clinical scenario of an RTA with no imaging abnormality along with a disproportionate clinical manifestation suggests diffuse axonal injury.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: 11-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to right shoulder pain. The patient first noticed the pain 4 days ago after volleyball practice. She has been placing cold compresses over the shoulder and taking PCM with initial improvement, but the pain has awakened her from sleep the last 2 nights. Today she is unable to lift her right arm to brush her teeth. Four months ago, the patient was diagnosed with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the wrists, knees, and ankles. She is taking methotrexate, and her symptoms had been gradually improving after dose adjustments. Temperature is 38.5⁰C (101.3⁰F). The patient holds her right arm at her side, and she resists attempts to move the shoulder due to pain. The overlying skin is warm. Bilateral wrists, knees, and ankles are mildly oedematous. The shoulder joint is aspirated, and synovial fluid analysis reveals leukocyte count of 55,000 cells/mm3, with 80% polymorphonuclear cells and 20% lymphocytes. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
options: Add a biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Begin antibiotic therapy

• Children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) who develop acute monoarticular pain with fever and restricted joint movement should be evaluated for septic arthritis, especially if they are on immunosuppressive therapy (eg, methotrexate).
• Synovial fluid WBC >50,000/mm³ with neutrophil predominance (>75%) strongly suggests septic arthritis, even in patients with underlying inflammatory arthritis.
• Septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency due to rapid cartilage destruction and requires immediate empiric IV antibiotic therapy after joint aspiration and cultures.
• Immunosuppressive escalation (steroids, biologics, methotrexate increase) is contraindicated until infection is ruled out.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which one of the following drugs inhibits neutrophil recruitment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Colchicine

Colchicine inhibits neutrophil (granulocyte) recruitment.

Colchicine acts by preventing the polymerisation of microtubules by binding to tubulin. This reduces neutrophil recruitment to inflamed tissue and also decreases the secretion of chemotactic factors by activated neutrophils, thus reducing the inflammatory response overall.

Colchicine is used in gout and Mediterranean fever.
questions.learning: Colchicine Colchicine inhibits neutrophil (granulocyte) recruitment. Colchicine acts by preventing the polymerisation of microtubules by binding to tubulin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient underwent LASIK for myopia and now is undergoing cataract surgery. What is the formula used for lens power calculation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Haigis L

Among the given options, the Haigis-L regression formula is used for calculating the lens power in a patient who is undergoing cataract surgery with a previous history of refractive surgery.

Haigis formula uses Axial Length (L), Corneal curvature (K), and Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD) for the calculation of IOL power (biometry).

• Keratometry measures the curvature of the anterior corneal surface.
• A-scan ultrasonography is used to determine the axial length.

Standard IOL calculations are unsuitable in any type of corneal refractive surgery as they are likely to result in residual refractive errors even after IOL implantation in these patients. In these patients, several other methods of calculating corneal refractive power are used which are then added to the standard and specific formulas such as the Masket, modified masket, Haigis L formula, and double-K method.

Other options:

Options A and B: SRK 1 and SRK 2 are the basic formulas used for IOL power calculations.

SRK formula: P = A-2.5L-0.9K where P is the power of IOL, A is a constant for the lens, L is the axial length and K is corneal curvature.

Option C: Hoffer Q formula is used for IOL power calculation in short eyes (hypermetropia). It uses only two variables; Axial length (L) and corneal curvature (K).
questions.learning: Haigis L Among the given options, the Haigis-L regression formula is used for calculating the lens power in a patient who is undergoing cataract surgery with a previous history of refractive surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of tuberculosis presents with dysuria and sterile pyuria. The cystoscopy image of the patient is provided below. Based on the patient’s history and the cystoscopic findings, which of the following conditions is most likely associated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Golf hole ureter

The cystoscopic findings are suggestive of  a "golf hole ureter", which is most likely associated with genitourinary tuberculosis(TB).

Genitourinary TB is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is thus always a secondary TB. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB. It can affect the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, prostate, seminal vesicles, epididymis, and vas deferens.

Lesions caused by tuberculosis in the kidney include:

• Golf hole ureteric orifice - This is due to fibrosis causing the rigid withdrawn dilated ureteric orifice to look like a golf hole (cystoscopic finding).
• Papillary ulcer - earliest lesion
• Pyonephrosis - caused by multiple scattered papillary ulcers undergoing caseous necrosis, which later become filled with pus
• Perinephric abscess -  by extension of pyonephrosis or tuberculous renal abscess
• Pseudocalculi - occurs when calcium gets deposited in a papillary ulcer healed with fibrosis
• Ghost calyces - caused by the destruction of the calyces
• Thimble bladder -the entire urinary bladder gets fibrosed, stiff, and unable to dilate and accommodate urine (IV urogram finding).
• Putty/cement kidney - amorphous dystrophic calcification eventually involves the entire kidney (seen in X-ray and CT)

The following X-ray KUB shows a thimble bladder:

Ureteric lesions can also be seen in genitourinary tuberculosis. They include:

• Kerr’s kink - kinking of the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ)
• Ureteral stricture
• Beaded ureter
• Shortening of the ureter
• Golf hole ureter - Longitudinal fibrosis leads to the shortening of the ureter and pulling up the orifice as a gaping hole. Reimplantation of ureter is done.
questions.learning: Golf hole ureter — The cystoscopic findings are suggestive of a "golf hole ureter", which is most likely associated with genitourinary tuberculosis(TB).

questions.text: The recommended calorie intake for a pregnant woman in the second trimester, who is a sedentary worker would increase by _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 350 kcal/day

The recommended calorie intake for a pregnant woman who is a sedentary worker would increase by ~ 350 kcal/day.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Mention the purpose of the instrument shown below in the image:
options: To differentiate between chronic inversion and fibroid polyp
It is used to diagnose cervical stenosis
It is used in Fallopian tube recanalization
It is used to measure the uterine cavity and the cervical length
questions.explanation: The instrument shown in the image is a uterine sound. This is a graduated, flexible or rigid metal probe with a bulbous tip. Its primary clinical purpose is to measure the depth of the uterine cavity and the length of the cervical canal (Option D). This measurement is essential before procedures like IUD insertion, dilatation and curettage, or hysterosalpingography to ensure safety and proper device placement. Uterine sounding can also help determine the position (anteversion/retroversion) of the uterus. While it can be used to differentiate between a fibroid polyp and chronic inversion (Option A) by checking the depth of the fornix, its most common and fundamental use is measuring cavity length. It is not a primary tool for diagnosing stenosis (Option B) or recanalizing fallopian tubes (Option C). Therefore, measuring uterine depth is the definitive functional identification for this tool
questions.learning: The instrument shown in the image is a uterine sound. This is a graduated, flexible or rigid metal probe with a bulbous tip.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with cyclical pelvic pain every month. She has not achieved menarche yet. On examination, a suprapubic bulge can be seen in the lower abdomen. PR examination reveals a bulging swelling in the anterior aspect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transverse vaginal septum above the vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

The given case scenario is suggestive of cryptomenorrhea due to an imperforate hymen.

Cryptomenorrhea is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract. The menstrual fluid gets collected in the reproductive tract.

Imperforate hymen is a urogenital anomaly. Imperforate hymen results due to failure of canalization of the inferior end of the vaginal plate. This anomaly usually remains unrecognized until puberty. It can lead to mucocolpos in early infancy. Patients present with amenorrhea, cyclic abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a hypogastric lump on abdominal examination. A bluish bulging membrane at the vaginal opening is noted on genital examination and the Valsalva maneuver.

Ultrasound of the pelvis reveals normal internal genitalia and hematocolpos. Laparoscopy should be performed along with hymenectomy to exclude endometriosis.

Most common causes of cryptomenorrhea:

• Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen
• Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen

Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis. A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood and restores the reproductive capacity in most cases.

Other options:

Option A: Transverse vaginal septum occurs due to the failure of Müllerian duct fusion or failure of vaginal plate canalization. On examination, the vagina may appear shortened and the cervix may not be identifiable. Secondary sexual characteristics appear normal. The diagnosis can be confirmed with ultrasound or MRI.

Option B: Vaginal atresia is characterized by the absence of the lower portion of the vagina with well-differentiated superior structures like the uterus. On examination, the hymenal ring is normal, proximal to which only a vaginal dimple or small pouch is found.

Option D: Cervical agenesis is the congenital absence of the cervix typically with a normal uterus. These patients also lack the upper vagina in most cases. They present with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pelvic pain. If a functional endometrium is present, a patient may have a distended uterus, and endometriosis may develop. The absence of a cervix is seen on examination.
questions.learning: Imperforate hymen — The given case scenario is suggestive of cryptomenorrhea due to an imperforate hymen. Cryptomenorrhea is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A case involving the death of a married woman within three years of marriage is reported. Who is responsible for conducting the inquest in this case?
questions.explanation: In India, according to Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a Magisterial Inquest is mandatory in cases involving the death of a woman within seven years of her marriage under suspicious circumstances. Since this case involves a death within three years of marriage, it falls strictly under the purview of a Magistrate (Executive or Judicial) to investigate potential foul play, such as dowry death or homicide. A Police Inquest (Option B) is the standard procedure for most unnatural deaths, but it is superseded by the Magistrate in this specific legal context. "Judicial" (Option A) is a broad term; while a Judicial Magistrate can perform the inquest, the correct specific authority is the Magistrate. The Coroner system (Option C) does not exist in modern India, as its functions were replaced by the Magisterial system. Therefore, a Magistrate must conduct the inquiry to ensure a thorough and impartial legal investigation
questions.learning: In India, according to Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a Magisterial Inquest is mandatory in cases involving the death of a woman within seven years of her marriage under suspicious circumstances.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of Kaposi sarcoma?
options: A white, striated lesion that cannot be scraped off
questions.explanation: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignancy caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV/AIDS. The characteristic lesions typically begin as flat, reddish-purple macules and progress into raised, palpable plaques and nodules. This violaceous (purple-red) appearance is a pathognomonic sign resulting from the deposition of hemosiderin and extravasated red blood cells within the tumor. A yellow lesion with pus (Option A) indicates a bacterial infection like an abscess. A white, striated lesion (Option B) describes lichen planus or oral hairy leukoplakia. Small red erosions (Option D) are non-specific findings for various inflammatory skin conditions. Therefore, the raised purple-red morphology is the definitive clinical description for Kaposi sarcoma lesions
questions.learning: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignancy caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV/AIDS.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The following finding was found in an autopsy. Identity the weapon.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bullet

The given image shows a well-defined punched-out hole in the inner table of the skull. Hence, it could most probably be an entry wound produced by a bullet.

Entry wound: The initial contact of the missile punches a clean hole through the outer table of the skull. Where the bullet emerges internally, the inner table is then unsupported and a cone-shaped plug is detached, forming a crater that is appreciably larger than the external hole.

Bevelling: inner table
Punched out hole: outer table

Exit wound: If the bullet traverses the cranium and penetrates the opposite side, then the same pattern occurs, but this time with the small hole on the inner table and the crater on the outside.

Bevelling: outer table
Punched out hole: inner table

The sequence of bullet injuries is given by Puppe’s rule.

Puppe’s rule: It is possible to determine the sequence of injuries in skull fractures caused by blunt injuries to the head because the second fracture ends at the point where a break in cohesion is already present. The fracture lines created by every other shot extend only up to the fractured lines produced by the previous shot without continuing over them. Even though this rule is true for all blunt injuries to the skull, it is of particular importance in gunshot wounds.

Other options :

Option B: Hammer: When a hammer is used, the fracture is circular or in the shape of an arc of a circle. The diameter of the fracture is the same as the striking surface. There are generally no radiating linear fractures. A depressed fracture is caused by blows from a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. It is also called a signature fracture as the pattern of fracture resembles the weapon or object used.

The following is an image of a depressed fracture:

Option C: Iron Rod: An irregular missile such as an iron rod would produce several irregular lacerated wounds, and the exit wounds are larger than the entrance wounds.

The following is an image of the famous 3D model of Phineas Gage's skull, who survived a workplace injury of a tamping iron rod through his skull.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male came to the emergency department after sustaining a fall. X-Ray showed a fractured neck of the femur and was operated on for the same. On post-operative day 2, he experienced a sharp, severe, constant, burning pain over his right back. On examination, the lesion is as seen below. The area is tender to light touch with a rash over the area. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Valacyclovir

This patient had a traumatic accident. He then developed burning pain followed by a rash localized on the right back unilaterally suggestive of herpes zoster.Oral valacyclovir is the most appropriate treatment in the given options.

Herpes zoster is due to varicella-zoster virus from the dorsal root ganglia of a sensory nerve following initial infection with varicella(chickenpox) during childhood. The risk of VZV reactivation is greatest in those with advanced age due to waning cell-mediated immunity. Recent trauma also increases risk due to traumatic sensory nerve stimulation.

It manifests as dermatomal pain (burning, throbbing, stabbing, pruritic) that precedes the rash by days or weeks followed by a unilateral dermatomal rash that begins as erythematous papules, grouped vesicles, and crusts within 7-10 days. The characteristic feature is cut-off at the mid-line. Mucous membranes within the affected dermatome are also involved. The lymph nodes are tender and enlarged.

Treatment involves starting oral aciclovir 800mg five times a day for 7-10 days or valacyclovir 1g t.i.d for 7 days when the patient presents with < 72hrs of rash.

The commonest and most intractable sequel of zoster is post‐herpetic neuralgia, generally defined as persistence or recurrence of pain more than a month after the onset of zoster, but better considered after 3 months.

Other Options:

* Option A: Oral amitryptiline, a tricyclic antidepressant is used to treat postherpetic neuralgia. It is not used in the acute phase of herpes zoster.

* Option B: Pain control is required however, the topical corticosteroid can lead to an increased risk of secondary bacterial infections.

* Option C : Muprocin is used for bacterial infections.
questions.learning: Valacyclovir — This patient had a traumatic accident. He then developed burning pain followed by a rash localized on the right back unilaterally suggestive of herpes zoster.Oral valacyclovir is the most appropriate treatment in the given options.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Calculate the anion gap from the following values: Na+ = 137 mmol/L K+ = 4 mmol/L Cl- = 100 mmol/L HCO3- = 15 mmol/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 22 mmol/L

The anion gap is the difference between measured cations and measured anions and is estimated as:

Anion gap = [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])

Substituting the given values, AG is 22 mmol/L. Normal AG is 6 to 12 mmol/L with an average of 10 mmol/L.

The concentrations of anions and cations in plasma must be equal to maintain electrical neutrality. Therefore, there is no real “anion gap” in the plasma.

However, only certain cations and anions are routinely measured in the clinical laboratory. The cation normally measured is Na+, and the anions are usually Cl− and HCO3−. The value of plasma potassium is omitted from the calculation of the anion gap.

Usually, the unmeasured anions exceed the unmeasured cations.

The anion gap will increase if unmeasured anions rise or if unmeasured cations fall.

The unmeasured anions include albumin, phosphate, sulfate, and other organic anions. The unmeasured cations include calcium, magnesium, and potassium.
questions.learning: 22 mmol/L The anion gap is the difference between measured cations and measured anions and is estimated as: Anion gap = [Na+] – ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) Substituting the given values, AG is 22 mmol/L.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

A. Morphine used in pulmonary oedema
B. Pethidine used in biliary colic
C. Indomethacin is used in headache
D. Aspirin used in peptic ulcer disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A, B and C

Statements A, B and C are true.

A. Morphine used in pulmonary edema
B. Pethidine used in biliary colic
C. Indomethacin is used in headache

Aspirin can also cause damage to the stomach and intestinal lining leading to the development of erosions or ulcers. Erosions may cause further complications like bleeding and perforations.

Note: Unlike Morphine, Pethidine/Mepiridine can be used for pain management in biliary colic as it has no effect on the tone of sphincter of Oddi.
questions.learning: A, B and C Statements A, B and C are true. Morphine used in pulmonary edema B.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old chronic smoker presented with a bright red velvety plaque on the floor of the mouth. Which of the following statements is correct about the diagnosis and management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Erythroplakia and biopsy

The given clinical scenario of a chronic smoker presenting with a bright red velvety plaque on the floor of the mouth is suggestive of erythroplakia and the next best step is to do an excision biopsy of the lesion.

Erythroplakia is a pre-malignant oral lesion that presents as a bright red velvety patch or plaque commonly at the lower alveolar mucosa, gingivobuccal sulcus and the floor of the mouth. The red colour is due to decreased keratinization and as a result, the red vascular connective tissue of the submucosa shines through.  Grossly, the lesion may be of three varieties—homogenous, speckled or granular, and erythroplakia, interspersed with areas of leukoplakia. Malignant potential is 17 times higher than in leukoplakia, hence excision biopsy and follow-up are indicated in such cases.

Other options:
Option A, B, D:  Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity characterized by whitish patches or plaques that cannot be rubbed off. Management includes smoking cessation and reduction in alcohol consumption. A biopsy should be done and a photographic record of the lesion is used for follow-up. Both erythroplakia and leukoplakia have malignant potential. Hence, only observation will not be appropriate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following immunizations are recommended for persons infected with HIV? 1. Hepatitis B vaccine 2. Influenza virus vaccine 3. Pneumococcal vaccine Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

People living with HIV (PLHIV) are at increased risk of vaccine-preventable infections due to impaired immunity. Therefore, inactivated vaccines such as Hepatitis B, Influenza, and Pneumococcal vaccines are routinely recommended, while the use of live vaccines depends on the patient’s CD4 count and degree of immunosuppression.

Why is D correct?

• 1. Hepatitis B vaccine✅: Recommended for all susceptible HIV-infected individuals because of the increased risk of chronic HBV infection.
• 2. Influenza vaccine✅: Annual inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for all PLHIV.
• 3. Pneumococcal vaccine✅: Recommended to reduce the risk of invasive pneumococcal disease; includes PCV followed by PPSV23 as per guidelines.
